Hi! I am Ivan Yi-fan Hu (胡 一帆, b. August 27, 2003—sharing a birthday with G. W. F. Hegel).

I received my B.A. in Chinese Language and Literature (汉语言文学) from Tsinghua University (2021–2026), where my thesis (Machine and Assemblage: Deleuze-Guattari and Tensions within the "Material Turn"), supervised by Prof. Min'an Wang (汪 民安), examined the theoretical tensions between Deleuze-Guattari and the "Material Turn" (specifically engaging with Manuel DeLanda and Levi R. Bryant) and was awarded the School-level Excellent Thesis.

Currently, I am an M.A. candidate at Literary Theory and Criticism (文艺学) track, Department of Chinese Language and Literature (中国语言文学系), School of Humanities (人文学院), Tsinghua University (2026–2029) continuing under the supervision of Prof. Wang, and an incoming joint graduate program (IGP–B) M.A. candidate at Decision Science & Technology Course (社会理工学コース), Department of Social and Human Sciences (社会・人間科学系), School of Environment and Society (環境・社会理工学院), Institute of Science Tokyo (2027–2028) supervised by Prof. Takamitsu Yamamoto (山本 貴光).

はじめまして。イヴァン・イーファン・フー（胡一帆　こ・いっぱん）と申します。２００３年８月２７日生まれで、G. W. F. ヘーゲルと誕生日が同日です。

２０２１年～２０２６年に清華大学中国語文学科（漢語言文学）に在学し、学士号を取得しました。在学中は汪民安（おう・みんあん）教授の指導のもと、機械とアッサンブラージュ：ドゥルーズ-ガタリと「物質的転回」内の緊張、特にマニュエル・デランダとリーヴァイ·R·ブライアントの議論を取り上げて検討した卒業論文を執筆し、学院レベル優秀卒業論文賞を受賞しました。

現在は２０２６年～２０２９年の予定で、清華大学人文学院中国言語文学系文芸学（文学理論・批評）コースの修士課程に在籍しており、引き続き汪教授の指導を受け研究を進めています。また２０２７年～２０２８年には、東京科学大学環境・社会理工学院社会・人間科学系社会理工学コースの国際共同大学院プログラム（IGP-B）修士課程に入学予定で、山本貴光（やまもと・たかみつ）教授の指導を受ける予定です。

你好，我是胡一帆（英文名Ivan Yi-fan Hu），生于2003年8月27日，与哲学家 G. W. F. 黑格尔同日生日。

2021–2026年我就读于清华大学汉语言文学专业，获文学学士学位。本科毕业论文由汪民安教授指导，题为机器与装配：德勒兹-加塔利与“物转向”的张力。该文聚焦德勒兹-加塔利的理论同“物转向”思潮之间的理论张力，重点围绕曼纽尔·德兰达、列维·R·布莱恩特的相关论述展开分析，获评院级优秀毕业论文。

目前我为清华大学人文学院中国语言文学系文艺学硕士研究生（2026–2029），继续师从汪民安教授开展研究；同时已获东京科学大学录取，将于2027–2028年就读该校环境·社会理工学院社会·人间科学系社会理工学课程（决策科学与技术方向）的国际联合研究生院项目（IGP-B）硕士项目，导师为山本贵光教授。

My research fields encompass SF (Speculative Fiction), Critical Theory and HPHSS (History and Philosophy of Humanities and Social Sciences), DH (Digital Humanities) & CSS (Computational Social Sciences), HPST (History and Philosophy of Science and Technology, esp. Logic, Language, and Intelligence), STS (Science, Technology and Society), MTS (Media and Technology Studies), and HPMSR (History and Philosophy of Magic, Science, and Religion).

Grounded in these disciplines and with a particular emphasis on Play/Game Creation and Studies, esp. AI4PG (AI for Play/Game), my current inquiries focus on these areas: Critical Theory and Practice in the Age of Digintelligence; SF Literature and Art (esp. Video Games) as a Practice of Futurology; AI Consciousness and the Question of Spirit; and Christian Theology and Modern/Contemporary Thought.

私の研究領域は以下の通りです：思弁フィクション（SF, Speculative Fiction）、批判理論と人文社会科学の歴史と哲学（HPHSS, History and Philosophy of Humanities and Social Sciences）、デジタル·ヒューマニティーズ（DH, Digital Humanities）と計算社会科学（CSS, Computational Social Sciences）、科学技術の歴史と哲学（HPST, History and Philosophy of Science and Technology、特に論理·言語·知能を中心）、科学·技術·社会（STS, Science, Technology and Society）、メディア·技術研究（MTS, Media and Technology Studies）、巫術·科学·宗教の歴史と哲学（HPMSR, History and Philosophy of Magic, Science, and Religion）。

これらの学問的基盤のもと、現在はプレイ/ゲーム創作·硏究（特にAIを活用したプレイ/ゲーム制作、「AI4PG (AI for Play/Game)」）に主たる関心を置き、以下のテーマを中心に研究を進めています：デジタルインテリジェンス時代の批判理論と実践、未来学の実践としての思弁的フィクション文学·芸術（特にビデオゲーム）、AI 意識と精神の問題、キリスト教神学と現代思想。

我的研究领域涵盖：思辨虚构（SF, Speculative Fiction）、批判理论、人文与社会科学的历史与哲学（HPHSS, History and Philosophy of Humanities and Social Sciences）、数字人文（DH, Digital Humanities）与计算社会科学（CSS, Computational Social Sciences）、科学技术的历史与哲学（HPST, History and Philosophy of Science and Technology，尤其逻辑、语言与智能）、科学技术与社会（STS, Science, Technology and Society）、媒介与技术研究（MTS, Media and Technology Studies），以及巫术、科学与宗教的历史与哲学（HPMSR, History and Philosophy of Magic, Science, and Religion）。

立足上述学科背景，我当前的核心方向为玩/游戏创作与硏究（尤其聚焦人工智能赋能玩/游戏领域，「AI4PG (AI for Play/Game)」），重点探讨以下议题：数智时代的批判理论与实践；作为未来学实践的思辨文艺（尤其是电子游戏）；人工智能意识与精神问题；以及基督教神学与现当代思想。

Have You Had a Good Summer?良い夏を過ごしましたか？你的夏天还好吗？

2026.8.11–12

It started like this: the deepest, most grounding sleep I've had in six months surprisingly found me in this old Beijing dorm room, a place suffocating under its own heavily 1980s aura. Which exact year the building was constructed no longer has any real archaeological value (though out of curiosity I did look it up: rumor has it this place was a central hub for mainland Chinese campus folk music in the 1980s and 90s; whether the singing ever truly died out is hard to say, but the dorm itself remains impeccably preserved in its original state). The peeling wall paint, the furniture, the window frames, the air conditioner, and the smell of the corridor collectively forge a profoundly stubborn historical continuity. The AC, in particular—when you turn it on, it wheezes a few times before it starts violently clanking and vibrating, barely spitting out a breath of cool air, behaving like a temp worker well past retirement age with zero passion left for his labor. I am much the same. Having finally secured my degree after a delayed graduation, I should, by all logic, have shed my student identity. Instead, I am staying right here at the same university to keep studying. How many years that will take—two, three, or even longer—is impossible to say. The situation has become rather absurd: I haven't truly left, nor have I truly started over; I've simply morphed from a student into someone who graduated once but is somehow still stuck here. If this drags on, this campus might very well become the physical location where I've spent the longest chunk of my life, yet right now, I can't even predict which year will be my last. Staying the longest doesn't mean liking it the most; it merely proves that some things are far better at procrastinating than planning, and I just happen to be the one dragged along.

During the day, I can still perform the choreography of a structured life—reading, writing, replying to messages, hitting the cafeteria or ordering takeout, doing laundry, taking a shower—maintaining the superficial order expected of a normal young adult. But after midnight, that order begins to loosen. An unchaired, agenda-less meeting with no closing time convenes in my head with absolute punctuality: What exactly did I do today? What am I doing tomorrow? What happens after I get this degree? What's next? And after that? Where will the money come from? Where do I find a job? Which city will I live in? What about my parents? Do I actually have the capability to walk this path all the way to the end? Money, degrees, jobs, cities, parents, the future—these are inescapable, brute facts. None of them need to be elevated to the status of a "philosophical question" to warrant anxiety; they are the material bedrock of philosophical questions. After thinking all night to no avail, at 3 AM I have no choice but to climb out of bed and whip up a bucket of Cup Noodles. I drop two blocks of fermented bean curd into the bowl, as is my ritual. The salt, grease, and fermented stench rush up together, and my attention finally descends from unsolvable life crises back to the surface of the soup—at least, in this exact moment, the next confirmed step is to finish the food (though the black-packaged Red Tonkotsu broth always tastes a bit off). Meanwhile, others are likely living out their own summers: some doing fieldwork, some interning at corporations, some meeting with advisors or bosses. Some have already begun processing their summer vacation into a resume—projects, conferences, surveys, volunteer work, neatly stacked line by line—so that when the fall semester begins, they can proudly declare they weren't idle, channeling that classic line: "Sweet highs, crisp mids, deep lows—in a word, total transparency." I have no grounds to criticize this. People have to make a living, and making a living has never been a shameful thing. It's just that I personally don't have that much raw material to process, so I simply stare at the blank document on my computer, watching the cursor flash patiently. It's quite fair, really. It never asks about my career plans, nor does it inquire about the status of my applications; it just sits there blinking, reminding me that the page is still blank.

I eventually fell asleep, but the dream shipped me straight back to my hometown. In the dream, I was still a teenager studying in the city, only returning for the holidays, jolting along in a three-wheeler across the muddy roads of the Yellow River floodplains—jolting so hard it numbed the bones—clutching a stack of unfinished exam papers. The relative sitting next to me had already aged into the man he is today (upon waking, I realized no such specific relative actually exists, yet he felt vividly real in the dream). The smell of his cheap tobacco was the same; his way of speaking was the same. He was still tirelessly urging me toward a stable future: best to get into the system, best to secure a respectable identity, best to become an official. I don't know why the dream had to specify becoming a "county magistrate," but that was the gist of it: read all the books you want, but eventually, you have to land somewhere that gives the family face. In the dream, I didn't even argue. Instead, I listened intently, as if I were waiting for this man to grade my paper, to tell me whether all these years of testing, advancing, leaving, and leaving again had been a mistake. Outside the window, it was raining endlessly. The apple orchards were soaked in standing water, the muddy water in the ditches blending seamlessly into the fields, the tires endlessly skidding. After waking up, I thought about it for a long time. What was truly unsettling wasn't the relative himself, but the fact that, even now, I take these questions so seriously in my dreams. It turns out you can leave a place, but you might never graduate from its metric of judgment. What a hometown truly leaves you with isn't just poverty or an insular society of acquaintances; it's an entire, ingrained system of risk calculation: Is the job stable? Is the money enough? What if you fail? What if you go out and can't come back? What happens when your parents get old? If all plans go to hell, do you even have a place to retreat to? These things do not automatically vanish just because your train pulled out of the county station. You change cities, they are still there; you change degrees, they are still there. Even when you start discussing overseas PhDs and the "academic job market," they just squat there in the background, reminding you to first factor in rent, income, and your exit strategy.

But I rarely go back now—two or three days during the holidays, sometimes arriving and leaving on the exact same day. Calling it a "return to the hometown" feels exaggerated; it's more like a short-term visiting scholar gig. I recognize what many streets used to look like, but I have no idea why they look the way they do now. Whose child has grown up, whose shop has closed, where someone's elderly parents have moved—I have to ask my relatives to re-map it all for me. When I was a kid, I thought that place was the whole world. I went out and realized it was just a tiny sliver of the world. Now, returning, I realize I need to get to know even this tiny sliver all over again. Yet, during the New Year, there are always these very strange afternoons. The village elders finish lunch and sit in the courtyard. The winter sun is weak. On the table, there is tea, sunflower seeds, and cigarettes. Someone hands me a smoke, and I take it. The chat usually starts with whether it's cold this year, how the harvest was, or whose kid has found a job. But somehow, as they talk, the conversation inevitably loops around to domestic politics. Because I usually use a VPN to watch YouTube, I'm exposed to plenty of gossip about national politics and officialdom. I don't treat it as serious research; mostly, it's sheer morbid curiosity—seeing what bizarre thing happened where, who made the news recently, how some official fell from grace, or what absurd story leaked from a certain department. It's a bit like a sexually repressed man watching porn: you don't necessarily believe it, nor do you genuinely care about the truth, you just watch it for the spectacle. But when I return home for the Spring Festival, this content I consume for mere entertainment suddenly finds a new utility. These old men aren't going to jump the firewall to watch YouTube themselves, so they listen to my secondhand political gossip. I tell a story, and they start guessing: Is this guy going to get purged? Is that place doomed? Why did this leader do that? What on earth is that country up to? The information isn't reliable, of course—barely three out of ten stories could pass a fact-check—but the old men listen with a mix of fear and fascination, and I get more excited the more I talk. The smoke gathers above our heads, and when I hit the climax of a story, my hands start gesturing wildly (they say Italy and China are remarkably alike, and perhaps that's true). It feels less like I'm telling internet rumors to a few village elders in a courtyard, and more like I'm delivering a lecture to students in a dilapidated classroom. I reach a particularly absurd detail, everyone laughs, and I press on. After finishing the final segment, I flick my cigarette butt—burned down to the filter—into the dry winter mud beside the yard. The gesture actually carries the flair of a university professor tossing a piece of chalk back into the tray after finishing a lecture. In that fleeting moment, a bizarre sense of shared glory emerges. It feels as if some version of the 1980s—an era I never actually lived through—has been briefly resurrected on that table. Ordinary people, having finished their meal, can sit around and earnestly discuss the affairs of state, worry about a distant war, critique an official who doesn't even know they exist, and speculate on the next decade. It's as if the world, though vastly beyond any individual's control, still has enough room for everyone to sit down and offer a few opinions. "It's my duty!" It turns out that over all these years, I've simply grown accustomed to wrapping these matters in academic jargon. The form of knowledge has become more complex, but it doesn't mean a person is any closer to the truth of the world. Sometimes I even feel that an old man's crude remark is far more honest than my so-called theoretical analysis. And precisely because of this, I've become increasingly reluctant to write off my hometown simply as a low-lying swamp that must be escaped. Of course it is a place I want to leave—for many years, my strongest desire was simply to get as far away from it as possible—but on those absurd afternoons, it also gave me a genuine sense of participation. At that dinner table, it allowed me to temporarily feel that I was fundamentally no different from these people; at the very least, we all felt we had the right to say a few words about the world.

My trip to Dazexiang early this year passed with this exact, somewhat suspect sense of participation. The event itself carried zero historical nostalgia. During the Spring Festival, my relative brought along a friend who supposedly had some clout in the local public security system, and a whole group of us went to take a look. Today, it's a standard tourist trap. The wild grass grows well, the tourists are highly cooperative, and the ground is strewn with the bamboo skewers of starch-sausages, crushed water bottles, and assorted wrappers. A speaker in the distance blasts overly loud DJ tracks, and right next to it stands a brightly colored propaganda board touting construction and development. The late Qin peasant uprising and modern cultural tourism coexist here in perfect harmony. Standing to the side, my relative enthusiastically explained that if I could get into the system, getting things done for the family would be much easier, and everyone could bask a bit in my reflected glory. I nodded, of course, but in my head, I remembered that the first great act of the famous young men who made this place historical wasn't building a "Beautiful Dazexiang," but slaughtering the county magistrate. Naturally, I couldn't say that out loud. If I did, a normal Spring Festival outing would instantly devolve into a Confucian-Legalist debate, and likely ruin everyone's appetite. History has indeed progressed to this day. When the ancients were driven to a dead end, they raised their banners in armed rebellion; when modern youth are driven to a dead end, they open a registration website, upload their documents, revise their CVs, prepare for an interview, and draft a three-to-five-year career plan to prove to themselves that there is still a way forward. The ancients took up swords; moderns take up Excel. Let's put aside how much more "civilized" the tools are—at the very least, there are far more spreadsheets. If I actually went in the direction my relative hopes for, I probably wouldn't instantly turn into some cartoon villain. Ordinary people usually lack that much dramatic flair. Most of the time, they just slowly learn highly "normal" things: what to say to whom at the dinner table, when to offer a toast, when to shut up, how to reframe personal interest as the collective good, how to package dissatisfaction as "constructive feedback," and how to tell yourself there's no point making a fuss even when you know something is deeply wrong. You cede five cities today, ten cities tomorrow. One small step forward, one giant leap for civilization. You look back a few years later, and usually, no major, recordable event has taken place. It's just that the things you once found unacceptable have become reality; the things you once found shameful have become your job; and the person you never wanted to be can now naturally explain why they had no choice but to be exactly this way. A person doesn't seem to need a definitive moment of corruption—most of the time, all it takes is a few dozen un-audited micro-decisions.

Summer is almost over, and my peers are gradually taking their places. Some have entered the system, some are continuing to take exams, some have started working, some are taking a gap year to apply, and some are cultivating a different, exceptionally strict hierarchy in Honor of Kings ranked matches. Nowadays, very few people flee into the mountains overnight because they were wronged. Modern escapes require paperwork: you must give notice before quitting, apply for a visa before going abroad, prepare a writing sample for a PhD application, and calculate rent and deposits before leaving a city. Even failure now demands a standard format—best packaged as an explainable gap in your professional history rather than an unprofitable flight. Yet I am still left here at this university, and whether the next chapter will be two years, three years, or longer, I still do not know. When you stay in a place this long, the classrooms, the dorms, the cafeterias, the library, the roads by the school gates, the people you knew and subsequently lost touch with—they all begin to form a secret geography known only to you. It is no longer just a school, nor is it the campus folk songs of the 80s and 90s or the youthful melo-artistic angst of the 2010s; it feels more like a stage that was never properly dismantled after the song-and-dance performance ended. Just like the dorm I am currently in: when I moved in a month ago, I was told it would be renovated a year later, at which point I'd have to pack up and move somewhere else. Counting down the arrival of the deadline on my fingers, I've gradually come to feel that this entire year's stay has, oddly enough, gained an even richer flavor because of it. A victory for negativity; a victory for dialectics.

And so, ultimately, I return to the dorm. The instant noodles I cooked at 3 AM are gone, but the smell of fermented bean curd still lingers by the desk. The document on the screen remains largely blank. After all that tossing and turning, I finally fell asleep, waking up well past noon as the sun slanted through the gap in the curtains. I washed my face, felt a craving for a cigarette, and wanted to wander out for a smoke or two, so I went downstairs to buy a pack. The cigarette shop is south of campus, and to get there you have to cut through a shantytown-like family quarter—rumor has it that Chen Yinke also once lived here back when it was an old courtyard compound. Now it's just a few rows of old buildings, narrow alleys, underwear and trousers hanging off airborne power cables, and junk piled against the walls. Passing through a little-known side gate brings you to a residential complex where many of today's professors and university leaders supposedly live, its name carrying a rather distinct air of old Manchu nobility. Finishing this fixed smoke-buying route and heading back, I found the mud from last night's rain hadn't completely dried. My soles stepped into the muck, pulled out, walked a few paces, and sank in again. The mud wasn't actually deep, but every time I pulled my foot up, the edges of my shoes took some of the wet earth with it. The sun had shifted a bit. There was hardly anyone in the family quarter, save for an occasional bicycle gliding past with a gentle clinking of its bell. I tore open the cigarette pack, lighting one after another, smoking until I was almost at the entrance of my dorm building before looking down and realizing the soles of my shoes were an absolute mess. So I squatted on the edge of the curb, using a wooden stick to meticulously scrape the mud out of the grooves. Suddenly, it occurred to me that for all these years, my actions have amounted to little more than this: yanking my feet out of the exact same mud pit, over and over, then looking down, and wondering if I can still keep walking.

Ivan Yi-fan Hu
2026.8.11–12
Graduate Dormitory, Tsinghua University, Beijing

事の始まりはこうだった。この半年でいちばん安心して眠れた一夜を、よりによって北京の、八〇年代の気配が濃厚すぎるこの古い寮で過ごすことになった。何年に建てられた棟なのか、いまさら考証する価値もない（とはいえ気になって調べてみると、ここはかつて八〇〜九〇年代の中国大陸におけるキャンパス・フォークの中心地だったらしい。歌声が絶えたかどうかはともかく、寮が当時の姿を保っていることだけは確かだ）。壁の塗装、家具、窓枠、エアコン、廊下の匂いが一体となって、じつに頑強な歴史的連続性をかたちづくっている。とりわけエアコンは、動きだす前に何度か息を切らし、それからガタガタと震えて、やっとのことで少しだけ冷風を吐く。定年を迎えたのに臨時の穴埋めで働きつづけている老労働者のようで、自分の労働にかける情熱などかけらもない。私も似たようなものだ。卒業を延期した末にようやく学位を取り、本来なら学生という身分から離れてよいはずなのに、そのまま同じ大学で学びつづけることになった。しかも何年かかるかは、いまのところわからない。二年か、三年か、それ以上か、どれもありうる。そこで事態はずいぶん不条理なものになってきた。ほんとうに出ていったわけでも、ほんとうにやり直したわけでもなく、ただの学生から、一度卒業したあともここに居つづける人間になっただけなのだ。このままずるずると続けば、この大学はこれまでの人生で最も長く過ごした場所になるかもしれない。だが、その最後の一年がいつなのかさえ、いまは予言できない。最も長くいたからといって、最も好きだったことにはならない。ある種の物事は計画よりも引き延ばしに長けていて、私はたまたま、それに引きずられる側だったというだけのことだ。

昼のあいだは、まだ物事を秩序立って進めているように見せられる。本を読み、ものを書き、メッセージを返す。学食か出前、洗濯かシャワー。普通の若者らしい表面上の秩序くらいは、なんとか保てる。ところが真夜中を過ぎると、その秩序がゆるみはじめる。頭のなかでは、議題も司会者も閉会時刻もない会議が、時間どおりに開かれる。今日は結局何をしたのか、明日は何をするのか、学位を取ったらどうするのか、その次は、そのもっと先は。金はどこから来る、仕事はどこで見つける、どの街で暮らす、親はこの先どうする。そもそも自分には、この道を最後まで歩けるだけの力があるのか。金、学歴、仕事、街、親、未来。それらはもともと避けようのない事実の集まりであって、哲学的問題に格上げされてはじめて不安に値するようなものではない。それらこそが、哲学的問題の物質的な土台なのだ。一晩考えても答えは出ず、午前三時、仕方なくベッドを出てカップヌードルを一つ作る。いつものように腐乳を二かけ入れると、塩と油と発酵した匂いがいっぺんに立ちのぼり、注意はようやく解決不能な人生の問題からスープの表面へと戻ってくる。少なくともこの瞬間、次にすることは食べ終えることだと決まっている（黒いパッケージの赤豚骨濃湯味は、どうも妙な味がする）。そのころ、ほかの人たちはそれぞれの夏休みを過ごしているのだろう。社会実践に出かける人、企業でインターンをする人、指導教員に会う人、上司に会う人。もう休みを履歴書へと加工しはじめている人もいる。プロジェクト、会議、調査、ボランティアを一つずつきれいに並べ、秋の新学期には、何もせずにいたわけではないと言えるようにする。「高音は甘く、中音は正確、低音は深い。ひと言で言えば、すべてが透き通っている」。もちろん、非難する筋合いはない。人は生計を立てなければならないし、生計を立てることは一度だって恥ずかしいことではない。ただ、私にはいまのところ、加工できる材料がそれほどない。だからパソコンの空白の文書を見つめ、ひたすら辛抱強く点滅するカーソルを眺めている。これはじつに公平だ。キャリアの計画があるのかとも、出願がどこまで進んだのかとも聞かない。ただそこにいて、紙はまだ空白だと知らせてくる。

やがて眠りに落ちたが、夢は私を故郷へ送り返した。夢のなかの私はまだ十代で、街の学校に通い、休みにしか帰省しない。黄河の氾濫原のぬかるんだ道を、骨までしびれるほど揺れる三輪車に乗って走り、解き終わっていない問題用紙を抱えている。隣にいる親戚は、もう現在と同じように年を取っていた（目が覚めてから、じつはそんな親戚は存在しないと気づいたが、夢のなかでははっきり記憶があった）。煙草の匂いも、話し方も変わらない。相変わらず根気よく、安定した将来を目指せと説く。できれば公的な組織に入り、できれば世間体のよい身分を得て、できれば役人になれ。なぜ夢がわざわざ県長にまで話を具体化したのかはわからないが、要するにそういうことだ。本を読むのは結構だが、最後は家族が人に話して面目を保てるような場所に落ち着かなければならない。夢のなかで私は反論するどころか、真剣に聞いていた。この人が答案を採点してくれるのを、ここまで何年も試験を受け、進学し、出ていき、また出ていったことが間違いだったかどうかを教えてくれるのを、まだ待っているかのようだった。窓の外では雨が降りつづき、りんご畑は水に浸かり、溝の泥水と田畑がひと続きになって、車輪は何度も滑る。目が覚めてから、長いこと考えた。ほんとうに不安にさせられたのは、その親戚ではない。いまでも夢のなかで、こういう問いを真剣に受け止めてしまう自分だった。人はある場所を離れられても、その場所から与えられた判断の仕方からは卒業できないことがある。故郷が人に残すものは、貧しさや顔見知りばかりの社会だけとは限らない。それ以上に、リスクについての一揃いの計算を残す。仕事は安定しているか、金は足りるか、失敗したらどうするか、出ていって戻れなくなったらどうするか、親が年老いたらどうするか、すべての計画がうまくいかなかったとき、自分には帰れる場所があるのか。そうしたものは、列車が県の駅を離れたからといって自動的に消えはしない。街を変えても残り、学歴を変えても残る。海外の博士課程や academic job market について話しはじめても、なお底のほうにうずくまり、まず家賃と収入と退路を考えろと念を押してくる。

とはいえ、いまではほとんど帰省しない。祝日に二、三日、時には来たその日に帰る。故郷へ帰ると言うのさえ大げさで、短期訪問に近い。昔の姿なら覚えている通りも、どうしていまの姿になったのかはわからない。どこの子が大きくなり、どこの店が閉まり、どこの家のお年寄りがどこへ引っ越したのか、そのたび親戚に聞き直さなければならない。子どものころは、そこが世界のすべてだと思っていた。外に出てから、世界のほんの小さな一角なのだと知った。いま帰ってみると、その小さな一角さえ、もう一度知り直さなければならなくなっている。それでも旧正月には、いつも妙な午後がある。村のお年寄りたちが食後に庭へ出て座っている。冬の日差しは弱く、卓上には茶とひまわりの種と煙草がある。一本差し出されれば、私も受け取って吸う。話はもともと、今年は寒いか、畑の収穫はどうか、どこの子に仕事が見つかったか、といったことなのに、いつのまにか国内政治へと回り込んでいく。普段、私はファイアウォールを越えて YouTube を見ているので、国内政治や官界の噂話をそれなりに耳にする。別に真面目な研究として見ているわけではない。たいていはただの物珍しさだ。どこからまた妙な話が出たのか、誰が最近ニュースになったのか、どの役人がどんな目に遭ったのか、どの部署で何があったのか。少し、性的に抑圧された人がポルノを見るようなところがある。信じているとも限らず、真相に関心があるわけでもなく、もっぱら面白半分に見ている。ところが春節に帰省すると、自分の暇つぶしだったものに、突然新しい使い道が生まれる。お年寄りたちは自分でファイアウォールを越えて YouTube を見ないから、私の口から又聞きの政界ニュースを聞くのだ。一つ話すと、そのたびみんなで推測する。この人は失脚するんじゃないか、あの土地は遅かれ早かれ駄目になるんじゃないか、あの指導者はなぜあんなことをするのか、あの国はいったい何をやっているんだ。情報はもちろん、あまり当てにならない。十件のうち、検証に耐えるものは三件もないかもしれない。それでもお年寄りたちは怖がりながら夢中で聞き、私も話せば話すほど興奮してくる。煙がゆっくりと頭上にたまり、話に熱が入ると手まで動きはじめる（イタリアと中国はよく似ているというが、本当なのかもしれない）。村のお年寄り数人にネットで読んだ雑談を聞かせているというより、とても粗末な講堂で学生に授業をしているような気分になる。途方もないくだりに来るとみんなが笑い、私はさらに話しつづける。最後のひとくだりを話し終え、フィルターまで燃えた吸い殻を庭の脇の冬枯れの土へ放る。その仕草には、一コマの講義を終えた大学教授がチョークを黒板受けに放り返すような風情さえある。その一瞬、妙な誇らしさが湧いてくる。自分が実際には経験したことのない八〇年代の何かが、卓上でひととき蘇ったようなのだ。普通の人も食後には大真面目に国家の大事を論じ、遠くの戦争を心配し、自分たちの存在すら知らない官僚を批評し、次の十年がどうなるかを予想できる。天下は個人の手に負えないほど大きくても、誰もが腰を下ろしてひと言ふた言、意見を述べる余地はまだあるかのように。「It's my duty!」結局この何年かで、私はこうした事柄をさまざまな専門用語で包むことに慣れただけなのだ。形式が複雑になっても、それだけで人が世界に近づくとは限らない。お年寄りの粗っぽいひと言のほうが、自分のいわゆる理論的分析よりもずっと正直だと感じることさえある。だからこそ、その後ますます、故郷をただ抜け出すべき低地として書きたくなくなった。もちろん、そこは私が離れたい場所であり、長いあいだ私の最も強い願いは、少しでも遠くへ行くことだった。それでも、ときにあの不条理な午後は、確かな参加の感覚をくれた。一つの食卓を囲みながら、私もこの人たちと根本的には変わらないと、しばし思わせてくれた。少なくとも、自分にはこの世界についてひと言ふた言、語る資格があると、誰もが思っていた。

今年の初めに大沢郷へ行ったのも、そういう、いくぶん怪しげな参加の感覚を伴ってのことだった。訪問そのものに懐古の意図はまったくない。春節のあいだ、親戚が、地元の公安組織でかなり顔が利くという友人を連れ、一行で見に行っただけだ。いまやそこは標準的な観光地で、雑草の生え具合もよく、観光客たちもよく調和していた。地面にはでんぷんソーセージの竹串、踏みつぶされたミネラルウォーターの瓶、さまざまな包装が散り、遠くのスピーカーからは大音量の DJ 音楽が流れ、傍らには色鮮やかな開発宣伝の看板が立っている。秦末の蜂起と現代の文化観光事業が、ここでは平和に共存していた。親戚は横で興奮気味に、将来お前が体制のなかに入れたら、家の用事もずいぶん通しやすくなるし、みんなも恩恵にあずかれる、と話す。私はもちろんうなずいたが、内心では、この土地の歴史で最も有名な若者たちが最初にやった大仕事は、「美しい大沢郷」を建設することではなく、県令を殺すことではなかったか、と思い出していた。もちろん、そんなことは言えない。口にした途端、普通の春節旅行が儒家と法家の闘争になり、最後には誰も気分よく食事ができなくなるだろう。歴史が今日まで進んできて、確かに進歩したこともある。昔の人は行き詰まると竿を掲げて蜂起できたが、現代の若者は行き詰まると応募サイトを開き、書類をアップロードし、CV を直し、面接を準備し、さらに三年から五年の計画を立てて、まだ進む道はあるのだと自分に証明する。昔の人は刀を持ち、現代の人は Excel を持つ。道具がどれほど文明的になったかはひとまず措くとして、少なくとも表の数はずいぶん増えた。本当に親戚の期待する方向へ進んだからといって、私もたちまち悪役になるわけではないだろう。普通の人には、たいていそれほどの演劇的才能はない。多くの場合、ひどく当たり前のことを少しずつ覚えるだけだ。宴席で相手に合わせて何を話すか、いつ乾杯を差し出すか、いつ黙るか、自分の利益を集団の利益として語り、不満を建設的な意見として語るにはどうするか。何かがおかしいとわかっていても、気にするほどのことではないと自分に言い聞かせる。今日は五城を割譲し、明日は十城を割譲する。前へ小さな一歩、文明には大きな一歩。何年かして振り返っても、記録に値する重大事件はたいてい何も起きていない。ただ、かつて受け入れがたかったものが現実となり、恥ずかしいと思っていたことが仕事となり、なりたくなかった人間が、そうするしかなかった理由を自然に説明できるようになっている。人には、はっきりした堕落の瞬間など必要ないのかもしれない。多くの場合、真面目に帳簿につけられなかった数十の小さな決断さえあれば、それで足りる。

夏が終わろうとしている。同世代の人たちも、少しずつそれぞれの持ち場へ戻っていく。体制のなかに入った人、試験を受けつづける人、働きはじめた人、出願のためにギャップ期間を取る人。そして『王者栄耀』のランク戦で、別の序列を経営する人もいる。いまでは、何か理不尽な目に遭ったからといって、一夜のうちに山へ逃れる人はほとんどいない。現代人の逃亡には手続きがある。退職は事前に通知し、出国にはビザを取り、博士課程への出願には writing sample が要る。街を離れる前には、家賃と敷金を計算しなければならない。失敗さえ、標準書式を持ちはじめた。何の収穫もない逃亡として書くより、説明可能な職歴として書くほうがよい。私はといえば、まだこの大学にいる。この先が二年なのか三年なのかも、依然としてわからない。ここで長く過ごしすぎたせいで、教室、寮、食堂、図書館、校門の前の道、知り合ってから連絡を取らなくなった人たちが、自分にしかわからない地理をかたちづくりはじめている。もはや単なる大学ではない。八〇〜九〇年代のキャンパス・フォークでも、二〇一〇年代の青春の痛みを描く文芸でもなく、歌と踊りの公演が終わったあと、撤去されずに残った舞台に近い。いまいるこの寮もそうだ。一か月前に越してきたとき、一年後には改修されるので、そのときはまた別の場所へ移らなければならないと告げられた。指を折って終わりの日の到来を数えるうち、かえってこの一年の寮暮らしに、ますます味わいが出てきたように思えてくる。否定性の勝利。弁証法の勝利。

だから最後には、やはり寮へ戻る。午前三時にベッドを出て作ったカップ麺はもう食べ終え、腐乳の匂いだけが机の辺りに残り、画面の文書には相変わらず大きな空白がある。ひとしきりもがいた末にようやく眠り、昼を過ぎて目を覚ますと、カーテンの隙間から日差しが斜めに差し込んでいた。顔を洗うと煙草が欲しくなり、一本か二本、散歩がてら吸いたくなったので、下へ買いに出た。煙草屋は大学の南側にあり、そこへ行くにはバラック街のような教職員家族用の住宅地区を通り抜ける。ここが共同住宅だったのか、大きな邸宅だったのか、そんなころに陳寅恪も住んでいたという。いまは古い建物が数列並び、狭い道が通り、空中を渡る電線には長袖や半ズボンが掛かり、壁際には雑物が積まれている。あまり知られていない小さな門を抜けると、いまの教授や幹部が大勢住んでいるという住宅地に出る。その名前にも、どこか満洲の古老めいた趣がある。いつもの煙草買いの道をたどって戻ると、昨夜の雨がまだ残り、道端の泥が乾ききっていなかった。靴底を一度踏み入れ、引き抜き、数歩進むとまた沈む。泥はさほど深くない。ただ足を引き抜くたび、靴の縁に湿った土が少しずつついてくる。日はもう少し傾いていた。住宅地区に人影は少なく、ときおり自転車が鈴を鳴らしながら脇をすり抜ける。私は煙草の箱を開け、一本また一本と火をつけ、寮の建物のすぐ近くまで吸いながら来て、ようやく足元を見た。靴底は泥まみれだった。そこで縁石の脇にしゃがみ、木の棒で溝の土くずを少しずつかき出していると、ふと、この何年か自分がやってきたことも、結局こんなものだったのだと思えた。何度も何度も同じぬかるみから足を引き抜き、それから地面にこすりつけてみる。まだ歩きつづけられるだろうか、と。

胡一帆
2026.8.11–12
大学院生寮、清華大学、北京

事情刚开始是这样的，半年以来睡得最踏实的一觉，居然是在北京这间八十年代气质过于浓厚的旧宿舍里睡出来的。楼栋究竟建于哪一年其实已经没有考据价值（出于好奇还是查证了一番，据说此地曾为上世纪八九十年代中国大陆校园民歌之中心聚落，弦歌辍没辍不好说，宿舍则确为原风原貌），墙皮、家具、窗框、空调和楼道的气味共同构成了一种十分顽强的历史连续性，空调尤其如此，启动先喘几下，接着哐啷哐啷地震动，好不容易吹出一点凉风，像一个已经到了退休年龄却还在临时顶班的老工人，对自己的劳动毫无热情。我也差不多。延毕以后终于拿到学位，按道理已经应该离开学生身份，结果还要继续留在原来的学校读下去，而且究竟会读几年现在也说不好，两年、三年，甚至更久，都不是没有可能。于是事情变得颇有些荒诞，我既没有真正离开，也没有真正重新开始，只是从一个学生变成了一个毕业过一次、接下来还要继续待在这里的人。倘若事情一直这样拖下去，这个学校甚至很可能成为我人生中至今待的时间最长的地方，只是现在连最后一年究竟是哪一年都还没有办法预言。待得最久并不代表最喜欢，只是说明有些事物比计划更擅长延宕，而我恰好又是那个被拖着走的人而已。

白天尚且能够把事情做得像有章法，读书，写东西，回消息，食堂或外卖，洗衣或洗澡，总还能维持住一个正常青年应有的表面秩序。到了午夜以后，秩序便开始松动，脑子里准时召开一个没有议程、没有主持人、也没有闭幕时间的会议，今天到底做了什么，明天到底干什么，学位拿到了以后怎么办，接下来怎么办，再往后怎么办，钱从哪里来，工作往哪里找，究竟要在哪座城市生活，父母以后怎么办，自己到底有没有本事把这条路一直走下去。钱、学历、工作、城市、父母、未来，本来就是一组无法回避的事实，没有任何一个需要被提升成哲学问题以后才值得焦虑，它们本身就是哲学问题的物质底座。想了一夜仍然没有结果，凌晨三点只好下床弄一桶合味道吃。面里照例掰两块腐乳，盐、油和发酵气味一齐冲上来，人的注意力便终于从无法解决的人生问题回落到汤面上来，至少此时可以确定下一件事情是把饭吃完（黑色包装赤豚骨浓汤风味总感觉怪怪的）。与此同时，别人大概正在过自己的暑假，有人去社会实践，有人去企业实习，有人见导师，有人见领导，有人已经开始把假期加工成履历，项目、会议、调研、志愿服务，一项一项排得齐齐整整，到秋天开学的时候便可以说自己没有闲着，“高音甜、中音准、低音沉，总之一句话，就是通透。”这当然无可指摘，人总要谋生，而且谋生从来就不是一件可耻的事，只是我个人暂没有那么多东西可以拿来加工，于是便只是盯着电脑里的空白文档，看那个光标极有耐性地一闪一闪。它倒是很公平，从来不问我有没有职业规划，也不问我申请做到了哪一步，只是在那里提醒我，纸还空着。

后来睡着了，梦却把我送回老家。梦里的我还是十几岁，在城里读书，只有节假日才回去，坐一辆在黄泛区泥路上颠得人骨头发麻的三轮车，怀里抱着没做完的卷子，旁边那个亲戚已经老成了现在的样子（醒来后我意识到其实并没有这么一个亲戚，但梦里却很有记忆），烟味没变，讲话的方式也没变，依然孜孜不倦地劝人奔一个稳定的前途，最好进单位，最好有个体面的身份，最好能做官。我不知道梦里为什么一定要把事情具体到县长，反正大致就是这么个意思，读书归读书，最后总得落到一个能让家里人说出去有面子的地方。我在梦里居然没有反驳，反而听得很认真，像还在等这个人替我判卷，告诉我这些年考试、升学、离开、再离开究竟有没有走错。车窗外一直下雨，苹果园泡在积水里，沟里的泥水跟田地混成一片，车轮不停打滑。醒来之后我想了很久，真正令人不安的倒不是那个亲戚，而是我到现在还会在梦里认真对待这种问题。原来人可以离开一个地方，却未必能从那个地方给他的判断方式里毕业。故乡真正留给人的未必只是贫穷或者熟人社会，更是一整套关于风险的计算，工作稳不稳，钱够不够，失败以后怎么办，出去以后回不来怎么办，父母老了怎么办，如果所有计划都不顺利的话，自己到底还有没有地方可以回去。这些东西不会因为火车离开县城便自动消失，换了城市还在，换了学历还在，甚至开始讨论国外博士和academic job market的时候，它们也依旧蹲在底下提醒你先考虑房租、收入和退路。

不过我现在已经很少回乡，节假日两三天，有时甚至当天来当天走，说是返乡其实都有些夸张，更像短期访问。很多街道我认得它原来的样子，却不知道如今为什么变成这样，谁家的孩子已经长大，谁家的店关门，谁家的老人搬去了哪里，都要重新向亲戚打听。小时候觉得整个世界就是那里，后来出去以后知道那里只是世界很小的一块，如今再回去，连这一小块也变得需要重新认识。可是过年总有一些非常奇怪的下午，乡里的老头老太太吃完饭坐在院子里，冬天太阳不强，桌上有茶、有瓜子、有烟，谁递来一支，我便接过来抽。聊天原本还是今年冷不冷，地里收成如何，谁家的孩子工作了没有，讲着讲着不知道怎么就会绕到国内政治。因为平时我会翻墙去看油管，里面有不少国内政治和官场的小道消息，我看这些东西本来也不是什么严肃研究，大多时候纯粹是猎奇，看哪个地方又传出什么奇事，哪个人最近又出了什么新闻，某个官场人物怎样倒霉，某个部门又发生了什么听起来离谱的故事，有一点性压抑者看A片的意思，未必相信，也并不关心什么真相，主要是看乐子。春节回乡后，这些本来供自己消遣的东西忽然有了新的用途，因为老人们不会自己翻墙去看油管，他们听的是我讲给他们听的二手政闻。讲一个，他们便跟着猜一个，这个人是不是要出事，那个地方是不是迟早要完，某个领导为什么如此，某个国家到底在干什么。信息自然不很可靠，十件里未必有三件经得起核查，可老人们听得又怕又迷，我也越讲越兴奋，烟雾慢慢在头顶聚起来，讲到兴处手都开始跟着比划（据说意大利和中国很像，也许看来是真的），仿佛坐在那里不是给几个乡里老人讲网上看来的闲闻，而是在一间非常简陋的讲堂里给学生授课。说到一个离谱处，大家一阵笑，我继续往下讲，说完最后一段，把已经烧到滤嘴的烟头往院子旁边冬天干枯的泥里一抛，动作倒颇有几分大学教授讲完一堂课以后把粉笔丢回黑板槽的味道。那一瞬间竟然会生出一种奇怪的与有荣焉，好像某种我从未真正经历过的八十年代在桌面上短暂复活了，普通人吃完饭也能一本正经地谈国家大事，担心一个遥远的战争，评价一个不会知道自己存在的官员，猜测下一个十年会怎样，仿佛天下虽然大到个人根本管不了，却仍旧容得下每个人坐下来发表两句意见。“It's my duty!”原来这些年我不过是慢慢习惯把这些事情用各种黑话包装，形式复杂了，人未必因此更接近世界。有时甚至觉得老人家一句很粗糙的话比自己的所谓理论分析诚实。也正因为如此，我后来越来越不愿意把故乡简单写成一个必须摆脱的低地。它当然是我想离开的地方，而且很多年里我最强烈的愿望就是离得再远一点，可它也在某些很荒谬的午后给过我一种真实的参与感，让我在一张饭桌上暂时觉得自己和这些人没有什么根本区别，至少大家都觉得自己有资格对这个世界说上几句。

今年年初的大泽乡之行便带着这种多少有些可疑的参与感过去了。事情本身没有任何怀古意味，春节期间亲戚带了一个据说在当地公安系统里颇有些面子的朋友，一群人一起去看看。如今那里已经是标准的景区，荒草很好，游客也很配合，地上散着淀粉肠竹签、踩瘪的矿泉水瓶和各种包装物，远处音响放着过于响亮的DJ，旁边竖着一块颜色鲜艳的建设宣传牌，秦末起义和现代文旅项目在这里和平共处。亲戚站在旁边很兴奋地说，如果以后我能进体制，家里办事情就会容易很多，也会跟着沾点光。我当然点头，心里却想起来，这地方在历史上最出名的一批年轻人做的第一件大事似乎并不是建设什么美丽大泽乡，而是把县令杀了。这话自然不能说，说出来一场正常的春节旅游立刻就得变成儒法斗争，最后大概谁也吃不好饭。历史发展到今天，确实还是有一些进步，古人走投无路的时候可以揭竿而起，现代青年走投无路则打开报名网站、上传材料、修改CV、准备面试，再给自己做一个三到五年的规划，以自证说还是有路可走的。古人拿刀，现代人拿Excel，工具到底文明了多少暂且不谈，至少表格多了不少。真要按照亲戚所期待的方向进去，我大概也不会立刻变成什么反派人物，普通人通常没有那么大的戏剧天赋，大多数时候只是慢慢学会一些非常正常的事情，饭桌上见什么人说什么话，什么时候敬酒，什么时候闭嘴，怎样把自己的利益说成集体利益，把不满说成建设性意见，明知某件事情不太对劲却告诉自己没有必要计较。今日割五城，明日割十城，向前一小步，文明一大步，几年以后再回头，往往没有发生任何足以记录的重大事件，只是原来很难接受的东西已经变成了现实，原来觉得可耻的事情已经变成了工作，原来不愿意成为的人也已经能够自然地解释自己为什么只能这样。人似乎并不需要一个明确的堕落时刻，很多时候只需要几十个没有被认真记账的小决定。

夏天快结束了，同龄人也逐渐各归各位，有人进了体制，有人继续考试，有人开始工作，有人gap申请，有人则在《王者荣耀》的排位里经略另一种等级制。现在已经很少有人因为受了什么委屈就连夜上山，现代人的逃亡也讲手续，辞职要提前通知，出国要办签证，申博需要writing sample，离开一座城市以前要先算清楚房租和押金。甚至连失败都开始有标准格式，最好写成一份可以解释的职业经历，而不要写成一场没有任何收益的逃亡。我却还留在这所学校里，接下来究竟是两年、三年，仍不知道。这里待得太久以后，教室、宿舍、食堂、图书馆、校门口的路、认识过后来失去联系的人，都开始形成一种只有自己知道的地理。它已经不只是学校，不是八九十年代的校园民歌，也不是二零一零年代的青春伤痛文艺，而更像一块在歌舞表演结束后，没有被及时拆掉的舞台。如正置身其中的宿舍，一个月前搬来时，被告知说一年后便将被重修，届时又要搬到其他地方，掰着指头计算终末线的降临，又渐自觉得这整一年的住宿却由此愈有滋味。否定性的胜利，辩证法的胜利。

所以最后还是回到宿舍。凌晨三点下床煮的泡面已经吃完了，腐乳的味道还留在桌边，屏幕上的文档依旧空着一大片。一阵折腾以后终于睡着，一觉睡到中午后才醒，太阳已经从窗帘缝里斜照进来。我洗了把脸，觉得烟瘾起来了，想遛一两根，于是下楼去买烟。烟店在学校南边，出去要穿过一片棚户式的家属区，据说陈寅恪也曾在大杂院还是大宅院的时候住过这，现在则是几排旧楼、窄路、飞线上的长衣短裤和墙根堆着的杂物。穿过一道鲜为人知的小校门，就是据说当今住了很多教授领导的小区，小区名也颇有点满洲耆老的情调。趟完这条固定买烟线路，往回走的时候，发现昨夜下过的雨还留着，路边的泥没有干透，鞋底踩进去一次，再拔出来，走几步又陷进去一次。泥其实并不深，只是每次拔脚都要从鞋边带走一些湿土。太阳已经偏了一点，家属区没有什么人，偶尔一辆自行车从旁边叮叮当当地滑过，我拆开烟盒，点了一支又一支，抽到快到宿舍楼下了，才低头发现鞋底已经沾得乱七八糟。于是跐在路牙石边上，用木棍一点点剔掉凹槽中的屑，忽然觉得自己这些年，所作所为也不过如此，一次又一次把脚从同一片泥坑里拔出来，然后在地上蹭蹭看，还能不能继续走。

胡一帆
2026.8.11–12
研究生宿舍，清华大学，北京

Critical Theory in the Age of Digintelligenceデジタルインテリジェンス時代の批判理論数智时代的批判理论

TRI and Weishan CthulhuTRI、ビザン·クトゥルーTRI、微山克蘇魯 · 2026.7–8

Introduction to the Critical Theory in the Age of Digintelligence Summer Reading Group

At the height of Fordism and industrial capitalism—the early or even "classical" phase of modernity familiar to us—large-scale machine production rested on rigorous spatial enclosure and the linear division of time. Capital forcibly concentrated labour in standardized factory production lines, physically disciplining the proletariat in the dual dimensions of body and time. This mode of exploitation, based on dense spatial concentration, objectively furnished an indispensable organizational precondition for classical class solidarity, trade-union movements and the awakening of collective political consciousness. Workers' physical co-presence under one roof transformed the visibility of exploitation into the cohesion of resistance. Yet with the advent of the post-Fordist phase dominated by cybernetics, the topology of exploitation underwent a fundamental ontological transformation. The logic of capital accumulation no longer relied solely on the direct extraction of absolute surplus value in physical space, but turned toward the continuous extraction of immaterial labour, cognitive surplus and the "behavioural surplus" persistently captured by digital platforms.

Within today's digintelligent platforms and algorithmic capitalism, the physical factory in its traditional sense has been thoroughly dismantled and reorganized. Labour is dispersed by APIs, crowdsourcing platforms, outsourced data-labelling networks and algorithms for allocating gig work, taking on a highly distributed, black-boxed and decentralized form. The medium of control has shifted from visible masonry walls and the supervisor's gaze into invisible TCP/IP protocols, deep packet inspection (DPI) and covertly operating predictive machine-learning models. Against this backdrop, traditional struggles over physical space, exemplified by Occupy Wall Street, face a serious structural mismatch at the instrumental and epistemological levels, and cannot avoid losing their efficacy before the underlying network architecture in which "code is law." If exploitation no longer takes the form of direct violent coercion, but becomes interface interactions and personalized recommendations seamlessly embedded in everyday life, do the physical points of purchase for resistance dissolve along with it?

This summer reading group seeks to suspend conventional humanist moral criticism and overly simple doctrines of technological refusal, directing theoretical inquiry into protocols, cryptographic infrastructures, the planetary computational Stack and the micropolitical networks through which heterogeneous subjects operate. The "age of digintelligence" is not a convenient label for technological progress, but a field of problems that must be historicized and theorized. Digital platforms, machine learning, cloud computing, data centres, automated management and generative AI are rearranging relations among capital accumulation, state governance, mediation, labour organization, knowledge production and political subjects. These changes can neither be described simply as a replacement for industrial capitalism nor reduced to old institutions acquiring a technological interface. More pressing questions concern which institutional relations have had their scale, speed and visibility changed by computation; which forms of power have merely gained more fine-grained operating conditions through new media; and which phenomena labelled "ruptures" actually continue the long histories of management science, advertising, colonial governance, infrastructure and the division of labour. Digitization and intelligentization thus constitute new objects of research while also forcing critical theory to reconsider the limits of its own concepts.

The first line of inquiry concerns forms of control and the production of computational subjects. From Wiener's feedback and communication to Foucault's analysis of disciplinary apparatuses, and then to Deleuze's modulation, Galloway's protocol and Rouvroy's algorithmic governmentality, these theories do not describe successive upgrades of a single mechanism of power. Discipline depends on spatial partition, timetabling, examination and normalization; protocols organize interoperability through technical standards; algorithmic systems may shape environments of action through classification, scoring, prediction, ranking and recommendation. These mechanisms may overlap, but may also generate conflicts among state jurisdiction, corporate governance and technical architectures. The question is therefore not whether "the algorithm has become the new sovereign," but how computational results enter institutional procedures; which organizations translate probabilistic outputs into eligibility, risk or punishment; who holds the power to interpret, modify and appeal; and how uncertainty within models is solidified into real consequences through organizational processes.

The second line of inquiry addresses surveillance, extraction, coloniality and infrastructuralization. Data are not naturally existing resources awaiting collection; they are continually produced through sensing, logging, labelling, identity systems, platform interfaces, business models and demands for governance. Zuboff's surveillance capitalism, Couldry and Mejias's data colonialism, Browne's historical analysis of racialized surveillance, and Mbembe's political reflections on coloniality, enmity and the exposure of life offer explanatory frameworks that are not fully compatible with one another. Concepts such as "colonial," "feudal" and "imperial" acquire analytical significance only when their corresponding mechanisms can be specified: resource appropriation, legal asymmetry, epistemic authority, compulsory dependence, spatial partition and differentiated risk are not interchangeable rhetorical figures. Likewise, the "cloud" cannot remain an interface metaphor. Data centres, submarine cables, chips, energy, minerals, land, spectrum, standards, logistics and maintenance labour together constitute the material conditions of computation. Platform power must therefore be discussed alongside infrastructure, territory, rent and the costs of exit.

The third line of inquiry concerns the political economy of platforms, labour and new relations of dependence. Varoufakis's and Durand's theses of technofeudalism are examined here in relation to platform capitalism, monopoly, theories of rent and infrastructure studies. What needs to be distinguished is not the rhetorical question of whether "capitalism is dead," but whether cloud gateways, network effects, intangible assets and platform governance produce structures of dependence that traditional theories of capital cannot fully explain, and in what respects platform rent and feudal ground rent are or are not comparable. Research on platform labour brings these macro-level questions back to orders, ratings, dispatching, microtasks, data labelling, content moderation, entrepreneurial subjects and global labour chains. The theory of affect and temporality offered by Berlant's Cruel Optimism is especially important here: why can precarious "freedom," "flexibility" and "self-enterprise" remain objects of attachment that subjects find hard to relinquish, and how might institutional change address ownership, the distribution of risk, lived time and expectations of the future together?

The fourth line of inquiry turns to mediation, publics and organization. Digital politics is often described in terms of falling connection costs, faster information circulation and weakened gatekeeping, yet publicness is not equivalent to traffic, nor organization to instantaneous assembly. Kelty's recursive public asks whether publics can maintain and modify the technical and institutional conditions of their own existence; Warner and Fraser discuss circuits of circulation, counterpublics and unequal participation; Kornbluh's Immediacy, or The Style of Too Late Capitalism critiques the fascination with transparency, immediacy, immersion and disintermediation through an analysis of cultural forms. Political action often depends on procedures, representation, memory, delay, interpretation, chains of responsibility and sustainable organization, while platform media may elevate "immediate visibility, immediate response, immediate circulation" into values in themselves. Decentralization is therefore not inherently democratic, and mediation is not inherently oppressive; the more important question is whether mediation can be held accountable, modified and collectively shaped by participants.

The fifth line of inquiry centres on general intellect, the concentration of computing power and technological futures. In the "Fragment on Machines" in the Grundrisse, Marx explores the tensions among social knowledge, fixed capital, labour time and the value-form; Virno further stresses that general intellect is not only crystallized in machines, but also exists in language, judgement, memory, cooperation and shared capacities. Generative AI brings this problem into view in a new form: model training depends on public texts, code, images, feedback, labelling labour and enormous physical computing resources, while these social conditions can be repackaged as private models, interfaces and cloud services. What requires analysis is therefore not whether "the LLM is general intellect," but through which mechanisms of property and infrastructure the cognitive traces of collective social production are concentrated; how rights of access, training, deployment and returns are distributed; and which layer of relations can be changed by open weights, public computing resources, interoperability and cooperative governance respectively.

The concluding discussion of AI, automation and posthuman futures does not aim to predict a timetable for AGI. Turing, Russell, Bostrom, Brassier, Land, Negarestani, Haraway, Hayles and Braidotti understand "intelligence," "the human," "machines," "control," "emancipation" and "the future" in profoundly different ways; Crawford, Bender and Hanna, Narayanan and Kapoor, and Hao continually bring these philosophical questions back to actual technologies, organizations and resource relations. Philosophical speculation, engineering judgement, industrial forecasting, political economy and empirical social research have different standards of evidence and cannot substitute for one another. Descriptive judgements, causal explanations and normative judgements should likewise remain distinct: exposing a mechanism of power does not automatically entail a single political programme, and the technical feasibility of an institutional arrangement does not establish its legitimacy. In this reading group, we seek to build testable connections among conceptual history, empirical mechanisms and normative questions, so that classical theories are neither revered as universal keys nor deprived, by differences between historical periods, of their capacity to reinterpret the present.

SessionCore Question
Session 1: Cybernetics, Control and the Birth of Digital Governance控制论、规训、控制社会与协议如何构成数字治理的历史前提？
Session 2: Algorithmic Governmentality and Biopolitics分类、预测、评分与排序如何制造可计算主体并获得制度效力？
Session 3: Surveillance, Extraction and Data Coloniality数据提取、监控、种族化分类与殖民性之间如何建立严格而非修辞性的联系？
Session 4: Planetary Computation and Infrastructure Space云、平台、数据中心与基础设施如何重组空间、权威、租金和退出成本？
Session 5: Recursive Publics, Mediation and Digital Politics公共性如何拥有并修改自身媒介条件？为什么中介与延迟可能是政治组织的条件？
Session 6: Platform Labour, Precarity and New Class Relations平台劳动、算法管理和不稳定生活如何重组劳动关系与集体行动？
Session 7: General Intellect and Resistance to Compute Concentration社会共同智力如何被固定资本化、基础设施化，又可能如何重新公共化？
Session 8: Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Posthuman Futures如何区分 AI 的现实能力、产业 hype、风险论证与后人类未来想象？

Part I: The Topology of Control (Weeks 1–2)

Session 1: Cybernetics, Control and the Birth of Digital Governance

This session begins with a prehistory often overlooked in theories of digital politics: before "algorithm" became an everyday word, the twentieth century had already developed an intellectual vocabulary that redescribed machines, organizations and societies through communication, feedback, information and control. Wiener's cybernetics, Cold War command-and-control, industrial management's demand for information processing, distributed communication networks and software protocols together constitute the historical conditions of digital governance. These conditions do not, however, form a linear chain necessarily leading to contemporary algorithmic governance. Foucault's disciplinary power depends on spatial partition, timetabling, examination and normalization; Deleuze's modulation points to continuous and variable forms of control; Galloway's protocol addresses how distributed networks stipulate operability while permitting connections. Their differences are, first of all, differences of object, scale and mechanism.

Within this genealogy, control cannot be reduced to whether a "centre" exists. Standards, protocols, interfaces, identities, permissions, hardware and law impose constraints at different levels; execution can be highly distributed while standard-setting, resource ownership and rights of modification remain concentrated. Baran's distributed communication is first an engineering design; May's crypto-anarchism is a political manifesto; Berners-Lee's Web proposal originates in an information-management problem; DeNardis shows that technical standards always occupy the intersection of transnational institutions, corporations and state power. The same network topology can serve military resilience, open collaboration, commercial platforms or surveillance systems. Its political character therefore cannot be deduced directly from architectural labels such as "distributed," "open" or "encrypted."

This session thus establishes a multilayered concept of control: technical systems may delimit operability by encoding rules, but may also depend on market concentration, organizational procedures and state jurisdiction to acquire practical efficacy. "Protocol politics" does not replace legal politics; it results from the nesting of standards, software, institutions and sovereignty. This distinction provides the basis for the next session on algorithmic governance. Only after specifying whether rules operate at the level of architecture, protocol, organization or law can we analyse how scoring, prediction and recommendation systems transform behaviour into computational objects.

Required Readings:

  1. Wiener, Norbert. The Human Use of Human Beings: Cybernetics and Society. Houghton Mifflin, 1950. (Read: Chapters 1–2, pp. 15–47).

    [Note: Wiener redescribes relations among humans, machines and social organizations through communication, feedback and control. The aim here is not to treat cybernetics directly as a theory of algorithmic governance, but to examine how a language of knowledge for "managing systems through information and feedback" took shape. It provides a historical background for the protocols and algorithms that follow, while reminding us that some basic imaginaries of what is now called "data-driven governance" did not begin with the Internet but have a longer cybernetic genealogy. More importantly, we should first establish the original text's object and technical level, and only then look for structural homologies; whenever the legal environment, organizational actors or material conditions differ, analogy must be treated as inspiration rather than evidence. In applying this framework to contemporary digital objects, the key is to identify the level at which a similarity occurs; changes to the legal environment, organizational actors or material conditions also alter the concept's explanatory scope. Wiener's The Human Use of Human Beings: Cybernetics and Society further grounds the "historical differences among cybernetics, discipline, societies of control and protocol governance" in institutional relations. The key to digital governance is not whether a centre disappears, but how command, feedback, standards and rights of maintenance are recombined across organizations. Execution can be highly distributed while standard-setting and resource ownership remain concentrated; network topology and political decentralization must therefore be assessed separately. Wiener's significance also lies in his refusal to treat feedback merely as a technical process inside machines: by connecting communication, entropy and organization, he formed a language capable of crossing engineering and social theory. Precisely because this language was highly transferable, it later exerted influence in management, military systems and computational culture far beyond its original engineering context. Rereading cybernetics today is better suited to examining when feedback becomes a principle of management, and when it is mythologized as a universal model of social self-regulation.]

  2. Foucault, Michel. Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison. Translated by Alan Sheridan. Vintage Books, 1977. Originally published 1975. (Read: Part III, Chapter 3, "Panopticism," pp. 195–228).

    [Note: This chapter provides a comparative theoretical starting point. Foucault discusses not "surveillance" as such, but how discipline produces governable bodies through spatial partition, timetabling, examination, record-keeping and the institutionalization of visibility. Panopticism depends not on a watcher constantly staring at someone, but on placing the observed person in a condition of always being potentially visible, thereby transforming external coercion into the subject's self-adjustment. We must maintain some distance when transferring this framework to digital platforms: data systems do not simply reproduce the positioning of bodies in architectural space. Instead, they may use logs, permissions, scores, recommendations and identity systems to turn action into data objects that can be computed and called up again. We can therefore ask: when surveillance shifts from "who is watching me?" to "what systems can record and process my actions?", how must the theory of panopticism be rewritten? The relation between platform datafication and disciplinary apparatuses can only be established through comparison of specific mechanisms, not deduced directly from their shared vocabulary of "visibility." What is genuinely comparable between digital platforms and panopticism is not the appearance of "seeing," but how visibility is institutionalized and enters the formation of subjects. Platform records often serve commercial prediction, risk control and organizational management simultaneously, and their data visibility is not symmetrically available to all actors. Digital surveillance is therefore better understood as a recombination of disciplinary techniques and data infrastructures than as the mere electronic conversion of Bentham's architectural model. Furthermore, digital environments change the temporal structure of disciplinary power. Conventional examinations often occur at definite moments, whereas platform records allow continuous accumulation and retrospective recalculation; a past act that once seemed irrelevant may acquire new meaning under a new model or policy. This retraceable, recomputable visibility means that digital governance both inherits discipline's logic of record-keeping and develops a politics of time different from that of prison architecture.]

  3. Deleuze, Gilles. "Postscript on the Societies of Control" October 59 (1992): 3–7. Originally published 1990.

    [Note: Deleuze's "societies of control" is not an empirical prediction of the Internet, but a highly compressed model of changing forms of power. Its core is the shift from the closed disciplinary mold to continuous modulation; the "dividual" means that an individual can enter different systems as multiple data fragments, credit, passwords and forms of identity. The text should be treated as a generator of questions, rather than translating the dividual directly into a "data profile." To apply it to digital governance today, what most needs to be added is not more technical terminology but the chain of implementation: where rules are encoded, who deploys and maintains them, and which legal and market relations make them effective. Thus, in Deleuze's "Postscript on the Societies of Control," the claim that "distributed topology and political decentralization are not the same thing" is more than a conceptual issue. The key to digital governance is not whether a centre disappears, but how command, feedback, standards and rights of maintenance are recombined across organizations. Execution can be highly distributed while standard-setting and resource ownership remain concentrated; network topology and political decentralization must therefore be assessed separately. Deleuze's distinction between mold and modulation is especially useful for describing power's shift from periodic certification to continuous updating: account status, credit limits, prices, permissions and recommendations can all be adjusted in real time as data flow. Yet "societies of control" is not an umbrella term for every digital phenomenon. Modulation has analytical force precisely because it identifies continuously changing conditions of access and the partitioning of identities, while state law, organizational rules and physical coercion may continue to coexist with them. What is most worth retaining from "societies of control" is not a label for a historical stage, but its account of power's temporality: through passwords, limits, qualifications and constantly updated statuses, control continually adjusts the space of action. Control and discipline are not mutually exclusive. Enclosed institutions such as schools, prisons and corporations remain, but increasingly combine with continuous assessment and data flows across settings.]

  4. Galloway, Alexander R.. Protocol: How Control Exists after Decentralization. MIT Press, 2004. (Read: Introduction; Chapter 1, "Physical Media"; and Chapter 2, "Form," pp. 1–92).

    [Note: Galloway's central contribution is to move the question of control away from a simple "centre–periphery" model. He asks how protocols establish rule relations in decentralized networks: systems such as TCP/IP and DNS allow large numbers of nodes to communicate, while specifying which actions can occur through standardized addresses, formats, permissions and modes of conversion. It is particularly important to distinguish "protocol is control" from "protocol is law": Galloway discusses the political form of technical systems, rather than claiming that state law has been replaced by network protocols. Theoretically, his work takes up Foucault's problem of discipline while providing a conceptual bridge toward algorithmic governance, blockchains and cloud platforms. We should further ask: when platforms write registration, identity, interfaces, ranking and access permissions into technical structures, does control become less dependent on explicit commands? Extending this text to platforms, the cloud or AI requires preserving both historical continuities and differences of mechanism: the former explain why a problem recurs, while the latter set boundaries that concepts cannot cross. Protocol politics thus exhibits an apparently paradoxical structure: the more communication depends on shared standards, the more a network may be distributed at the level of execution while generating new concentrations in standard-setting, naming systems or key resources. Galloway's value lies precisely in restoring "decentralization" from a normative compliment to an analysable technical and political relation, so that topology, governing authority and ownership are no longer conflated. Protocols also shift political conflict into versions, compatibility and the evolution of standards. Who may propose modifications, which changes lead to forks, and whether older nodes can still connect are all questions of governance within technical communities. Protocol is thus not a static rule, but a continually maintained institutional process; control occurs not only during execution, but also when standards are formulated and updated.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Lessig, Lawrence. Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace. Basic Books, 1999. (Read: Chapter 7, "What Things Regulate," pp. 85–99).

    [Note: The most noteworthy feature of Lessig's account of "code" is precisely that it does not draw a sharp divide between technical systems and legal institutions. He argues that behaviour is shaped jointly by four regulatory forces: law, social norms, markets and architecture. Code on networks can therefore regulate by changing the conditions of action, but its efficacy remains embedded in legal, economic and social relations. Rather than turning "Code is Law" into a slogan, we should analyse how a platform uses passwords, interfaces, authentication, defaults, payment rules and content ranking to transform an act from being "unlawful" into being "impossible to perform at all." This question is fundamental to understanding "architectural power." The political efficacy of technical structures always passes through organizations and institutions. Protocols prescribe interoperability; hardware determines the range of implementation; market concentration shapes exit costs; and state jurisdiction determines when rules carry coercive force. These layers together constitute the actual form of digital control. Lessig's four regulatory forces—law, norms, market and architecture—prevent digital governance from being reduced to "code determines everything." Architecture may make certain actions technically impossible or increase their costs, but the design and execution of code are themselves shaped by corporate business models, legal liability and social norms. What most deserves study in platform governance is how these four forces overlap: defaults, pricing mechanisms, community rules and state regulation often operate together within the same interface. Lessig's framework also suggests that the most stable form of platform power is often not a single mode of regulation, but multiple forces reinforcing one another. Commercial incentives may, for example, drive a particular interface design; the interface then changes users' norms; and law subsequently takes the platform's established technical conditions as its object of governance. The politics of digital architecture arises from this circuit, not from code possessing an independent sovereignty above society.]

  2. Beniger, James R.. The Control Revolution: Technological and Economic Origins of the Information Society. Harvard University Press, 1986. (Read: Introduction and Chapter 1).

    [Note: Beniger situates modern information society within the "crisis of control" brought about by industrialization: as production, transport, distribution and consumption accelerated, established organizational forms became increasingly unable to handle the resulting complexity, prompting the continuing development of information-processing and management technologies. This avoids a narrative in which "the Internet suddenly invented control" and places platforms, logistics and algorithmic scheduling within a longer history of management. The focus is on the economic and organizational demands that control serves. The political efficacy of technical structures always passes through organizations and institutions. This long-term perspective is particularly useful for explaining platform logistics, real-time pricing and algorithmic scheduling: these are not forms of "intelligence" appearing out of nowhere, but managerial responses to continued increases in speed, scale and complexity. Beniger thus reconnects the history of information technology with the organizational history of capitalism. Studying the so-called digital transformation must also involve examining how accelerating production and circulation generate new pressures for coordination, and who has the capacity to undertake that coordination. From the perspective of organizational history, the "crisis of control" also reveals the symbiosis between information processing and expansion of scale. Firms can sustain coordination over a wider area only when they can track inventory, transport, consumers and labour processes; new information technologies both respond to complexity and make further expansion possible. The growth of digital platforms can likewise be placed within this cycle, rather than described as a purely technological breakthrough. Information-processing capacity can therefore itself be understood as a productive condition of organizational expansion: it resolves existing complexity while opening space for centralized coordination on a larger scale. This reciprocal reinforcement between organization and information also makes Beniger an important mediator between the history of industrial management and that of platform governance. It places management technology and the capitalist problem of scale within a single historical framework. The information revolution is thus recast as a result of the co-evolution of organizational capacities and economic structures. This perspective also helps explain why "real-time" capability has become a persistent goal of modern management.]

  3. Baran, Paul. "On Distributed Communications Networks" IEEE Transactions on Communications Systems 12, no. 1 (1964): 1–9.

    [Note: Baran's article should be read as a text in engineering history. Its central problem is how communication systems can improve redundancy and survivability in high-risk environments, not how to establish "decentralization" in a political sense. For precisely this reason, it is well suited to testing later analogies in digital politics: why can the same distributed topology be interpreted as military resilience, network freedom, platform elasticity or even surveillance infrastructure? A technical structure does not carry a single political direction within itself. Through Baran's "On Distributed Communications Networks," the proposition that "distributed topology and political decentralization are not the same thing" enters the organizational and institutional levels. The political efficacy of technical structures always passes through organizations and institutions. At the scale of Baran's "On Distributed Communications Networks," this proposition requires attention to both continuity and transformation: old institutions may gain new modes of operation through new technologies, while new technologies may be reabsorbed into existing institutions. Baran's engineering argument also reminds us that a distributed network is first a solution for reliability, not a political institution. Node redundancy can improve a communication system's capacity to survive destruction, but cannot answer who owns the network, who sets its protocols or who can cut off access. Later interpretations that directly translate "distributed" into freedom, autonomy or democracy effectively turn engineering topology into an unproven normative judgement. Engineering redundancy also reveals the difference between "resilience" and "autonomy." Multipath design may make a network harder to destroy, while a small number of institutions still control equipment, spectrum and access licences. Baran's value lies in preserving this distinction within technical history, requiring subsequent political imaginaries of distributed networks to address ownership and governance rather than infer power relations from topology alone.]

  4. DeNardis, Laura. The Global War for Internet Governance. Yale University Press, 2014. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–24).

    [Note: DeNardis places the Internet's technical governance directly within global politics. IP addresses, domain names, standards, routing and security are not purely "technical issues," but neither can they simply be reduced to state sovereignty. Read alongside Galloway, this work shows how protocols, corporations, international organizations and state agencies jointly produce network order. The "connection among technical design, maintenance labour and the legitimacy of governance" revealed by DeNardis's The Global War for Internet Governance extends beyond conceptual debates internal to the text. The political efficacy of technical structures always passes through organizations and institutions. DeNardis's The Global War for Internet Governance allows this connection to be delimited to specific objects and causal chains; analogies beyond that scope require new evidence rather than relying on terminology alone. DeNardis brings Internet governance to a more precise level: domain names, address allocation, routing, security certificates and technical standards have engineering properties while also constituting global power relations. Network order is not a choice between the state and the Internet; it is sustained jointly by governments, standards organizations, operators, platform firms and technical communities. Infrastructure governance therefore often takes place at technical layers that are difficult for publics to perceive, yet profoundly alter conditions of access and expression. The complexity of Internet governance also shows that the technical layer is not a stage prior to politics. How standards organizations reach consensus, how operators exchange traffic, and how certificate authorities establish trust are seemingly backstage arrangements that are themselves institutions. DeNardis thus breaks network sovereignty into identifiable points of governance, exposing both blanket claims that "the state controls the Internet" and that "the Internet transcends the state" as excessively crude.]

  5. Turner, Fred. From Counterculture to Cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the Rise of Digital Utopianism. University of Chicago Press, 2006. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 11–39).

    [Note: Turner traces the historical translation among American counterculture, the Whole Earth network and personal computing culture. The book is useful for testing a familiar account of Silicon Valley's origins: the communities, individual autonomy, technological media and network imaginaries of the 1960s did not naturally lead to platform capitalism, but were continually recomposed through different organizational, commercial and cultural forces. At the analytical scale of Turner's From Counterculture to Cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the Rise of Digital Utopianism, the "historical differences among cybernetics, discipline, societies of control and protocol governance" first appear as a set of concrete relations. More importantly, the account makes feedback, information and adaptation part of organizational thinking, while later discipline, protocols and platform governance reorganize these relations in different ways. Turner's history shows that the relation between countercultural communities and later digital capitalism is not simply one of betrayal. Individual autonomy, the rejection of bureaucracy, networked collaboration and entrepreneurial culture were recombined in particular organizational environments, gradually forming a technological culture that combined communal imaginaries with market logic. Understanding this transformation helps explain why openness, participation and innovation can simultaneously serve anti-establishment politics and corporate management. This history also explains a persistent paradox in Silicon Valley culture: anti-bureaucratic discourse frequently coexists with highly centralized corporations. Individual freedom is emphasized in user interfaces and entrepreneurial myths, while backstage infrastructures, capital control and labour management may become more concentrated. Countercultural legacies are therefore not simply the opposite of platform capitalism, but one of the sources of its cultural legitimacy.]

  6. Kittler, Friedrich. Optical Media. Translated by Anthony Enns. Polity, 2010. Originally published 2002. (Read: "Theoretical Presuppositions," pp. 29–46).

    [Note: Kittler emphasizes how the physical conditions of media and their technical capacities for storage and transmission shape cultural forms. Read before protocol politics, his work helps prevent us from understanding code as purely abstract symbols: protocols must run on hardware, spectrum, storage and computing capacity. His media determinism requires critical reading, but this extreme position is precisely what forces digital media studies to take the material foundation of digital power seriously. Kittler's Optical Media, Turner's From Counterculture to Cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the Rise of Digital Utopianism and Barbrook's "The Californian Ideology" place the "layered relations among standards, protocols, software, hardware and institutional power" within different intellectual traditions. Kittler's Optical Media frees these layered relations from overly abstract judgements about historical eras. The contribution of Kittler's Optical Media to this problem lies precisely in keeping theory open to refutation. Emphasis on media materiality also changes the direction of analysis in software politics. The "cloud," "real time" and "seamless experience" all depend on concrete devices for storage, transmission, display and computation; these devices determine what information can be recorded, how fast it circulates and where distortions occur. Although Kittler's forceful media theory cannot replace institutional analysis, it prevents critique from remaining at the level of interfaces and discourse.]

  7. Barbrook, Richard, and Andy Cameron. "The Californian Ideology" Science as Culture 6, no. 1 (1996): 44–72.

    [Note: This article critiques the ideological form in which digital technological culture combines liberal individualism, anti-bureaucracy and technological progress. Together with Turner, it forms a historical and ideological pairing: this article examines how cultural imaginaries are reorganized, while Turner provides the historical genealogy. "The Californian Ideology" should not be treated as an all-purpose explanation of Silicon Valley; we should examine the real tensions it reveals. Through Barbrook's "The Californian Ideology," the claim that "distributed topology and political decentralization are not the same thing" can be broken down into several interrelated components. From this perspective, the claim cannot stand apart from institutional authorization and resource allocation; technical forms produce stable social consequences only when combined with organizational power. What most deserves retention is not a fixed label of "Silicon Valley ideology," but the political mixture the article reveals: anti-bureaucracy, individual emancipation and market freedom can intertwine in technological utopias. Open networks and personal computers therefore do not naturally correspond to either left- or right-wing politics; their political direction depends on property structures, labour relations, and how public investment is narrated and distributed. The critique of "The Californian Ideology" also concerns how public investment is erased from technological myths. The Internet, computers and research systems have long depended on state and university resources, yet commercial success is often retold as a victory for individual entrepreneurship and market spontaneity. This politics of memory helps shape Silicon Valley's distinctive attitudes toward regulation, taxation and public responsibility. This ideology has remained effective partly because it can repackage conflicting values as a coherent narrative: individual autonomy and venture capital, anti-bureaucracy and corporate expansion, open culture and intellectual property can coexist under the name of "innovation." The task of critique is not to seek a pure origin, but to analyse how these contradictions are provisionally stitched together by a temporal narrative of technological progress.]

  8. May, Timothy C.. "The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto" In High Noon on the Electronic Frontier, edited by Peter Ludlow, 41–44. MIT Press, 1996. Originally written in 1988 and circulated in the early cypherpunk milieu; read at the September 1992 founding meeting. (Read: entire manifesto, pp. 41–44).

    [Note: This text is first a document of its historical context, rather than a theoretical authority capable of independently grounding normative judgements. May imagines strong encryption, anonymous communication, digital cash and electronic contracts as technical conditions for weakening state capacities for regulation, taxation and information control, while also revealing marked libertarian and technological-determinist tendencies in cypherpunk culture. Its significance here is that it shows the political imaginary in which terms such as "decentralization," "privacy," "anonymity" and "code autonomy," subsequently reused by different camps, were initially connected. It should especially be compared with Galloway and Lessig: if technical architectures do possess regulatory capacities, why can encryption be understood both as a tool against state surveillance and as an infrastructure of new private power? May's "The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto," Barbrook's "The Californian Ideology" and Berners-Lee's "Information Management: A Proposal" together bring the "connection among technical design, maintenance labour and the legitimacy of governance" down from macro-level judgements to mechanisms. May's contribution to this connection lies in forcing broad judgements back onto identifiable institutional mechanisms. His text also shows that cryptography's political significance has never been singular. Privacy technologies can limit the visibility available to states or corporations, but may also weaken the conditions for implementing taxation, labour protections and public regulation. Debate about encryption therefore cannot remain confined to a binary opposition between "state and individual"; platform capital, financial intermediaries, infrastructure operators and public responsibility must all enter the analysis.]

  9. Berners-Lee, Tim. "Information Management: A Proposal" CERN, 1989. (Read: entire proposal).

    [Note: This is not a mature manifesto of Web utopianism, but an engineering proposal to solve CERN's information-management problems. It matters as an original design document because it reveals the initial intentions behind hypertext, links, network sharing and open information. Comparison with later walled gardens, platform economies and cloud services allows us to discuss how design visions shift through commercialization, standardization and capital accumulation. Starting from Berners-Lee's "Information Management: A Proposal," the "historical differences among cybernetics, discipline, societies of control and protocol governance" acquire clearer causal levels. Engineering design carries no fixed political direction. Openness, encryption, distribution and modularity can have opposite consequences in different institutions; assessing their political implications still requires returning to rights of standard-setting and modification, resource ownership and authority over fault resolution. Looking back from this original proposal to the platformized Web also reveals a historical divergence between "linking" and "controlling gateways." Open hypertext emphasizes extensible connections among heterogeneous information, whereas platformization increasingly organizes visibility through account systems, recommendation logics and proprietary interfaces. This difference reminds us that network technologies' political effects often arise from subsequent commercial and institutional structures, rather than being predetermined by their initial engineering designs. Berners-Lee's proposal also retains an institutional problem that later becomes increasingly significant: open protocols can guarantee interconnection, but cannot ensure that the information ecosystem will not be reconcentrated around a few gateways. The Web's basic standards remain open, yet search, social media, identity and cloud services can form new bottlenecks on top of them. The coexistence of an open lower layer and a concentrated upper layer is a structure that cannot be ignored in understanding contemporary Internet politics. It makes the relation between open standards and platform concentration an important thread in Web history: interconnection at the base does not automatically prevent gateways at the upper level from forming monopolies again.]

  10. Edwards, Paul N.. The Closed World: Computers and the Politics of Discourse in Cold War America. MIT Press, 1996. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on command-control systems and Cold War computing).

    [Note: Edwards places Cold War computing, military command-and-control systems and a broader political imaginary of the "closed world" within a single historical framework. His value lies not in attributing all digital technology to the military, but in showing how computational architectures, simulations, chains of command and political narratives once shaped one another. For this session, the book supplies an indispensable mediation in institutional history between Wiener's cybernetics and later network governance, while reminding us not to treat "control" as merely an abstract form at the software level. Engineering design carries no fixed political direction. Edwards's closed world situates Cold War computers within military command, simulation and imaginaries of closed systems. Computation is not just a tool; it also participates in shaping a political epistemology of enemies, environments, decisions and controllable worlds. The history of digital governance therefore cannot be traced solely through the civilian Internet: military organizations' demands for real-time information, command-and-control and systems integration were also deeply involved in forming computational infrastructures.
