The closure of the closed world also manifests in modes of knowledge production: complex realities are transformed into systems that can be simulated, computed and commanded, giving decision-makers an imaginary of "seeing the whole from the centre." Today's data dashboards and real-time surveillance continue part of this epistemological impulse, but their organizational structures differ from Cold War military systems. Comparison should focus on how system visualization shapes decision-makers' beliefs in controllability. From this perspective, dashboards, simulations and real-time situational awareness do more than improve decision-making efficiency: they shape standards for "complete information" and "rational control." The more systems emphasize visualizing the whole, the more they may treat local knowledge, ambiguities and political disputes that cannot enter the model as noise. The epistemological boundaries of computational governance are thus directly connected to organizational power. This systems perspective also affects how responsibility is allocated: when failures are attributed to "insufficient information" or "incomplete models," organizations often pursue further data expansion rather than reflect on the setting of objectives itself. The closed world is therefore also a logic of governance that continually demands greater computability.]

  11. Pickering, Andrew. The Cybernetic Brain: Sketches of Another Future. University of Chicago Press, 2010. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on British cybernetics).

    [Note: Through particular figures and experiments in the British cybernetic tradition, Pickering stresses that cybernetics did not have only one historical path toward centralized management, prediction and optimization. From a performative and adaptive perspective, he presents another conception of machines continually coupled with unknown environments. Following Wiener and Beniger, the book importantly puts the brakes on the linear genealogy that "cybernetics necessarily leads to societies of control": the same concepts of feedback, adaptation and systems may acquire very different political meanings in different institutions and practices. With Pickering's The Cybernetic Brain: Sketches of Another Future, the claim that "distributed topology and political decentralization are not the same thing" can be transformed from a rhetorical proposition into institutional analysis. Engineering design carries no fixed political direction. In Pickering's The Cybernetic Brain: Sketches of Another Future, this claim does not lead to a single conclusion, but requires comparison of configurations of power in different organizational settings, so as to establish concepts' explanatory scope and the conditions of their failure. Through the heterodox tradition of British cybernetics, Pickering shows that cybernetics does not necessarily lead to centralized control. Experiments by Ashby, Pask and others attend more closely to adaptation, emergence and dancing with complex environments, developing a technological imaginary distinct from command-and-control. This difference prevents us from treating "cybernetics" as a single political genealogy, and demonstrates that the same concepts of feedback can lead to different engineering practices and social philosophies. Pickering's "performative" cybernetics also offers another politics of technology: rather than presupposing that an environment can be fully represented, it allows a system continually to adapt to unknown environments through feedback. This stance is not inherently democratic, but provides an important counterexample to the dataist assumption that "more accurate prediction means better governance." Complexity need not always be addressed through more comprehensive models; it can also be handled through open relations of adaptation.]

  12. Chun, Wendy Hui Kyong. Programmed Visions: Software and Memory. MIT Press, 2011. (Read: Introduction; Chapter 1, "On Software, or the Persistence of Visual Knowledge").

    [Note: Chun asks why software is experienced as something both invisible and apparently capable of directly commanding machines, placing its executability, interfaces, memory and discourses of control within media history. This corrects the tendency to treat protocol or code as purely logical rules: code's effects of power depend on compilation, hardware, interfaces, institutions and user practices, and "programmability" is not a frictionless sovereign command. Engineering design carries no fixed political direction. Chun's Programmed Visions: Software and Memory ultimately turns the "connection among technical design, maintenance labour and the legitimacy of governance" into a problem that empirical research can continue to dissect, rather than a diagnosis of the era completed in advance. Chun particularly reveals software's duality: it is presented as transparent, executable command, yet can operate only through numerous invisible layers of abstraction and material processes. Software acquires its distinctive governing efficacy precisely between this "visible sense of control" and "invisible technical mediation." For digital politics, analysing code means asking not only what it says, but how it is compiled, deployed, updated and embedded in organizations. Software's "executability" can also produce an illusion of immediacy, as if writing code were enough to realize an intention without friction. In fact, execution always passes through operating systems, hardware, libraries, networks and user environments; errors, compatibility and updates are normal features of systems. Chun thus returns software from abstract command to a medium with historical and material conditions. Software should therefore be understood as an institution of mediation: it turns complex hardware into operable interfaces while concealing numerous conditions of execution through abstraction layers. Users' experience that "a click makes it happen" comes from a continually maintained technical chain, not from the absence of distance between command and result. It is through this hidden mediation that software acquires powerful effects of everyday governance.]

Session 2: Algorithmic Governmentality and Biopolitics

This session moves from "how rules prescribe action" to "how computation organizes the possibilities of action." Rouvroy's algorithmic governmentality does not presuppose a reconstruction of subjects' worlds of meaning. Instead, through data collection, correlation analysis and probabilistic prediction, it produces structures of classification, risk and opportunity before action occurs. Cheney-Lippold's algorithmic identity further shows how subjects can be divided into continually updated data categories. Bucher rejects the image of "the algorithm" as a single, mysterious black box, stressing that code, training data, platform objectives, engineering practices, user behaviour and institutional environments together constitute algorithmic power. The computational subject is therefore not a person completely "known" by a machine, but an actor recoded, grouped and ranked in different institutional settings.

The political efficacy of algorithms cannot be explained solely by model performance. A probabilistic output becomes part of governance only when it is given consequences for action within organizational procedures such as loan approval, welfare eligibility, border screening, recruitment, content distribution or insurance pricing. Prediction, explanation, judgement and justification must therefore be distinguished: statistical correlation is not causal explanation, and a model's risk score cannot automatically serve as a legal or ethical reason. Amoore's analysis of uncertainty and probabilistic judgement, Eubanks's empirical research on welfare automation and Pasquale's discussion of black boxes and accountability all point to the same question: how are technical outputs translated within institutions into decisions that impose real constraints?

This session also returns "algorithmic bias" from a general value judgement to a chain of institutional processes. Training data, labelling systems, target variables, evaluation metrics, threshold settings, deployment environments, human review and channels of appeal can each generate or amplify inequality. Classification does not merely describe the world: once adopted by organizations, it helps shape structures of opportunity and social identities. Algorithmic governmentality therefore concerns not only knowledge but also administrative procedures, organizational responsibility and the protection of rights. The expansion of computability has not abolished political judgement; in many settings, it has changed how judgement is concealed, distributed and held accountable.

Required Readings:

  1. Rouvroy, Antoinette. "The End(s) of Critique: Data Behaviourism versus Due Process" In Privacy, Due Process and the Computational Turn, edited by Mireille Hildebrandt and Katja de Vries, 143–167. Routledge, 2013.

    [Note: This chapter is the conceptual core of the session. Rouvroy's algorithmic governmentality describes a form of governance that need not first understand subjects' meanings, motivations or intentions, but intervenes before action through data collection, correlation analysis and prediction. The key is to distinguish correlation from causation, prediction from justification, and profiling from judgement: algorithms do not need to "truly know who you are"; they only need institutions to believe, probabilistically, that certain classifications suffice to support action. Only then can we understand the real tension between algorithmic governance and traditional legal procedures. More specifically, the conflict with due process is not that "machines lack humanity," but that data behaviourism tends to transform subjects from legal and political persons capable of giving reasons and answering accusations into probabilistic behavioural profiles. Correlation analysis can support pre-emptive intervention without establishing causal explanations, making critique itself difficult: if a system no longer asks who you are or why you are as you are, but merely adjusts the environment you will encounter on the basis of past data, is a traditional critique centred on exposing ideology or correcting false representations still sufficient? This chapter should therefore be read alongside Yeung, Eubanks and Amoore to test, through regulation, welfare administration and security judgements respectively, whether algorithmic governmentality holds in the same way across institutions. Rouvroy's data behaviourism forms the core of algorithmic governmentality because it attempts to bypass the intentions, narratives and normative judgements of the traditional subject, discovering behavioural patterns directly in correlations across vast datasets. Governance can thus probabilistically shape subjects' spaces of opportunity before they have expressed themselves. A fundamental jurisprudential problem then emerges: correlation may support prediction, but cannot automatically supply reasons; procedural justice requires not merely accurate outcomes but contestable normative grounds.]

  2. Cheney-Lippold, John. "A New Algorithmic Identity: Soft Biopolitics and the Modulation of Control" Theory, Culture & Society 28, no. 6 (2011): 164–181.

    [Note: Cheney-Lippold introduces algorithmic identity to explain how digital systems produce dynamic categories from behavioural data. Read alongside Deleuze, this shows that identity is no longer determined solely by subjects' self-declarations or fixed demographic attributes, but can become a probabilistic object continually recalculated from behaviour. The limits are equally clear: algorithmic classification still draws on existing social categories, rather than being purely mathematical classification detached from history. The continuity between algorithmic identity and conventional population classifications must be specified through the origins, institutional uses and updating mechanisms of categories, rather than remain a correspondence between terms. The computational subject is not an individual fully known by a model, but an object divided into scores, probabilities, categories and behavioural traces in different institutional settings. Once classification enters welfare, credit, recruitment or content distribution, it in turn shapes opportunity structures and subjects' actions. Algorithmic identity turns identity from a stable attribute into a continually updated probabilistic classification. Systems need not establish who "the real you" is; they only need to place individuals provisionally into operable categories on the basis of behavioural traces, and use these to decide advertising, prices, risk or visibility. Cheney-Lippold thereby reveals a new dimension of identity politics: subjects may not know which category they have been assigned to, and have even greater difficulty participating directly in its definition and revision. Dynamic classification has another important consequence: identity is no longer confirmed only at registration, but can be inferred anew after every click, movement and purchase. Subjects confront not one fixed dossier but a series of continually changing and potentially contradictory probabilistic identities. Appeals are therefore especially difficult, since those affected may not even know which inference triggered differential treatment, or when. The political difficulty of algorithmic identity thus involves not only "being misjudged," but also subjects' difficulty in knowing which categories describe them and how those categories travel across settings.]

  3. Bucher, Taina. If...Then: Algorithmic Power and Politics. Oxford University Press, 2018. (Read: Chapter 2, "The Multiplicity of Algorithms," pp. 19–40; Chapter 3, "Neither Black nor Box," pp. 41–65).

    [Note: Bucher's important contribution is to reject the image of algorithmic power as a mysterious, unified, invisible "black box." Algorithmic power is distributed across code, data, platform objectives, user behaviour, engineering practices and institutional arrangements. This helps ground Rouvroy's broad concept of governance in concrete systems: we do not face "the algorithm" as a single actor, but a set of different software, institutions and practices. "Algorithmic transparency" must therefore also be redefined: transparent code does not automatically mean transparent governance. Predictive systems often need only construct sufficiently operable proxies, without developing a complete theory of identity; this is precisely where algorithmic identity and traditional identity politics are related yet cannot be equated. Bucher's If...Then: Algorithmic Power and Politics thus offers a limited but effective explanatory scale for the "institutional chain linking quantification, data production and algorithmic systems": it can identify mechanisms, but does not replace further analysis of organizations, law and material conditions. Bucher rejects the algorithm as a single black-box subject, emphasizing that algorithms are jointly constituted by code, data, commercial goals, user practices and organizational institutions. Algorithmic power is therefore relational power: it resides not only in ranking logics, but also in engineering teams' choices, platform metrics and users' adaptations to systems. Transparency understood merely as releasing source code cannot encompass this complex sociotechnical assemblage. Bucher's attention to algorithmic imaginaries also shows that algorithmic power resides not only in what systems actually do, but in what people believe they can do. Users adjust their expression to accommodate imagined recommendation rules, while institutions may expand automated deployments in the belief that "algorithms are more objective." Algorithms' social efficacy thus arises partly from the expectations and uncertainties that form around them.]

  4. Amoore, Louise. Cloud Ethics: Algorithms and the Attributes of Ourselves and Others. Duke University Press, 2020. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–24).

    [Note: Amoore examines how probabilistic judgements acquire the capacity to produce action in border, security and risk governance. The important question is not whether algorithms can "predict accurately," but when institutions turn probabilistic outputs into actual decisions, and how that translation changes the politics of responsibility and uncertainty. Transparency is not a single solution either. This session places explainability within a broader understanding of due process and institutional accountability. Placed in the session's overall context, Amoore's Cloud Ethics: Algorithms and the Attributes of Ourselves and Others gives more concrete structure to the question of "how transparency, explanation, appeal and responsibility are redistributed in automated decision-making." The computational subject is not an individual fully known by a model, but an object divided into scores, probabilities, categories and behavioural traces in different institutional settings. Once classification enters welfare, credit, recruitment or content distribution, it in turn shapes opportunity structures and subjects' actions. Amoore shifts algorithmic ethics from "whether a model is correct" toward how probabilistic judgements are put into action. Border, security and risk systems often operate under uncertainty; the key is not to eliminate uncertainty, but to examine how institutions choose thresholds, give certain attributes greater weight and allow partial correlations to have real consequences. Responsibility therefore cannot be transferred to the model: the institutional allocation of uncertainty is itself a political decision. Amoore thereby advances the ethical question into attribution itself: systems infer the potential properties of a person or event from partial traces and pre-allocate attention, suspicion and resources accordingly. Probability is not a neutral waiting state, but can become a reason for action. The politics of risk governance lies in who is made to bear the costs of uncertainty, and which errors institutions deem acceptable.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Gillespie, Tarleton. "The Relevance of Algorithms" In Media Technologies, 167–194. MIT Press, 2014.

    [Note: Gillespie discusses how "relevance" itself becomes one of platforms' most important public decisions. Search, recommendation and ranking do not merely compute information; they decide what deserves to be seen and considered important. This adds a dimension of media and public culture to algorithmic governmentality. Theoretical similarity does not automatically imply institutional identity. Predictive accuracy, statistical correlation and administrative legitimacy belong to different levels; a risk score truly becomes governance only when it acquires consequences through thresholds, human review, appeals and enforcement procedures. "Relevance" is therefore normative rather than purely technical. What platforms call relevance commonly compresses click probabilities, dwell time, commercial objectives and content value into one ranking process. Algorithms do not directly adjudicate truth, yet can alter the conditions under which public issues emerge by allocating attention. Gillespie thus moves algorithm studies from inside models to platform institutions: what requires explanation is how criteria of relevance are set, adjusted and legitimized. Recommendation systems also have a public dimension because they alter the visible structure of a "common world." When users receive highly personalized rankings, public issues no longer have identical gateways, while platforms retain the authority to adjust recommendation goals and content boundaries. Research on algorithmic relevance must therefore connect media institutions to business models, rather than merely measure ranking accuracy. Platform ranking is both information processing and the allocation of attention; when relevance becomes a function of commercial objectives, media power enters the core of algorithmic design. Gillespie further reminds us that the normativity of algorithmic ranking often appears in the name of "user demand" or "relevance," thereby turning value judgements into technical matters. What deserves recommendation, what counts as spam and which content should be downranked all presuppose some public order. If algorithm studies ignore the institutional objectives behind these classifications, they will misrepresent platforms' most important political judgements as purely engineering optimization.]

  2. Eubanks, Virginia. Automating Inequality. St. Martin's Press, 2018. (Read: Introduction, pp. 1–14; Chapter 1, pp. 17–36).

    [Note: This book brings abstract algorithmic governance into welfare, poverty and administrative systems. Its core is not to prove that algorithms "are biased," but to observe how technical systems reorganize the allocation of social resources and how historical inequalities enter risk classifications. It shifts analysis from "platform experience" toward state administration and social policy. Eubanks's Automating Inequality does not provide a final name for "how organizations translate probabilistic outputs into judgements with real consequences," but a theoretical point of entry open to testing against competing explanations; this openness is itself part of its research value. Eubanks's Automating Inequality also shows that automated governance first falls on populations with the least capacity to exit. When technical systems repackage resource scarcity, welfare screening and risk management as questions of efficiency, poverty itself can readily become suspicion and computable risk. Eubanks's cases show that automated welfare systems do not simply substitute machine for human judgement; they reorganize screening within existing frameworks of resource austerity, administrative reform and the governance of poverty. Technology can speed up assessment, but can also fix historically entrenched suspicion and punishment of the poor into data rules. Algorithmic fairness therefore cannot be separated from the institutional objectives of the welfare state: a system that accurately enforces harsh policies can still produce profound injustice. Eubanks's empirical material also reveals a common political asymmetry in technological reform: administrative agencies deploy systems to reduce costs and prevent fraud, while those undergoing assessment bear the temporal costs of data errors, complex processes and automatic refusals. Efficiency calculated only from the institution's side excludes the extra labour borne by vulnerable groups from performance measures. The criteria for evaluating automated governance must themselves therefore be politicized. These cases also show that automation in poverty governance produces more than isolated errors; it can change the relationship between the state and welfare applicants. When face-to-face explanation and case-specific discretion are replaced by database verification and risk scoring, applicants must shoulder more responsibility for proving their eligibility. Digitizing procedures can thus transfer administrative burdens from inside institutions to those with the fewest resources.]

  3. Pasquale, Frank. The Black Box Society. Harvard University Press, 2015. (Read: Introduction; Chapter 2, "The Digital Poorhouse," pp. 35–58).

    [Note: Pasquale focuses on information asymmetry and accountability in automated decision-making. His work can test whether "open-source code" is a sufficient answer: even a system with open code may remain unaccountable because of its data, model complexity, commercial secrecy or organizational permissions. Through Pasquale's The Black Box Society, the "institutional chain linking quantification, data production and algorithmic systems" enters the organizational and institutional levels. At the scale of Pasquale's The Black Box Society, this chain must be approached through both continuity and transformation: old institutions may gain new ways of operating through new technologies, and new technologies may be reabsorbed into existing institutions. Pasquale's The Black Box Society also suggests that analysing this institutional chain requires preserving differences among objects and institutional boundaries, rather than substituting concepts' rhetorical force for empirical explanation. Pasquale's The Black Box Society extends invisibility from the technical to the institutional black box: commercial secrecy, control of data, professional barriers and organizational permissions together determine who can explain a system. Explainability can therefore become real accountability only when joined to auditing, appeals and the allocation of responsibility. Pasquale's black box encompasses technical complexity, trade secrets and institutional information asymmetry simultaneously. The opacity of financial scoring, search ranking and platform decisions cannot all be solved by "explaining the model"; those affected often also lack access to data, channels of appeal and bargaining power. Accountability must therefore extend from disclosure to organizational responsibility, specifying who has the authority to decide, who must give reasons and who can correct mistakes.]

  4. Harcourt, Bernard E.. Exposed: Desire and Disobedience in the Digital Age. Harvard University Press, 2015. (Read: Chapter 1, "The Expository Society," pp. 1–28).

    [Note: Harcourt discusses exposure, desire and surveillance together. Subjects' self-display should not simply be explained as "voluntarily submitting to surveillance"; we should analyse how platform design, social norms, the desire for visibility and commercial data extraction reinforce one another. Transparency is not a single solution either. The question of "how transparency, explanation, appeal and responsibility are redistributed in automated decision-making," revealed by Harcourt's Exposed: Desire and Disobedience in the Digital Age, extends beyond conceptual debate within the text. Harcourt's Exposed: Desire and Disobedience in the Digital Age allows this question to be delimited to specific objects and causal chains; analogies beyond that scope need new evidence and cannot rest on terminology alone. Harcourt's "exposure" also reveals an important turn in surveillance studies: subjects do not always exist as passive objects, but actively produce visibility through social interaction, consumption and self-display. The question is not whether this activity cancels coercion, but how commercial architectures capture desire and turn it into resources for prediction and governance under asymmetric data-access rights. Harcourt makes "exposure" more than a loss of privacy: it becomes a social relation. Through sharing, searching, location-tracking and consumption, subjects continually produce themselves, while platforms retranslate these expressions into computational resources. Desire and surveillance are therefore not opposing forces: precisely because digital environments satisfy needs to be seen, connected and expressive, data extraction can penetrate everyday life in the forms of participation and convenience. The paradox of the expository society is that subjects gain freedom of expression and connection while handing ever more traces of their lives to platforms they cannot observe reciprocally. Freedom and surveillance do not simply grow at one another's expense; they may increase together within the same architecture of interaction.]

  5. Beer, David. The Data Gaze: Capitalism, Power and Perception. Sage, 2018. (Read: Introduction and Chapters 1–2).

    [Note: Beer uses the concept of the data gaze to discuss how datafication changes relations of "seeing" and "being seen." This connects algorithmic classification with social perception: as life becomes increasingly datafied, institutions are not alone in "seeing" us; people increasingly understand themselves through metrics as well. At the analytical scale of Beer's The Data Gaze: Capitalism, Power and Perception, "how classification, prediction, scoring and ranking constitute computational subjects" first appears as a set of concrete relations. So-called algorithmic bias cannot remain a value judgement. Training data, labelling systems, target variables, evaluation metrics, deployment environments and existing institutional inequalities may each produce different problems; only tracing them layer by layer reveals where bias arises. The data gaze is not merely an institutional gaze upon people, but a perceptual mechanism through which subjects reconceive themselves in terms of metrics. Step counts, credit scores, popularity, rankings and performance data translate life into comparable quantities that in turn shape goals for action. Beer thus connects algorithmic governance to quantified subjectivation: data describe reality while also helping determine what kind of reality deserves pursuit. The metricized self does not arise entirely from coercion. People actively organize their lives with rankings, health data and social feedback, but this voluntary use occurs within the measurable dimensions that platforms have predefined. Subjectivity therefore includes both the desire to quantify oneself and guidance by metric architectures. Beer's analysis moves power beyond an external gaze into the technical forms of everyday self-evaluation. Such self-quantification further shows that data power is often realized through subjects' active participation, rather than solely through external surveillance or compulsory collection. The power of metrics thus comes both from measurement and from people reorganizing their actions around metrics. It is precisely in this self-adjustment that the data gaze enters subject formation.]

  6. Yeung, Karen. "Algorithmic Regulation: A Critical Interrogation" Regulation & Governance 12, no. 4 (2018): 505–523.

    [Note: This article offers a corrective from the perspectives of institutions and the rule of law. Algorithmic regulation does not simply improve technical efficiency; it concerns how machines execute, monitor and dynamically adjust rules. It helps build a clearer theoretical bridge between Rouvroy and Lessig. Yeung's "Algorithmic Regulation: A Critical Interrogation," Beer's The Data Gaze: Capitalism, Power and Perception and Seaver's "Algorithms as Culture: Some Tactics for the Ethnography of Algorithmic Systems" place "how organizations translate probabilistic outputs into judgements with real consequences" within different intellectual traditions. Yeung's "Algorithmic Regulation: A Critical Interrogation" frees this problem from overly abstract diagnoses of the era. So-called algorithmic bias cannot remain a value judgement. Yeung's contribution to this question lies precisely in keeping theory open to refutation. Her institutional perspective further shows that the key to algorithmic regulation is not merely its degree of automation, but how feedback loops change rule enforcement. Continuous monitoring can shift governance from retrospective punishment toward real-time adjustment, but dynamism may also compress procedural review and stable expectations. There is consequently a real institutional tension between efficiency and adaptability, on one hand, and the foreseeability and explainability demanded by the rule of law, on the other.]

  7. Seaver, Nick. "Algorithms as Culture: Some Tactics for the Ethnography of Algorithmic Systems" Big Data & Society 4, no. 2 (2017). (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Seaver opposes treating algorithms merely as technical objects that can be read directly from code, arguing instead that algorithmic systems are cultural objects jointly constituted by engineers' classifications, organizational cultures, models of users, data practices and maintenance work. This is crucial for this session: if algorithmic governmentality involves prediction and classification, researchers must ask not only how models work mathematically, but how categories such as "relevance," "user," "anomaly" and "success" are defined within organizations. Through Seaver's "Algorithms as Culture: Some Tactics for the Ethnography of Algorithmic Systems," the "institutional chain linking quantification, data production and algorithmic systems" can be broken down into several interrelated components. So-called algorithmic bias cannot remain a value judgement. From Seaver's perspective, this institutional chain cannot stand apart from institutional authorization and resource allocation; technical forms produce stable social consequences only when combined with organizational power. Seaver's cultural-anthropological approach returns algorithms from "independently operating code" to organizational life. How engineers understand users, which metrics count as success and how teams handle anomalies are all cultural practices that help constitute algorithmic systems. The significance of algorithmic ethnography thus lies not in entering secret code repositories, but in observing how technical objects are continually produced through everyday work, narratives and institutional routines.]

  8. Fourcade, Marion, and Kieran Healy. "Classification Situations: Life-Chances in the Neoliberal Era" Accounting, Organizations and Society 38, no. 8 (2013): 559–572. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Fourcade and Healy return scoring, ranking and classification to research on social stratification, emphasizing that modern classification systems do not neutrally describe, but change the opportunities, prices, resources and institutional treatment available to individuals. Their concept of the "classification situation" is especially useful alongside algorithmic identity: computational subjects are not only representations in data, but occupy real opportunity structures shaped by classification outcomes. Fourcade's "Classification Situations: Life-Chances in the Neoliberal Era," Seaver's "Algorithms as Culture: Some Tactics for the Ethnography of Algorithmic Systems" and Espeland's "A Sociology of Quantification" together move the question of "how transparency, explanation, appeal and responsibility are redistributed in automated decision-making" from broad judgements to mechanisms. Transparency is not a single solution either. Fourcade's contribution to this question lies in forcing macro-level judgements back onto identifiable institutional mechanisms. So-called algorithmic bias cannot remain a value judgement. "Classification Situations: Life-Chances in the Neoliberal Era" places this redistribution of transparency, explanation, appeal and responsibility back within historical conditions. Similar digital appearances need not arise from the same mechanisms, and the validity of concepts therefore depends on preserving differences. Fourcade and Healy's classification situations directly connect classification to life chances. Classifications in credit, insurance, education and consumption do not simply describe social differences: they determine interest rates, opportunities, treatment and visibility, thereby producing feedback effects. What digitization intensifies is not classification itself, but its capacity to enter everyday institutions at finer granularity, higher frequency and lower visibility.]

  9. Espeland, Wendy Nelson, and Mitchell L. Stevens. "A Sociology of Quantification" European Journal of Sociology 49, no. 3 (2008): 401–436. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Espeland and Stevens provide a methodological baseline for studying quantification: numbers, metrics and rankings compress complexity, but also use commensuration to place objects that were not directly comparable on a common scale. Bringing this article into algorithmic governance is not to claim that all algorithms are merely "scoring," but to see the social engineering that often occurs before predictive models can enter institutional decisions: objects must become quantifiable, metrics comparable and results rankable. Starting from Espeland's "A Sociology of Quantification," the question of "how classification, prediction, scoring and ranking constitute computational subjects" acquires clearer causal levels. Transparency is not the single solution to automated governance. Once commensuration is accomplished, political disputes are often rewritten as problems of metric design. University rankings, credit scores and risk models wield power not because numbers are inherently coercive, but because organizations begin allocating opportunities and resources according to them. The sociology of quantification therefore offers an important path: trace how classification standards change behaviour after entering institutions, while in turn stabilizing the classifications themselves. Espeland and Stevens also emphasize reactivity: those who are ranked and measured adjust their behaviour to fit evaluation systems. Once a metric becomes a target, it may change the object it was intended to measure. This mechanism is especially important in algorithmic governance, because deploying predictive models changes people's strategies and consequently changes future data. Quantification is thus not passive recording, but a social process capable of reshaping institutional settings. When metrics become goals of action, systems of quantification change the quantified objects themselves; this is the fundamental reason rankings and scores can generate institutional feedback. Commensuration and reactivity together constitute the basic mechanism through which quantification regimes continually reinforce themselves.]

  10. O'Neil, Cathy. Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality and Threatens Democracy. Crown, 2016. (Read: Introduction; selected case studies on education, employment, credit, and policing).

    [Note: Through a series of institutional cases, O'Neil shows how large-scale scoring models amplify inequality when opacity, closed feedback loops and high-impact settings coincide. This is not the endpoint of algorithmic theory, but an excellent stress test for concepts: only by placing models back within admissions, employment, credit or policing procedures can we see how errors are distributed, whether channels of appeal exist and how quantitative judgements acquire de facto coercive force. Transparency is not the single solution to automated governance. O'Neil's WMD concept stresses how models' scale, opacity and feedback properties jointly amplify harm. This accessible concept needs to be paired with more rigorous algorithm research, but it captures the core of institutional deployment: once a model enters high-stakes fields such as education, employment or justice, errors are no longer merely statistical deviations. They change people's opportunities and write their effects back into future data. Model evaluation must therefore include social feedback, not just offline accuracy. This feedback property connects WMDs with performativity in the social sciences. Model-generated judgements change educational resources, credit opportunities or policing attention, and those outcomes may then be treated as "real-world data" for the next round of training. Unless this cycle is interrupted, historical inequalities acquire renewed empirical legitimacy in the form of model performance. Evaluating models therefore requires not only asking whether predictions are accurate, but also whether deployed predictions generate new data that continually validate existing differences. The WMD framework also raises an accountability problem: when models are treated as objective tools, institutions can explain unpopular decisions as "results of the data," obscuring policy choices. Which variables are selected, which errors are acceptable and whether human overrides are permitted remain institutional decisions. Automation has not eliminated judgement; it has written some judgements into models and procedures in advance. Institutions therefore cannot treat responsibility for models as a one-off technical duty fulfilled by developers. Deployment, updating, threshold adjustments and human overrides continually change systems' consequences; accountability should cover their whole life cycle.]

  11. Kitchin, Rob. The Data Revolution: Big Data, Open Data, Data Infrastructures and Their Consequences. Sage, 2014. (Read: Introduction; chapters on data infrastructures and data assemblages).

    [Note: Kitchin restores big data from the slogan of "more data" to a data assemblage: collection devices, standards, databases, analytical tools, organizational objectives and institutional practices together determine how data are produced. This supplies the infrastructural component that can easily become abstract in Rouvroy's theory: data behaviourism does not confront naturally existing data, but objects that have been selected, cleaned, formatted and institutionalized. Through Kitchin's The Data Revolution: Big Data, Open Data, Data Infrastructures and Their Consequences, the "institutional chain linking quantification, data production and algorithmic systems" can be transformed from a rhetorical proposition into institutional analysis. Transparency is not the single solution to automated governance. Kitchin's analysis of data infrastructure prevents "big data" from being imagined as self-existing, like a natural resource. Data become usable objects only through collection protocols, database structures, cleaning standards, metadata and institutional objectives. "Data-driven" decisions therefore involve selection and exclusion from the outset; understanding model outputs requires tracing backward how data are produced, classified and maintained. Kitchin also distinguishes data openness from data power. Data can be technically open yet genuinely usable by only a few actors because of formats, computing resources, expertise and institutional permissions. The politics of open data thus cannot end with publishing files: it must address who has the capacity to analyse, link and turn data into resources for decision-making. Data infrastructure is itself a mechanism for distributing unequal capacities. Its governance also includes compatibility between standards and long-term maintenance. Whether different institutions can understand and reuse data often depends on metadata, formats and continual updating; this low-visibility work determines whether so-called "data assets" can exist at all.]

  12. Rieder, Bernhard. Engines of Order: A Mechanology of Algorithmic Techniques. Amsterdam University Press, 2020. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on ranking, recommendation, and algorithmic techniques).

    [Note: Rieder's mechanological approach shifts attention from the excessively broad noun "algorithm" to specific technical mechanisms—ranking, recommendation, classification—and their histories. Read after Bucher, it trains a finer-grained mode of critique: different algorithmic techniques have different inputs, objective functions, evaluation methods and organizational uses, and cannot all be described as a single omnipresent "algorithmic power." Transparency is not a single solution either. Transparency is not the single solution to automated governance. Rieder's fine-grained method is particularly useful for resisting the overgeneralization of "algorithm." Ranking, classification and recommendation have distinct problem formulations, technical traditions and evaluation metrics, and their power effects within organizations differ as well. Only by matching model types with specific institutional uses can algorithmic critique move from grand diagnosis to verifiable analysis of mechanisms. Mechanology also requires returning algorithmic techniques to genealogies of tools, rather than following only the latest models. Ranking, matching, clustering and recommendation all have longer histories and have produced different bodies of engineering common sense. Understanding technical genealogies helps distinguish governance effects arising from machine learning's new capabilities from those that actually derive from earlier information retrieval, statistical classification or database management. Such technical disaggregation also supplies more precise objects for governance: different mechanisms of ranking, matching and classification should face different requirements for transparency, auditing and responsibility. Rieder's emphasis on algorithmic techniques can also change auditing methods. Instead of requiring an abstract "algorithm" to be transparent as a whole, we can separately examine input data, ranking functions, feedback signals and organizational objectives. This disaggregation links responsibility to specific stages and frees critique from a binary choice between "black boxes are unknowable" and "releasing the code solves everything."]

Part II: Extraction, Coloniality and Infrastructure (Weeks 3–4)

Session 3: Surveillance, Extraction and Data Coloniality

This session further situates algorithmic governance within data production, resource extraction, and historical inequality. Zuboff's surveillance capitalism emphasizes how behavioral data become predictive assets; Couldry and Mejias's data colonialism places data relations within a longer history of colonial appropriation. Starting from the historical continuity of slavery, racialized identification, and surveillance technologies, Browne reveals how systems of classification embed differentiated visibility and exposure. These accounts are not equivalent: capital accumulation, colonial appropriation, racialized governance, and biopolitics have distinct historical mechanisms. Juxtaposing these concepts means testing what each can explain about the data economy and when an overextended analogy obscures differences.

Data extraction is not simply an exchange occurring after "user consent," either. Through identity systems, defaults, tracking infrastructure, advertising markets, data brokers, and network effects, platforms continually convert everyday actions into records that can be stored, linked, and used for prediction. Groups bear unequal risks when they are recorded, identified, or excluded; classifications in biometrics, credit scoring, targeted advertising, and public administration bring existing social differences into technical processes. Noble, Benjamin, Magnet, Dencik, and others approach these problems through information retrieval, racial technologies, identification, and data justice. "Data bias" consequently becomes more than model error: it is part of social classification, resource allocation, and relations of power.

Mbembe is not used here to produce facile analogies such as "account suspension equals digital death." He supplies a political context for understanding coloniality, enmity, borders, and differentiated exposure. An analysis of data coloniality holds only where compulsory dependence, relations of appropriation, epistemic authority, legal asymmetry, and exit costs can be specified. This session therefore does not seek the most dramatic historical name for digital society. It clarifies how datafication connects observation, extraction, classification, and governance, and how these mechanisms inherit or reorganize earlier structures of power in different institutional settings.

Required Readings:

  1. Zuboff, Shoshana. The Age of Surveillance Capitalism. PublicAffairs, 2019. (Read: Chapter 3, "The Discovery of Behavioral Surplus," pp. 63–96).

    [Note: Zuboff's concept of "behavioral surplus" connects data governance with capital accumulation. Focus on how she distinguishes user behavior, data extraction, prediction products, and commercialization. We must therefore test whether this model applies to the entire digital economy or chiefly explains the extractive mechanisms of Google and advertising platforms. Chapter 3 requires unpacking the whole argumentative chain of behavioral surplus: users leave behavioral traces in obtaining services; firms turn data exceeding the immediate needs of service improvement into additional inputs; computation then produces products predicting future behavior. What needs testing is whether this chain generalizes beyond advertising platforms and whether surveillance capitalism flattens differences among states, finance, logistics, and nonadvertising platforms. Read Zuboff as a strong model rather than a general theory of the digital economy: in which industries is it most explanatory, and where must platform capitalism, data colonialism, or administrative automation supplement it? A valid conceptual transfer must specify mechanisms such as coercion, ownership, spatial control, hierarchies of knowledge, or resource flows, while acknowledging important differences between classical colonial rule and platform data relations. Zuboff's behavioral surplus brings user activity, data extraction, and prediction markets into one process of capital accumulation. Its theoretical ambition extends far beyond online advertising, generating debate over whether surveillance capitalism has been overgeneralized. The most productive reading distinguishes businesses genuinely dependent on behavioral prediction from platforms whose revenues come chiefly from infrastructure rents, transaction commissions, or monopoly pricing, rather than fitting the entire digital economy into the concept.]

  2. Couldry, Nick, and Ulises A. Mejias. The Costs of Connection. Stanford University Press, 2019. (Read: Chapter 2, "Cloud Empire," pp. 37–68; Chapter 3, "The Coloniality of Data Relations"; Chapter 5, pp. 167–208).

    [Note: Couldry and Mejias use data colonialism to describe the ongoing conversion of social life into extractable data. "Cloud Empire" particularly suits this session because it connects clouds, platforms, data extraction, and social relations. The central questions are whether data colonialism can provide a historical framework for cloud infrastructure and where this framework may overextend the analogy with classical colonialism. The authors place data relations within a longer history of colonial resource appropriation, stressing the continuous translation of social life itself into commercially usable data flows. "Cloud empire" names the infrastructure and corporate power supporting this relation. We cannot merely seize on the forceful word "colonialism": we must closely read how the analogy is built through the appropriation of social life, the normalization of data extraction, and a new social order. Alongside Browne, ask whether a generalized colonial model centered solely on extraction overlooks historical differences, given coloniality's enduring entanglement with racialization, territorial appropriation, and violent rule. Surveillance has no single central agent. National security, advertising, employer management, financial risk control, and social platforms may share data and technologies, yet have different legal mandates and interests; one concept of surveillance capitalism must not erase these institutional differences. Describing data relations as a new form of colonial appropriation emphasizes how everyday life itself continually becomes an extractable resource. The concept's strength is connecting capital accumulation and relations of subjectivity; its risk is flattening historical colonialism's differences of violence, territory, and race. A valid comparison therefore specifies mechanisms of appropriation, resource flows, and structures of dependence rather than borrowing only the moral force of "colonial."]

  3. Browne, Simone. Dark Matters: On the Surveillance of Blackness. Duke University Press, 2015. (Read: Introduction; Chapters 1–2).

    [Note: Browne extends the historical depth of surveillance studies into slavery, racialized identification, and the continuous management of Black bodies, resisting accounts of digital surveillance as an entirely new problem that suddenly arrived with the internet. Her claim is not that all surveillance is alike, but that modern identification, border management, and regimes of visibility inherit and reorganize earlier technologies of racialized rule. Between Zuboff and data colonialism, this raises the question of whether explanations centered on commercial extraction adequately account for historical differences in surveillance power. Being seen and being datafied are also distinct. Many governing systems derive their power precisely from invisible backend classification and inference; critique must therefore investigate classificatory opportunities, risk distribution, and epistemic authority as well as privacy exposure. In Browne's Dark Matters: On the Surveillance of Blackness, the analytical gains and nonnegotiable historical limits of colonial analogy are consequently more than conceptual questions. The politics of extraction arise from asymmetry: some actors control collection, linkage, inference, and reuse, while others appear chiefly as those recorded, classified, and predicted. Privacy is only one layer; property rights, epistemic authority, and conditions of exit are equally important. Browne also forces surveillance history to revisit the historical continuity of race and the body. Biometrics, border checks, and database classifications seem to rely on new technologies, but who must be identified, who counts as a risk, and who must prove their identity have never been technically neutral arrangements. The history of digital surveillance must therefore trace the longer institutional genealogy of visibility and racialized rule rather than begin with internet firms. Browne's dark sousveillance also preserves resistance: monitored people do not merely accept surveillance but develop practices of counteridentification, counterrecording, and recoding visibility. Surveillance history is thus not only the history of expanding power but also that of classified subjects continually disrupting classification—a crucial point for research on digital identity and biometrics.]

  4. Mbembe, Achille. Necropolitics. Translated by Steven Corcoran. Duke University Press, 2019. Originally published in French as Politiques de l'inimitié in 2016. (Read: Introduction; "Necropolitics"; selected chapters on enmity, borders, and exposure).

    [Note: Mbembe's necropolitics concerns sovereignty, war, coloniality, and the political conditions under which lives are differentially exposed to death and injury. Applied to digital and intelligent technologies, it must never simply rename account bans, downranking, or platform exclusion "digital death": such analogies weaken the concept's historical force and obscure actual relations of violence. A more rigorous transfer asks how datafied borders, automated risk judgments, militarized surveillance, and resource allocation help produce different degrees of exposure, vulnerability, and freedom of action. Further questions concern who determines data standards, servers, models, and research agendas, and whether researched communities can exit, refuse, revise, and govern jointly. In the context of this session, Mbembe's Necropolitics gives a more concrete structure to the question of bringing data justice, epistemic authority, and differentiated exposure into one research framework. Extraction is political because relations are asymmetric: some actors control collection, linkage, inference, and reuse, while others appear chiefly as recorded, classified, and predicted subjects. Privacy is one layer; property rights, epistemic authority, and exit conditions matter equally. Necropolitics examines how sovereignty organizes life through exposure to death, warlike spaces, and differentiated conditions of survival; its historical background far exceeds digital governance. Within data coloniality, the theory should not inflate account bans or downranking into "digital death," but investigate when digital infrastructures enter borders, policing, war, or resource allocation and connect with actual biopolitics and necropolitics. Mbembe is therefore most useful here for calibrating scale. Datafied governance enters a necropolitical problem space only when linked to closed borders, military strikes, policing risks, or unequal distributions of basic resources. Retaining the concept in this intensive biopolitical context prevents digital critique from borrowing the rhetoric of death at the cost of historical weight.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Benjamin, Ruha. Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code. Polity, 2019. (Read: Introduction and Chapter 1).

    [Note: This connects algorithms with racialized power, supplementing Noble's approach through information retrieval. It reminds us that general intellect is not an undifferentiated "common human resource": whose knowledge, languages, and embodied experience most readily become training data is itself political. Theoretical resemblance does not automatically establish institutional identity. Benjamin's Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code therefore explains the historical relations among extraction, surveillance, racialized classification, and coloniality only insofar as corresponding institutional mechanisms can be identified empirically. The "New Jim Code" makes technological neutrality itself an object of critique: inequality need not appear as explicit discriminatory rules but may persist through apparently objective efficiency, optimization, and risk management. Benjamin accordingly situates algorithms within existing structures of housing, education, policing, and employment; technology's social consequences depend on the institutional histories it enters. Abolitionist tools also differ from mere fairness repairs. The question is not how existing systems can operate more evenly across groups, but whether some systems inherently serve unequal classification and punishment. Technological governance thus involves improving models and more fundamental institutional choices: which judgments should never be delegated to automation? Benjamin's abolitionist orientation is particularly useful in distinguishing technological reform from institutional reform. Even if a predictive system achieves statistical fairness across groups, fairness metrics cannot answer the deeper question of legitimacy when the system's purpose is to expand punishment, exclusion, or overpolicing. Technology ethics must therefore preserve the institutional negation that asks whether the system should exist at all.]

  2. Noble, Safiya Umoja. Algorithms of Oppression. NYU Press, 2018. (Read: Introduction, pp. 1–14).

    [Note: Noble shows that algorithmic ranking does not operate in a vacuum: it amplifies existing social prejudices. Unlike Crawford's data/labor perspective, it emphasizes classification and the politics of representation in information environments. Surveillance has no single central agent. Noble's Algorithms of Oppression offers not a final name for the mechanisms through which commercial datafication and state governance coexist rather than replace one another, but a theoretical opening testable against competing explanations; this openness is itself part of its research value. The central contribution of Noble's Algorithms of Oppression is not merely demonstrating biased search results. It shows how commercial ranking, advertising logic, and social representation jointly shape "relevance." Search becomes a site where cultural classification and market incentives overlap; racialized representation is not simply a data error. Through search engines, Noble shows how commercial ranking can repackage racial and gender prejudice as the "most relevant" results. Search is no neutral mirror of public knowledge: advertising markets, content ecologies, and platform design shape its classifications. Representation is therefore more than a cultural issue; when search becomes an entry point for understanding groups and social facts, ranking power also becomes epistemic power. Noble's cases further reveal infrastructure's cumulative effects. Search results respond to existing content while influencing subsequent clicks, content production, and public understanding, reinforcing certain associations. Using past behavior as a relevance signal can technologize prejudice through feedback loops. Algorithmic ranking both processes information and produces future information environments. The politics of search also concern epistemic authority. Once a platform organizes vast information algorithmically, users can easily take what appears first as the world's own natural ordering. Noble reveals this naturalization through the interface: technical ranking gives commercial and social biases the appearance of objectivity, making them harder to recognize as institutional choices.]

  3. Lyon, David. Surveillance Studies: An Overview. Polity, 2007. (Read: Introduction; chapters on surveillance as social sorting).

    [Note: Lyon gives surveillance studies a conceptual framework broader than "being seen," emphasizing surveillance as an institutional process of collecting information, classification, and social sorting. This is a useful foundation because platforms, states, and commercial databases often need not watch individuals continuously: they allocate opportunities through categories of identity, risk, consumption, and eligibility. Being seen and being datafied are distinct. Through Lyon's Surveillance Studies: An Overview, the analytical gains and nonnegotiable historical limits of colonial analogy enter organizational and institutional analysis. At the scale of Lyon's Surveillance Studies: An Overview, those gains and limits require attention to continuity and transformation together: old institutions acquire new operations through new technologies, while new technologies may also be reabsorbed into existing institutions. The value of Lyon's Surveillance Studies: An Overview is understanding surveillance as a relation of social organization rather than a single device. Identification, classification, visibility, and institutional purposes together determine surveillance's forms, furnishing a basis for comparing commercial platforms, state administration, and security systems. Lyon treats surveillance as social classification and organizational practice rather than mere "watching." Modern surveillance uses identity records, databases, and risk categories to allocate different treatment and rights of movement. Digital technology extends this capacity while continuing surveillance's long alliance with administrative organization. Situating surveillance studies within this sociological tradition helps avoid technocentric narratives confined to cameras, platforms, or privacy.]

  4. Andrejevic, Mark. Automated Media. Routledge, 2020. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on automation, surveillance, and decision systems).

    [Note: Andrejevic examines how automated media increasingly delegate perception, analysis, and response to data-intensive systems. The point is not to announce human replacement by machines, but to analyze how institutions expand monitoring beyond human processing capacity and manage information environments through automated correlations and predictions. Reading this alongside Zuboff distinguishes more carefully the relations among accumulation, media automation, and governing capacity. The question of bringing data justice, epistemic authority, and differentiated exposure into one framework, raised by Andrejevic's Automated Media, exceeds an internal conceptual debate. It therefore remains subject to empirical evidence and competing explanations beyond Andrejevic's Automated Media. Automated media's central problem is consequently not machine autonomy, but which judgments cease to receive public explanation when perception–analysis–response chains are compressed. Large-scale automation greatly expands monitoring and response, yet can distance the grounds of decisions from those affected. Andrejevic emphasizes precisely this politics of scale: automation changes how much institutions can see, how quickly they process it, and under what conditions they act. Automated media also alter political action's timescale. Systems flag, block, or recommend before humans understand; institutions may increasingly rely on machines reacting first and explanations arriving later. Speed becomes a resource of power: organizations that process enormous signal volumes in real time have a structural advantage over individuals who can only appeal afterward. The politics of automation must analyze this temporal asymmetry too. Once speed combines with institutional coercion, new procedural problems arise: flags occur instantly, while explanation and correction take a long time. Asymmetrical appeal costs thus become a significant measure of automated governance.]

  5. Turow, Joseph. The Daily You: How the New Advertising Industry Is Defining Your Identity and Your Worth. Yale University Press, 2011. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on behavioral targeting and audience classification).

    [Note: Beginning with organizational changes in advertising, Turow traces how audiences are segmented, valued, and continually targeted. This supplies an important industrial history for surveillance capitalism: extraction was not invented in a vacuum but connects with advertising markets, audience measurement, customer relationship management, and differential pricing. "Identity" here is primarily a commercial classification, not necessarily subjective self-identification. At the analytical scale of Turow's The Daily You: How the New Advertising Industry Is Defining Your Identity and Your Worth, the historical relations among extraction, surveillance, racialized classification, and coloniality first appear as concrete relationships. This industry's history also shows that data's value does not naturally reside in individual behavior: it is produced through market categories and tradable audience imaginaries. "High-value users," "customers likely to churn," and "high-risk populations" are categories organizations construct for specific purposes. Individualized marketing and social stratification may therefore reinforce one another on the same infrastructure rather than constitute independent processes. Turow's industrial history reveals personalization's other face: finer segmentation enables more differentiated treatment. Personalized recommendations not only improve matching efficiency but can allocate different prices, discounts, and information environments to different consumers. The boundary between commercial classification and stratified opportunity becomes blurred, giving advertising technology broader effects of social sorting. Advertising technology allocates not just product information but the attention and discounts businesses consider worth investing in, so commercial valuation directly participates in social differentiation.]

  6. van Dijck, José. "Datafication, Dataism and Dataveillance: Big Data between Scientific Paradigm and Ideology" Surveillance & Society 12, no. 2 (2014): 197–208. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Van Dijck distinguishes datafication, dataism, and dataveillance, helping us see "everything can become data" as both technical practice and cultural ideology with epistemological commitments. Data do not automatically possess the status of truth; platforms' and research institutions' trust in large-scale behavioral data itself requires explanation. This illuminates Rouvroy's governance through correlation, but here the emphasis is on the knowledge-cultural conditions legitimizing extraction. Van Dijck's "Datafication, Dataism and Dataveillance: Big Data between Scientific Paradigm and Ideology," Turow's The Daily You: How the New Advertising Industry Is Defining Your Identity and Your Worth, and D'Ignazio's Data Feminism place the coexistence rather than mutual displacement of commercial datafication and state governance within different intellectual traditions. Surveillance has no single central agent. Van Dijck's article releases these mechanisms from overly abstract diagnoses of an era. Dataism matters because it elevates datafication from a technical operation into an epistemological belief: if records are comprehensive enough and computation complex enough, social behavior seemingly becomes directly apprehensible. Critiquing this belief supplies algorithmic governance with a necessary epistemological dimension. Data volume cannot replace conceptual choices; correlation cannot itself answer questions of causality, meaning, or legitimacy.]

  7. D'Ignazio, Catherine, and Lauren F. Klein. Data Feminism. MIT Press, 2020. (Read: Introduction; Chapters 1–3).

    [Note: D'Ignazio and Klein place data practices within feminist intersectional analysis, emphasizing power, context, embodiment, and omitted experience. Rather than a generic AI fairness manual, this asks researchers who defines datasets, who is recorded, who is absent, and who bears classification's consequences. Alongside Browne, Benjamin, and Noble, it moves critique from system bias to the politics of data production itself. Being seen and being datafied are distinct. Through D'Ignazio's Data Feminism, the analytical gains and nonnegotiable historical limits of colonial analogy can be separated into interrelated elements. From D'Ignazio's Data Feminism, those gains and limits cannot stand apart from institutional authorization and resource distribution: technical forms produce durable social consequences only when combined with organizational power. Data Feminism embeds power analysis directly in data practices. From posing questions through classification and visualization to interpretation, it tracks who is represented, who is omitted, and who bears consequences. More data on women or minorities are not a sufficient answer; existing power structures and binary classifications must be challenged. Data justice therefore concerns not just correcting bias but redesigning knowledge production's purposes and participatory relations. Data Feminism particularly emphasizes context and pluralism. Detached from collection contexts, datasets readily abstract particular social relations into natural facts, while plural epistemic positions expose this abstraction's costs. Democratizing data practice thus entails more than open downloads: it includes documenting provenance, retaining uncertainty, and involving affected groups in defining problems.]

  8. Birhane, Abeba. "Algorithmic Colonization of Africa" SCRIPTed 17, no. 2 (2020). (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Birhane uses algorithmic colonization to describe asymmetrical power reproduced when digital technologies enter African societies through universalist, developmentalist, and efficiency discourses. Outside actors often control technology, capital, data, and standards, while affected communities become deployment sites or data sources. This speaks directly to Couldry and Mejias's data colonialism and insists that "colonial" must be demonstrated through specific ownership, epistemic authority, and institutional dependence, not merely used rhetorically. Birhane's "Algorithmic Colonization of Africa," D'Ignazio's Data Feminism, and Ricaurte's "Data Epistemologies, the Coloniality of Power, and Resistance" move the integration of data justice, epistemic authority, and differentiated exposure from macro-level judgment to mechanisms. Birhane's contribution is precisely to bring that broad judgment back to identifiable institutional mechanisms. Her article also resituates the question historically: similar digital appearances need not have identical mechanisms, and conceptual validity depends on preserving differences. Birhane returns "colonial" from metaphor to institutional relations: who designs models, cloud services, and standards, who defines knowledge needs, and where technological gains flow are concrete grounds for assessing coloniality. Algorithmic colonization then describes not all transnational technological circulation but persistent asymmetrical dependence and its erosion of local knowledge, autonomy, and public capacity.]

  9. Ricaurte, Paola. "Data Epistemologies, the Coloniality of Power, and Resistance" Television & New Media 20, no. 4 (2019). (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Ricaurte connects datafication to the coloniality of power, emphasizing knowledge production as well as resource extraction: what can be known, how it is classified, and who may define data results as social reality. This moves data colonialism beyond an economic metaphor toward epistemic authority and importantly introduces Latin American decolonial theory into data studies. Ricaurte's "Data Epistemologies, the Coloniality of Power, and Resistance" gives clearer causal layers to the historical relations among extraction, surveillance, racialized classification, and coloniality. She further situates data within knowledge production's coloniality: not all worlds are datafied alike, and not all forms of knowledge enter databases and models without loss. Choosing categories, variables, and measurable objects already embeds epistemological politics within infrastructure. Resistance therefore concerns not only privacy or property, but who may determine what counts as knowledge. This critique also concerns data sovereignty. If local communities supply only raw data while outside institutions monopolize categories, model design, and interpretation, knowledge production reproduces a center–periphery structure. Decolonization must redistribute power over research agendas, infrastructure, and interpretation, not merely add representative data. Data decolonization accordingly includes infrastructure: epistemic autonomy remains limited when computing, storage, and modeling depend on external actors. Data infrastructure itself becomes contested terrain for knowledge politics and decolonial practice. Rights over knowledge and infrastructure cannot be cleanly separated here.]

  10. Magnet, Shoshana Amielle. When Biometrics Fail: Gender, Race, and the Technology of Identity. Duke University Press, 2011. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on fingerprinting, facial recognition, and biometric failure).

    [Note: Through biometrics, Magnet shows how supposedly objective identity depends on databases, sensors, thresholds, and existing social classifications. Failure is more than an engineering error: it is distributed unevenly across bodies and may recode race, gender, and nationality as problems of identification. This supplies a highly concrete technical object for broader surveillance/data coloniality analyses. Surveillance has no single central agent. Biometrics particularly clearly reveal a loop between categories and bodies: systems train and validate against existing demographic categories, then return those categories to borders, security, and identity regimes as technical identification. Failure rates are not merely engineering defects; when identification carries compulsory consequences, errors are distributed unevenly along existing social differences. Magnet emphasizes that failure is no accidental event outside the system. When biometrics are declared objective, automatic, and universal, institutions treat misidentification as individual abnormality rather than a classificatory problem. Technical failure is thus politically distributed: some bodies must bear greater costs of verification, suspicion, and proving themselves. Accuracy must be assessed alongside these unequal consequences. Political assessment must relate error rates to the consequences of error, since the same statistical error imposes entirely different social costs in different identity regimes. Technical precision and institutional justice cannot be unrelated evaluative dimensions. In identity cards, borders, or welfare systems, biometric failure is not merely a user-experience issue: it can affect movement, access to resources, and the ability to prove legal status. Technical performance must therefore be linked to institutional consequences: the same misidentification rate has entirely different political weight in entertainment applications and compulsory identity systems.]

  11. Mejias, Ulises A., and Nick Couldry. Data Grab: The New Colonialism of Big Tech and How to Fight Back. University of Chicago Press, 2024. (Read: Introduction; chapters on data territories, colonialism, and resistance).

    [Note: This book continues and updates the authors' data colonialism argument, placing the ongoing datafication of everyday life and large technology firms' infrastructure expansion within colonial relations' long history. Compared with 2019's The Costs of Connection, it more explicitly addresses contemporary Big Tech and resistance strategies. It therefore works as subsequent debate within the same session rather than assigning two books the same function in separate sessions. Focus on colonial analogy's analytical gains and historical limits. Being seen and being datafied are distinct. Mejias's Data Grab: The New Colonialism of Big Tech and How to Fight Back turns those gains and nonnegotiable limits from a rhetorical proposition into institutional analysis. Data Grab continues the data colonialism framework but concentrates on Big Tech's conversion of connectivity, convenience, and infrastructure into continuing data appropriation. Its policy significance is shifting the problem from individual privacy choices to collective data relations: when leaving major platforms means losing work, social, or public-service opportunities, consent can hardly bear the entire burden of legitimacy. Resistance must therefore involve institutional restrictions and public alternatives. Mejias and Couldry further stress that the data grab does not depend on one-off coercive appropriation: it continues once connectivity becomes a condition of life. The harder platforms become to leave, the easier extraction becomes to package as a natural condition of service exchange. The institutional question then becomes whether data minimization, collective rights, and public infrastructure can make social participation cease to require unlimited surrender of data.]

  12. Taylor, Linnet. "What Is Data Justice? The Case for Connecting Digital Rights and Freedoms Globally" Big Data & Society 4, no. 2 (2017). (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Taylor proposes data justice to connect privacy and data protection with wider social justice. It helps shift critique into normative questions: if datafication produces inequalities of visibility, representation, resource allocation, and agency, institutional evaluation cannot focus solely on individual consent. It can close this session by converting diagnoses of surveillance and coloniality into an agenda on rights, capabilities, and global inequality. Data justice extends digital rights beyond individual privacy to structural distribution. Who accesses data, who can refuse datafication, who bears automated errors, and who benefits from the data economy cannot be resolved by consent alone. Taylor connects governance with social justice while preserving institutional differences for cross-national comparison. Locating data justice within global digital rights avoids universalizing European and North American privacy-law experiences. Countries connect infrastructure differently to social protection, identity regimes, and development policy, giving digital rights different urgencies. Transnational justice must address both individual freedom and resource allocation rather than replicate one legal paradigm.
