Data justice's unit of analysis is therefore not merely an individual data subject, but data relations constituted by states, platforms, communities, and infrastructure. It also connects usually separate policy domains: privacy concerns control over data, antidiscrimination concerns classification's consequences, and development justice concerns the distribution of infrastructure and capabilities. Taylor brings these into one normative space and reminds us not to assume an individual consumer with ample choices as the default subject of digital rights.]

Session 4: Planetary Computation and Infrastructure Space

This session returns the "cloud" to land, energy, chips, data centers, submarine cables, satellites, spectrum, cities, and legal arrangements. Bratton's The Stack describes planetary computation as a layered architecture; Easterling's Extrastatecraft analyzes how infrastructure space produces quasi-governing effects through standards, logistics, and spatial formats. Star reminds us that infrastructure usually recedes into the background when working smoothly and reappears through breakdown, conflict, or exclusion. Platform power therefore resides not just in interfaces, algorithms, and business models, but in conditions of connection, material resources, and maintenance systems.

Infrastructuralization also changes the relation between authority and territory. Sassen's reassemblage of territory, authority, and rights, Graham and Marvin's differentiated urban networks, and Plantin and colleagues' encounter between platform and infrastructure studies all show the increasingly unstable boundary between platforms and infrastructures. Through APIs, cloud services, identity systems, and payment interfaces, some platforms become underlying conditions other organizations cannot easily bypass. Traditional infrastructures, meanwhile, increasingly adopt platform logics of datafication, service provision, and tiered access. The political question is not whether platforms simply replace states, but how different authorities are redistributed through networks spanning multiple scales.

Varoufakis and Durand's technofeudalism theses become testable only against this infrastructural background. Whether cloud capital, intangible assets, platform gateways, rents, and exit barriers constitute dependencies distinct from traditional capital–labor relations requires point-by-point comparison with platform capitalism, monopoly capitalism, and rent theory. Critics such as Morozov are important precisely because they force the concept to specify its additional explanatory value. If "feudalism" merely renames monopoly, rent, and market power, its theoretical necessity is limited. If platform control of infrastructural conditions genuinely changes market entry, ownership, and dependence, the institutional levels at which this change occurs must be specified.

Required Readings:

  1. Bratton, Benjamin H. The Stack: On Software and Sovereignty. 10th anniversary ed., with a new preface by the author. MIT Press, 2026. Originally published 2016. (Read: new preface; "The Nomos of the Cloud"; "Platform and Stack, Model and Machine"; "Cloud Layer").

    [Note: Bratton's stack is not simply a theory of the cloud-computing state. "Nomos of the Cloud" examines planetary computation's challenge to political geography; "Platform and Stack" explains how computational architecture becomes a political model; "Cloud Layer" situates data centers, platforms, infrastructure, and state governance in one architecture. Rather than directly calling Google or Amazon states, closely examine how sovereignty is distributed across layers and organizations. Use MIT Press's 2026 tenth-anniversary edition: revisit the original architectural account of planetary-scale computation, then use the new preface to test its validity and blind spots a decade later. The six-layer model is illuminating not because reality neatly divides into Earth, Cloud, City, Address, Interface, and User, but because it traces relations across layers: how energy and minerals support the cloud, how addressing brings objects into a computable order, how interfaces present institutional rules as actionable choices, and how a user may be a person, organization, sensor, or machine agent. It is a model of models, not an empirical map. The 2026 edition invites the question of which changes in sovereignty, cloud platforms, AI agents, and geopolitics strengthen the stack and which require revising its hierarchical imagination. The Stack offers a cross-scalar architectural language: its six layers are not merely technical but analytical slices of computation's reorganization of territory, identity, and sovereignty. Its advantage is placing data centers, cities, and interfaces within a single planetary system; its risk is that architectural abstraction obscures regional differences. Use it as a comparative framework rather than a complete world map.]

  2. Easterling, Keller. Extrastatecraft: The Power of Infrastructure Space. Verso, 2014. (Read: Chapter 2, "Zone: The Infrastructure Commons," pp. 25–70).

    [Note: Easterling is not simply saying special zones are lawless spaces. She examines how infrastructure space, through spatial products, protocols, standards, logistics, and institutional arrangements, generates governing effects beyond traditional state planning. Applied to digital platforms, the analogy needs limits: Amazon's cloud and a free-trade zone are different spaces, although both show rules operating through infrastructure and standards rather than conventional legal texts. Calling platforms states, empires, or territories requires care. Free-trade zones and clouds are comparable only at the level of infrastructural regulation; their legal status, spatial structures, and economic relations must be treated separately. Infrastructure space is political precisely because it organizes conduct through technical specifications, spatial templates, and operational standards rather than always through explicit legal commands. Zones, logistics networks, and data centers are not vacuums outside the state; state policy, private capital, and transnational standards often produce them together. Easterling supplies a spatial language for analyzing quasi-governing effects. More importantly, infrastructure space frequently works through replication. Packaged as a standardized spatial product, a zone, industrial park, or logistics model spreads between regions carrying predetermined governing logics. APIs, cloud architectures, and service terms share this replicability, but their spatial and legal mechanisms differ. Comparison should remain at the level of rules spreading with infrastructure. This spatial politics shows how infrastructural power acts through default environments: once rules are embedded in spaces and systems, they are harder to identify than explicit commands. The core is not being outside law but how rules gain lasting force in spatial, standardized, and operational forms.]

  3. Star, Susan Leigh. "The Ethnography of Infrastructure" American Behavioral Scientist 43, no. 3 (1999): 377–391.

    [Note: Star provides this session's indispensable methodological foundation. Infrastructure is hard to see because it becomes work and life's background; breakdown, conflict, or exclusion suddenly makes it visible. Studying clouds therefore requires investigating electricity, networks, server rooms, maintenance labor, and standards, not just interfaces and software. If existing theories of capitalism adequately explain rents, network effects, and monopoly, "feudal" is rhetoric; if there are new dependencies, gateway controls, and nonmarket allocations, explain why they require a new concept of social formation. In Star's "The Ethnography of Infrastructure," the political-economic distinctions among rent, profit, gateway control, and exit costs thus exceed conceptual questions. Star also places maintenance, repair, and exceptional experiences at the center. For most users, stable infrastructure recedes into the background; for maintainers, excluded people, and users encountering failures, it remains visible. Social differences are often clearest in disconnection, service suspension, incompatibility, or denied permissions. Infrastructure's relationality also means one system does not become background identically for all. Stable broadband may be invisible to urban middle classes but remain an explicit constraint for remote communities, disabled users, or maintenance workers. Star's ethnography inherently attends to difference: whose infrastructure is it? The maintenance perspective also changes innovation narratives. Reliability often depends on long-term, repetitive, low-visibility repair work rather than original design alone. Failure logs and maintenance sites often reveal actual power relations better than promotional materials.]

  4. Plantin, Jean-Christophe, Carl Lagoze, Paul N. Edwards, and Christian Sandvig. "Infrastructure Studies Meet Platform Studies in the Age of Google and Facebook" New Media & Society 20, no. 1 (2018): 293–310.

    [Note: This article almost serves as the session's methodological manifesto: platforms and infrastructures can no longer be fully separated, since platforms acquire infrastructural properties while platform logics reorganize traditional infrastructures. It connects Star with Bratton and makes the cloud a form of social organization rather than merely a technical layer. Planetary-scale concepts can make particular places disappear. Macro models explain only when grounded in nodes—minerals, chips, data centers, cables, cities, labor, or jurisdictions—and when they test whether regions bear symmetrical costs. In the session's context, Plantin's "Infrastructure Studies Meet Platform Studies in the Age of Google and Facebook" gives the tension between planetary models and particular places, labor, and maintenance a concrete structure. The infrastructuralization of platforms and platformization of infrastructures captures Google's and Facebook's movement from optional services to nodes of social dependence. Once platforms become infrastructural, stability, universal access, and public responsibility become pressing; traditional infrastructures adopting platform logics may become datafied, commercialized, and organized through interfaces. Both changes blur public utilities and private platforms. This two-way transformation also rewrites public responsibility. Infrastructure is expected to be stable, universal, and available over the long term, while platform firms quickly change services, prices, and rules. When private platforms become unavoidable nodes for education, work, or public communication, corporate flexibility comes into conflict with infrastructural responsibility to society.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Sassen, Saskia. Territory, Authority, Rights: From Medieval to Global Assemblages. Princeton University Press, 2006. (Read: Chapter 7, "Digital Networks, Global Cities," pp. 323–377).

    [Note: Sassen's importance is that globalization does not simply make state sovereignty disappear: territory, authority, and rights are reassembled in transnational networks. This gives a more precise framework than the "platform state": different authorities coexist and overlap at particular spatial nodes. Digital infrastructure is therefore not naturally supranational space, but a site recombining old and new governing scales. Global assemblages undermine narratives of state withdrawal. Global digital networks need legal recognition, urban nodes, financial institutions, and cross-border rules; they can weaken some state capacities while reorganizing and strengthening others. Authority is reassembled across scales rather than simply transferred from states to platforms. Sassen also shows deterritorialization and reterritorialization often occurring together. Data flows seem to escape place, yet server siting, taxation, jurisdiction, and talent concentration anchor them anew in particular cities and countries. Global networks do not abolish space but reorder spatial relations across scales. Digital globalization thus recombines territory, authority, and rights within infrastructural networks rather than abolishing territory. Transnational digital networks always entail renewed concentration at nodes and competition among jurisdictions. The global is produced through particular places. Reorganizing authority also means firms and states are not in a zero-sum relation. States shape clouds through taxation, localization, and security policies; platforms use cross-border architectures to alter regulatory costs. Sassen's assemblage perspective analyzes this coproduction rather than reducing reality to who replaces whom.]

  2. Graham, Stephen, and Simon Marvin. Splintering Urbanism. Routledge, 2001. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–36).

    [Note: Differentiated urban infrastructure provision shows how networks produce spatial divisions. Alongside Easterling, it demonstrates that infrastructure need not produce publicness: prices, priorities, connections, and spatial choices can instead create service tiers. Calling platforms states, empires, or territories requires care. Splintering urbanism reveals that infrastructure has no inherently universalist direction. Networked services tier connectivity through prices, standards, and spatial investment, delivering speed, redundancy, and stability to high-value districts while peripheral areas suffer interruption and shortage. For digital infrastructure, this reveals connectivity itself as a new social difference. Fragmentation concerns not only access versus nonaccess, but connection quality, latency, bandwidth, reliability, and affordability. As infrastructure becomes a condition of work, education, and public services, technical differences become differences of opportunity. Infrastructure politics must exceed a single penetration-rate metric. Tiered connection quality eventually settles into tiered educational, employment, and participatory opportunities, making infrastructural equity explicitly distributive. Research must therefore examine service quality and spatial differences rather than merely count connections. Infrastructure differences ultimately become social opportunity differences. The distribution of quality connections, redundancy, and maintenance resources often reveals class and regional divisions in digital cities better than nominal access rates. Network equity must enter design and investment decisions. Splintering Urbanism also shows commercialization replacing universal-service logics with profitability. High-value users and areas gain priority investment; low-return spaces remain undermaintained. Digital networks relying wholly on similar commercial choices may further entrench existing urban class and regional divisions.]

  3. Mattern, Shannon. Code and Clay, Data and Dirt: Five Thousand Years of Urban Media. University of Minnesota Press, 2017. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on urban information infrastructures).

    [Note: Mattern extends urban media history across writing, maps, architecture, logistics, databases, and sensing systems, refusing to treat the smart city as a suddenly arriving digital revolution. Her key method juxtaposes code and clay, data and dirt: information infrastructures always depend on material carriers, spatial institutions, and maintenance labor. This provides Bratton's macro stack with a more historical, urban-scale correction. Through Mattern's Code and Clay, Data and Dirt: Five Thousand Years of Urban Media, the political-economic distinctions among rent, profit, gateway control, and exit costs enter organizational and institutional analysis. Mattern treats cities as media environments long constituted by writing, sound, masonry, maps, sensors, and databases, resisting smart-city accounts of digitization as sudden revolution. Urban computation must rest on existing roads, utility networks, administrative archives, and social memory. Digital infrastructure is therefore not an invisible network covering old cities, but something continually layered over and rubbing against historical material strata. Her long urban media history also resists data-city narratives that dismiss older infrastructure as obsolete background. Sensors depend on roads, databases inherit archival categories, and interfaces are constrained by architectural and administrative boundaries. Digitization is never a blank-slate redesign: it continually layers with existing materials, institutions, and histories. This perspective substantially reduces the sense of technological rupture in smart-city discourse. Mattern also expands media from screens to the city itself. Street signs, archives, building materials, and sensors jointly organize information; the smart city is another layer of this long history of mediation, not the first time the city becomes computable.]

  4. Hu, Tung-Hui. A Prehistory of the Cloud. MIT Press, 2015. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on cloud infrastructure, sovereignty, and labor).

    [Note: Through the cloud's prehistory, Hu dismantles language that imagines networks as placeless, frictionless space. Connecting clouds with earlier networks, military systems, mainframes, data centers, and labor relations, he shows the cloud as historically formed infrastructure and political imagination, not a natural technical layer. Alongside Bratton, compare architectural modeling and media archaeology as approaches to the same object. Planetary concepts can erase particular places. The tension between planetary models and specific sites, labor, and maintenance revealed by Hu's A Prehistory of the Cloud exceeds internal conceptual debate; it remains testable through empirical evidence and competing explanations beyond Hu's A Prehistory of the Cloud. Hu's A Prehistory of the Cloud confines that tension to particular objects and causal chains; analogies beyond this scope require new evidence, not terminology alone. Tracing the cloud metaphor's prehistory reveals how placelessness, weightlessness, and unlimited expansion obscure military, network, and data-center foundations. The cloud's virtuality is an interface effect, not a material fact. Concentrated data centers, dispersed terminals, and hierarchical network routes show that clouds create spatial abstractions while reorganizing concrete geographical dependencies. The metaphor also has political-psychological effects: users more readily understand storage and computation as natural environments rather than corporate infrastructure built and sold as services. Services seem as ubiquitous as air while depending on a few hyperscale operators. Hu's historicization exposes this naturalization as a cultural product of the technology industry.]

  5. Parks, Lisa. Cultures in Orbit: Satellites and the Televisual. Duke University Press, 2005. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on satellite infrastructures and global visibility).

    [Note: Parks extends media infrastructure into orbital space, examining how satellites connect ground, signals, images, and geopolitics. For planetary computation, this reminds us that "planetary" is not a rhetorical "global," but a vertical space composed of orbits, spectrum, ground stations, state licenses, and investment. Clouds also need locating in these material layers. At the scale of Parks's Cultures in Orbit: Satellites and the Televisual, the connection of clouds, platforms, and infrastructure with land, energy, standards, and sovereignty appears first as concrete relations. Technofeudalism must be compared with monopoly, rent, and platform capitalism. If "feudal" only renames market power, its explanatory gain is limited; if infrastructural control changes dependence, entry, and returns, identify the institutional levels involved. Satellite media bring infrastructure's vertical dimension into digital politics. Orbital positions, ground stations, spectrum allocation, and remote sensing jointly constitute communication conditions, so global coverage always depends on specific geopolitical arrangements. Parks turns planetary scale from macro rhetoric into traceable technical objects and resource competition. From satellite television to satellite internet, orbital infrastructure shows communication sovereignty's vertical space. State borders cannot fully explain signal coverage, yet launch capabilities, spectrum coordination, and ground reception remain institutionally controlled. Planetary computation's globality is concretely produced through scarce positions, technical licenses, and capital investment. Satellite networks thus show that global coverage does not abolish boundaries; boundaries extend from the ground into institutional arrangements for orbits, spectrum, and ground stations.]

  6. Lehdonvirta, Vili. Cloud Empires: How Digital Platforms Are Overtaking the State and How We Can Regain Control. MIT Press, 2022. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on platform governance and institutional power).

    [Note: Lehdonvirta compares large platforms as institutions capable of rulemaking, enforcement, and dispute resolution, asking why they assume some traditional governing functions in cross-border digital markets. "Overtaking the state" in the title is a proposition to test, not a factual description. Its value is distinguishing state sovereignty, private governance, market infrastructure, and user dependence rather than declaring platforms already to be states. Lehdonvirta's Cloud Empires: How Digital Platforms Are Overtaking the State and How We Can Regain Control, Parks's Cultures in Orbit: Satellites and the Televisual, and Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism place the two-way infrastructuralization of platforms and platformization of infrastructures in different intellectual traditions. Calling platforms states, empires, or territories requires care. Lehdonvirta's Cloud Empires: How Digital Platforms Are Overtaking the State and How We Can Regain Control frees this two-way process from overly abstract epochal judgments. Technofeudalism must be compared with monopoly, rent, and platform capitalism. If feudalism only renames market power, its explanatory gain is limited; if infrastructure control changes dependence, entry, and returns, identify the institutional levels involved. Describing platforms as empire-like governing structures concerns their powers of rulemaking, dispute resolution, identity management, and sanction, not a rhetorical analogy with states. Platform authority, unlike traditional states, derives from contracts and infrastructure dependence; it may reach across borders without territorial sovereignty. The comparison is most valuable in clarifying the sources and limits of different governing capacities.]

  7. Varoufakis, Yanis. Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism. Bodley Head, 2023. (Read: Chapter 3, "Cloud Capital," pp. 58–91; Chapter 4, "The Rise of the Cloudalists and the Demise of Profit," pp. 92–115; Chapter 7, "Escape from Technofeudalism," pp. 175–214).

    [Note: Varoufakis's central claim is that cloud capital changes the traditional relation of competition and profit, producing new dependencies through platform gateways, data, and cloud infrastructure. The useful question is not whether to accept the word technofeudalism, but whether it explains rents, network effects, monopoly, and user dependence. If monopoly capital and platform capitalism still explain them, what does feudalism add? Conversely, does it reveal power relations difficult to explain with traditional capital theory? Distinguish cloud capital from ordinary digital capital. The argument is not that large tech firms are feudal because they are large: platforms accumulate infrastructure that shapes behavior, organizes transactions, and extracts cloud rent from ecosystem participants, increasingly arranging markets inside private platforms. Read Chapters 3 and 4 together: the former defines cloud capital, the latter introduces cloudalists and changes in profit/rent relations. Chapter 7 shows the account must confront exit and political reorganization, not merely diagnose an era. Test whether Amazon Marketplace, app stores, and cloud services share this structure. The cloud-capital thesis argues platforms are no longer just firms in capitalist markets: cloud infrastructure and user behavior let them shape transaction environments and extract cloud rent from dependency. The crucial dispute is not whether "feudal" is striking, but whether relations among profit, rent, markets, and platform power have structurally changed. If conventional monopoly theory already explains these returns, technofeudalism's additional explanatory power must be demonstrated explicitly.]

  8. Durand, Cédric. How Silicon Valley Unleashed Techno-Feudalism: The Making of the Digital Economy. Translated by David Broder. Verso, 2024. Originally published as Technoféodalisme: Critique de l'économie numérique in 2020. (Read: Chapter 2, "On Digital Domination"; Chapter 3, "The Rentier Class of the Intangible"; Chapter 4, "The "Techno-Feudal" Hypothesis").

    [Note: Durand's structure particularly suits comparison with Varoufakis: Chapter 2 covers digital domination, Chapter 3 intangible assets and the rentier class, and only Chapter 4 systematically proposes the technofeudal hypothesis. Distinguish three levels: mechanisms of domination, forms of accumulation, and a hypothesis about social formation. Compare Marxist rent theory, monopoly capitalism, and platform capitalism rather than equating rent with feudal ground rent. Similar vocabulary conceals different paths: Durand emphasizes how digital domination, intangible assets, intellectual property, and rentier logics reorganize accumulation, placing technofeudalism at the boundary between capitalism's internal development and potential transformation of social form. Because Chapters 2–4 progress cumulatively, do not jump to the feudal hypothesis. Establish domination and intangible rent first, then ask whether these mechanisms warrant naming a social formation. Reading the books together is not a contest but a comparison of their criteria for feudalism. Durand's How Silicon Valley Unleashed Techno-Feudalism: The Making of the Digital Economy, Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism, and Thorhauge's The Economic Lives of Platforms: Rethinking the Political Economy of Digital Markets bring the scalar tension between planetary models and particular places, labor, and maintenance down from macro judgment to mechanisms. Planetary concepts can erase particular places. Durand's argument is best separated into three questions rather than accepted as an epochal name: how domination forms, how intangibles generate rents, and whether these changes amount to a new social formation. Feudalism then becomes a testable political-economic hypothesis, not a predetermined conclusion. Platform dependency, intellectual property, and monopoly rent must be analyzed separately.]

  9. Thorhauge, Anne Mette, Andreas Lindegaard Gregersen, Eva Iris Otto, Jacob Ørmen, and Morten Axel Pedersen, eds. The Economic Lives of Platforms: Rethinking the Political Economy of Digital Markets. Bristol University Press, 2024. (Read: "Rethinking the Political Economy of Digital Markets," pp. 1–16; "Modes of Connectivity," pp. 17–36).

    [Note: This collection provides finer-grained comparisons for the technofeudalism debate. Rather than begin with an overarching social formation, it examines how connectivity, market design, data, and mediation organize economic activity. After Varoufakis and Durand, it forces large terms such as cloud landlord and rent into researchable mechanisms: which gateways are controlled, how prices are set, how supply and demand are organized, and where exit costs actually occur. Platforms' economic lives exceed market intermediation. Connections, pricing, data accumulation, and rulemaking jointly determine value's creation and distribution, with significant differences across platform types. The collection moves political economy from a single business model to comparative analysis, preventing a few giant firms from standing for the whole platform economy. Connectivity modes also determine transaction entry, participants' statuses, and which relations become datafied. An economics confined to prices and network effects misses connections' institutional nature. Treating connection as designed relations reveals how market structures are written into technical interfaces. Platform political economy must study how interfaces institutionalize economic relations, not only seek power in financial statements or market shares. Connections themselves constitute institutional design, not just a precondition for transactions. This is an important distinction from ordinary market intermediaries. Defining eligibility, transaction units, and visible information already preorganizes market relations in interfaces. Platform power thus operates before market formation.]

  10. Mezzadra, Sandro, Niccolò Cuppini, Mattia Frapporti, and Maurilio Pirone, eds. Capitalism in the Platform Age: Emerging Assemblages of Labour and Welfare in Urban Spaces. Springer, 2024. (Read: "Introduction. The Platform Age," pp. 3–14; "Operations of Platforms," pp. 15–31; "The Politics of Platforms," pp. 81–95).

    [Note: This open-access collection advances from classic digital-labor theory to recent platform-labor research. It treats platforms as infrastructures organizing labor, urban space, welfare, and social cooperation, bringing valorization, algorithmic management, worker subjectivity, and alternatives into one framework. Alongside Scholz and Woodcock, ask whether platform cooperativism changes only ownership or also labor organization and social reproduction more broadly. Calling platforms states, empires, or territories requires care. Data centers, cities, borders, supply chains, and maintenance sites show how macro architectures are executed and whether environmental and labor costs are symmetrical across regions. Capitalism in the Platform Age moves platform studies into the intersection of cities, welfare, and labor reproduction. Platforms are not isolated apps: they may reorganize transport, delivery, care, and public services, jointly platformizing labor markets and urban space. Analysis must therefore track the rewriting of local institutions and redistribution of social-reproductive costs, not only firm valuations or extraction. The urban dimension shows platforms and local states do not simply replace each other. Delivery, ride-hailing, short-term rentals, and care platforms must encounter transport rules, housing policy, labor law, and welfare institutions. Expansion exploits local institutional differences while prompting local governments to redefine regulatory objects. Welfare effects particularly matter. As work splits into temporary tasks and multiplatform income, insurance, taxation, and protections founded on stable employment become harder to apply. Platform capitalism not only innovates corporate organization; it forces welfare states to redefine labor statuses and social rights. Cities are the institutional scale where this conflict first becomes visible.]

  11. Morozov, Evgeny. "Critique of Techno-Feudal Reason" New Left Review, nos. 133/134 (2022). (Read: entire essay).

    [Note: Morozov supplies a particularly useful opposition within this session. He questions the hasty treatment of digital monopoly, intellectual property, platform rents, and financialization as evidence that capitalism has yielded to feudalism, asking us to reconsider the continuing roles of competition, profit, and state policy. This prevents the two technofeudalism books from dictating the debate and makes their concept a falsifiable, comparable hypothesis. "Critique of Techno-Feudal Reason" transforms the political-economic differences among rent, profit, gateway control, and exit costs from rhetoric into institutional analysis. These differences do not lead to one conclusion; they require comparing configurations of power across organizational settings to determine explanatory scope and failure conditions. Morozov's critique offers a necessary counterargument: prematurely announcing contemporary capitalism as feudalism may obscure the continuing mechanisms of capital, competition, finance, and the state. Conceptual novelty cannot replace evidence for historical periodization. Productive debate compares theories' precision in explaining the same phenomena—platform rents, monopoly, infrastructural dependence. Morozov also reminds us that historical analogies shape strategy. Treating platforms as feudal lordships may favor restoring capitalist competition; treating the problem as capital concentration and privately owned infrastructure yields different priorities for antitrust, public ownership, and labor politics. Concept choice is therefore not a naming game: it organizes policy imagination.]

  12. Mosco, Vincent. To the Cloud: Big Data in a Turbulent World. Paradigm Publishers, 2014. (Read: Introduction; chapters on cloud computing, big data, and political economy).

    [Note: From political economy and communication studies, Mosco demystifies the cloud's industry structure, labor, data, and ideology. Predating stack and technofeudalism accounts, it provides a historical marker: from the outset, cloud computing involved corporate concentration, data centers, energy, labor, and state policy, not merely technical outsourcing. Planetary concepts can erase particular places. Preserve falsifiability rather than maximize conceptual coverage; extend a framework only where evidence supports its central mechanisms. The tension between planetary models and specific places, labor, and maintenance thus remains testable through evidence and competing explanations beyond Mosco's To the Cloud: Big Data in a Turbulent World. Demystification means showing that clouds do not eliminate place: language hides servers, data centers, electricity, and labor from users' experience. Ideological effects and material architecture require simultaneous study. The more weightless and ubiquitous a service appears, the more its fixed investments in land, energy, and capital need tracing. Cloud concentration also has economies of scale. Capital, energy purchasing, and technical operations give large data centers cost advantages, so on-demand convenience and highly concentrated backends grow together. Demystification therefore concerns industrial structure as well as language: the more clouds resemble ubiquitous public environments, the easier their ownership becomes to obscure. Mosco also returns clouds to global communication politics. Concentrated data centers and services give a few firms cross-sector infrastructural positions, turning traditional media, governments, and ordinary businesses into clients. Clouds create infrastructural dependence; the political issues concern control over outages, pricing, and standards as well as privacy.]

Part III: Mediation, Organization and Labour (Weeks 5–6)

Session 5: Recursive Publics, Mediation and Digital Politics

This session shifts from control and extraction to the institutional conditions of publicness. Kelty's recursive public is not a crowd discussing things online, but a public form able to participate in maintaining, modifying, and reproducing its own technical and institutional foundations. Free-software communities matter theoretically not only because their code is open, but because licenses, collaborative norms, discussion procedures, version control, and infrastructure jointly constitute a recursively modifiable public life. Warner's analysis of publics and counterpublics emphasizes that publics are not fixed, preexisting groups: circulation, responses, and recirculation continually call them into being. Fraser further places unequal participation and counterpublics within public-sphere theory.

Kornbluh's Immediacy, or The Style of Too Late Capitalism gives this discussion a tension at the level of media form. Immediacy, transparency, immersion, and the absence of mediation are often treated as digital culture's natural values. Political organization, however, depends on procedures, representation, delay, explanation, memory, and chains of responsibility. Tufekci, Dean, Gerbaudo, and others further show that inexpensive mobilization and rapid circulation do not automatically produce sustained organizational capacity. Connections quickly enlarge participation, yet may also make decision-making, resource accumulation, and long-term coordination fragile.

Digital politics therefore turns not on an abstract choice between centralization and decentralization, but on which mediations participants can understand, hold accountable, and modify. A public's owning its servers is not the sole criterion; more important is its ability to influence rulemaking, resource allocation, structures of visibility, and dispute resolution. Only when both media conditions and organizational forms can become political questions does publicness avoid shrinking into a temporary attention space supplied by a platform. Recursive publics thus connect media technology, institutional design, and collective autonomy.

Required Readings:

  1. Kelty, Christopher M. Two Bits: The Cultural Significance of Free Software. Duke University Press, 2008. (Read: Chapter 1, "A Recursive Public," pp. 27–63).

    [Note: This is the session's central text. Kelty's recursive public not only uses public media but can modify, maintain, and reproduce their infrastructural and institutional conditions. Focus on how software licenses, code, discussion, maintenance, and identity jointly form publicness. In comparison with the platform era, ask what remains of publicness when participants lose practical control over code, servers, accounts, and rules. Conversely, does enduring publicness require some autonomy over technical infrastructure? Participant counts and circulation speed cannot directly measure it. A highly visible group may still lack the ability to preserve archives, modify rules, own infrastructure, or determine exit conditions; distinguish these institutional dimensions from expression rights. Kelty's Two Bits: The Cultural Significance of Free Software grounds publics' ability to maintain and modify media conditions in institutional relations. Publicness is not synonymous with information traffic: it requires durable rules, memory, procedures, and media conditions. Platforms expand visibility but may place the interfaces, data, and communicative structures supporting publics under private governance. A recursive public is no ordinary online discussion group; it can reshape its own conditions of communication and collaboration. Free-software communities are recursive because members not only use code and licenses but maintain these institutional-technical foundations. This raises a sharp platform-era problem: how is organizational autonomy constrained when publics can form only on unmodifiable proprietary platforms? Recursion also means a public can in some sense repair itself. When software, licenses, or communication channels fail, members can change them through shared rules rather than wait for an outside platform's decision. Technical and democratic autonomy do not entirely coincide for Kelty, yet the right to maintain makes a crucial connection between them.]

  2. Kornbluh, Anna. Immediacy, or The Style of Too Late Capitalism. Verso, 2024. (Read: "Circulation," pp. 24–43; "Writing," pp. 65–112; "Antitheory," pp. 148–190).

    [Note: Kornbluh's book is not directly about technology; it belongs here precisely to broaden the question of why platform-era publicness increasingly seeks directness, instantaneity, immersion, and no mediation. She calls this cultural form immediacy and argues that it lowers tolerance for representation, distance, and mediation. This creates a tension for recursive publics: rules, procedures, discussion, and maintenance sustain publicness, yet immediacy culture experiences these mediations as obstacles. What happens to organization's necessary delays, explanations, and institutional procedures when political communication demands immediate reaction? Read "Circulation," "Writing," and "Antitheory" together. Immediacy is not one media phenomenon, but a late-capitalist style linking circulation, first-person expression, immersion, transparency, and antitheoretical attitudes. Her polemical intensity also requires critique: does reducing mediation always mean political regression? When marginalized subjects seek to speak directly, how should we discuss representation's institutional value? Positioning Kornbluh among Warner, Fraser, and Kelty avoids one-sided praise of mediation; distinguish necessary, accountable, and monopolistic mediations. Mediation is not inherently antidemocratic: can it be visible, accountable, and reconfigured? Critiquing immediacy connects cultural form with political organization. When directness, immersion, the first person, and instantaneous circulation become values, mediation looks like alienation or delay. Yet public politics depends on irreducible mediations of representation, procedure, explanation, and organization. Digital speed thus has two sides: it extends responsiveness while potentially eroding the distance and time required for sustained judgment.]

  3. Warner, Michael. "Publics and Counterpublics" Public Culture 14, no. 1 (2002): 49–90.

    [Note: Warner emphasizes that a public is not a fixed group existing before media: circulation, response, and recirculation continually summon it. This particularly matters for platforms, where recommendations, reposting, group chats, subscriptions, and algorithmic timelines alter public formation. Read with Kelty to examine how technical conditions produce publicness. Inexpensive mobilization and organizational capacity are distinct measures. Rapid assembly amplifies issues without necessarily accumulating trust, resources, divided roles, or conflict-resolution mechanisms; keep mobilization, organization, and institution distinct. "Publics and Counterpublics" offers a limited but effective scale for explaining differences among publics, counterpublics, networked publics, and recursive publics. It identifies mechanisms without replacing further analysis of organizations, law, and material conditions. Publics arise through texts' circulation and strangers' sustained responses rather than preexist them. Publicness is thus media-dependent: communicative rhythms, forms of address, and accessibility change who constitutes a public. Algorithmic timelines further intervene, so platform rankings and recommendations shape formation alongside participants' communicative acts. Counterpublics also organize themselves through expression and social rhythms different from the mainstream. Platforms lower their communicative costs while measuring all expression through standardized formats and metrics. This tension between standardization and counterpublic difference is essential to networked publicness.]

  4. Fraser, Nancy. "Rethinking the Public Sphere: A Contribution to the Critique of Actually Existing Democracy" Social Text, no. 25/26 (1990): 56–80.

    [Note: Fraser revises classical public-sphere theory through subaltern counterpublics, participatory parity, and identity differences. Rather than make a unified sphere the only ideal, she asks how multiple publics, counterpublics, and marginal publics coexist. In this session, "Rethinking the Public Sphere: A Contribution to the Critique of Actually Existing Democracy" gives a concrete structure to the distinction among expression, infrastructural ownership, and democratic governance. Publicness is not information traffic: it requires durable rules, memory, procedures, and media conditions. Platforms expand visibility but may privately govern the interfaces, data, and circulation structures that sustain publics. Counterpublics also revise the normative image of one shared public sphere. Social inequality means resources, languages, and visibility for discussion have never been equal; marginalized groups often first need their own counterpublic spaces. Digital networks expand differentiation while platform ranking and commercial logics shape encounters among publics. Participatory parity further shows that formal openness does not guarantee equal participation. Resources, status, and expressive habits affect who is heard. Platforms lower speaking thresholds yet create new inequalities through attention competition. Multiple publics must therefore be studied alongside actual differences in participation conditions. Counterpublics' value is preserving difference within publicness rather than requiring everyone first to adopt one language and expressive norm.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Gramsci, Antonio. Selections from the Prison Notebooks. Edited and translated by Quintin Hoare and Geoffrey Nowell Smith. International Publishers, 1971. Originally published in Italian selections from the prison notebooks, 1948–1951. (Read: "The Intellectuals," pp. 5–23).

    [Note: This reading does not simply rename programmers organic intellectuals; it reconsiders the links among knowledge, production, and organization. Gramsci examines intellectuals' emergence from particular social forces and their roles in culture, organization, and hegemony. In digital environments, examine separately the knowledge positions of software engineers, protocol developers, platform managers, data workers, and researchers. Technical competence does not naturally represent a political class. Participant counts and circulation speed cannot directly measure publicness. Gramsci's Selections from the Prison Notebooks moves publics' capacity to maintain and modify media conditions from macro judgment to mechanism analysis; validity ultimately depends on identifying institutional relations empirically. Organic intellectuals connect intellectual labor with social groups and organized practice rather than give clever people special status. In digital society, the concept examines engineers, researchers, technical communities, and labor organizations forming shared worldviews and organizational capacities. Expertise itself does not determine political alignment: how knowledge is organized, which social forces it serves, and how it becomes collective practice are decisive. Distinguish technical authority from political representation too. Knowing a system does not automatically entitle engineers to define other groups' public interests. Expertise becomes collective political capacity through organization, negotiation, and shared practice. This particularly matters for AI expert governance. Gramsci also emphasizes reciprocity: intellectuals organize social experience, while organizations give knowledge work sustained social positions. Publicness dependent solely on short-cycle opinion leaders struggles to develop this long-term function. How engineering communities, labor organizations, and public research institutions accumulate knowledge and transmit organizational memory is the real core of the "new organic intellectuals" question.]

  2. Habermas, Jürgen. The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere. Translated by Thomas Burger. MIT Press, 1991. Originally published 1962. (Read: Part V, pp. 141–180).

    [Note: This supplies public-sphere theory's historical baseline. The point is not to equate platforms with Habermas's mass media, but to understand the institutional, medial, and social conditions a public sphere requires and how commercialization changes them. Mediation is not inherently antidemocratic; it must be visible, accountable, and reconfigurable. Habermas still offers a key benchmark: publicness depends on institutional spaces, media forms, and social qualifications, not information circulation alone. The platform-era issue exceeds everyone's ability to speak: how business models, ownership, attention allocation, and inequality organize discussion, and which institutions sustain critical communication, matter more. Commercialization takes new infrastructural forms digitally. Traditional mass media shape discussion through ownership and advertising; platforms additionally control identity, ranking, circulation, and feedback. Theory must extend from content production to distribution architectures and private technical systems' specification of communicative conditions. Who controls infrastructure becomes unavoidable: media ownership and technical architecture require joint discussion. Publicness's material conditions now extend from newspapers, coffeehouses, and broadcasting to servers, interfaces, and recommenders. Media architecture becomes part of public-sphere institutions. Revisiting the sphere means not restoring old media orders, but analyzing how new infrastructures affect equal participation, issue formation, and public judgment. Habermas's normative framework cannot directly encompass fragmented network publics, but still offers measures: are participatory conditions equal, can agendas escape private control, and are reasons open to public contestation? Joined to platform infrastructures, these retain critical force without reviving the historical social model.]

  3. Benkler, Yochai. The Wealth of Networks. Yale University Press, 2006. (Read: Chapter 3, "Peer Production and Sharing," pp. 59–90).

    [Note: Benkler offers an institutional and economic analysis of peer production. With Kelty, ask whether commons-based peer production supplies organizational forms distinct from firms and markets, and how platforms reabsorb their public outputs. Inexpensive mobilization is not organizational capacity. Through Benkler's The Wealth of Networks, differences among publics, counterpublics, networked publics, and recursive publics enter institutional and organizational analysis. Peer production's political potential comes from changing the relation between productive cooperation and exclusive property, not networks themselves. Open licenses, modular collaboration, and shared resources lower participation barriers but still require governing rules, maintenance, and sustainable material foundations. This sharply contrasts with platformization: open collaboration is not free platform labor. Distinguish nonmarket cooperation from unpaid corporate contribution. The former usually has shared rules, common resources, and institutions through which participants influence production; the latter may leave platforms in unilateral control of infrastructure and revenue. Both use networks, but their property and governance structures differ completely. This is crucial for open-source models. Even freely downloadable weights leave a significant institutional distance from commons-based peer production if one company still decides training, governance, and deployment.]

  4. Coleman, Gabriella. Coding Freedom. Princeton University Press, 2012. (Read: Chapter 3, pp. 61–84).

    [Note: Coleman's ethnography brings free software and hacker culture from abstract technological freedom into particular communities. Focus on relations among technical ability, ethics, political identities, and organizational culture. The distinction between expression, infrastructural ownership, and democratic governance revealed by Coleman's Coding Freedom is not merely an internal conceptual debate. It remains subject to empirical evidence and competing explanations beyond Coleman's Coding Freedom. Coleman's Coding Freedom confines this distinction to particular objects and causal chains; analogies beyond that scope need new evidence rather than terminology alone. Coleman's Coding Freedom grounds free-software ethics in community practices: technical competence, humor, legal consciousness, hacker ethics, and organizational boundaries intertwine. Publicness arises not just from open licenses, but from participants' sustained commitments to code, rules, and shared identities. This ethnography particularly matters because free-software politics do not follow automatically from license texts. Humor, craft, reputation, legal consciousness, and everyday collaboration jointly shape community ethics. Technical autonomy is thus a practiced and organized cultural form, not a political property naturally appearing when code is opened. Coleman also shows how technological communities' politics often appear in legal details and everyday norms rather than grand declarations. Specific understandings of copyright, anonymity, free speech, and collaborative obligations shape conduct. Free-software culture is an institutionalized ethics stabilized by long practice, not by members sharing a single ideology.]

  5. Tufekci, Zeynep. Twitter and Tear Gas. Yale University Press, 2017. (Read: Introduction and Chapters 1–2).

    [Note: Tufekci examines how networked media lower mobilization costs without necessarily strengthening long-term organizational capacity. With Kornbluh, distinguish immediacy's rapid circulation from organization's needs for memory, trust, accumulated resources, and procedures. Participant counts and circulation speed cannot directly measure publicness. At the scale of Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas, publics' ability to maintain and modify media conditions appears first as concrete relations. Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas explains that ability only insofar as corresponding institutional mechanisms are empirically identifiable. Through Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas, the question becomes more rigorous: which mechanisms actually change, which involve only a change of medium, and who bears the consequences? Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas further insists on differences among objects and institutional boundaries; rhetorical force cannot replace empirical explanation. Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas particularly shows that networked movements can gain enormous communicative scale almost instantly without simultaneously developing negotiation, resource management, or internal conflict-resolution capacities. A capacity deficit is not a dismissal of network mobilization, but an account of asymmetry between organizational foundations and communication speed. Networked protests show that digital media dramatically reduce mobilization costs, quickly producing scale and visibility without necessarily developing bargaining, decision-making, and conflict resolution. The experience traditional organizations slowly accumulate may be precisely what rapid mobilization lacks. Network movements' fragility may therefore arise from unequal growth of organizational and communicative capacity rather than failure of communication.]

  6. Dean, Jodi. Crowds and Party. Verso, 2016. (Read: Chapter 3, "The Distributive Party," pp. 119–156).

    [Note: Dean questions the assumption that more connections mean stronger political organization. Networked circulation produces many individualized gatherings without necessarily producing enduring organizations. With Kelty, distinguish recursive publics from network crowds. Dean's Crowds and Party, Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas, and Gerbaudo's Tweets and the Streets: Social Media and Contemporary Activism place the conflict between immediacy and speed, on one hand, and organization's necessary mediations and delays, on the other, within different intellectual traditions. Mediation is not inherently antidemocratic; the question is whether it can be visible, accountable, and reconstructed. Dean's Crowds and Party frees this conflict from abstract epochal diagnoses. The contribution of Dean's Crowds and Party is to preserve theory's falsifiability. Dean's Crowds and Party does not simply reject crowd mobilization: it stresses the structural difference between momentary assembly and organizational forms capable of decisions, discipline, and sustained action. Digital media magnify the former without automatically producing the latter. This organizational question strips network connection of a naturally democratic aura. Rapid circulation produces shared feelings and short-term gatherings without necessarily creating organizations responsible for decisions, resources, and long-term commitments. The tension between crowd and party becomes crucial to digital activism: political capacity requires durable organizational forms as well as expression.]

  7. Gerbaudo, Paolo. Tweets and the Streets: Social Media and Contemporary Activism. Pluto Press, 2012. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–20).

    [Note: Gerbaudo's discussion of leaderless networks analyzes social media's redistribution of political visibility and leadership. It does not prove network movements undemocratic, but suggests interfaces may generate new centers. Low mobilization costs and organizational capacity are different measures. Gerbaudo's Tweets and the Streets: Social Media and Contemporary Activism separates distinctions among publics, counterpublics, networked publics, and recursive publics into connected elements. His correction to leaderless-network accounts is particularly important. Social media do not eliminate leadership: account visibility, emotional choreography, and calls to action produce new soft leadership. Networks can be formally distributed yet highly concentrated in attention and agenda-setting. Study implicit curation, coordination, and representation rather than judge decentralization from organizational self-descriptions alone. The choreography of assembly reveals organizational labor connecting online circulation and offline gatherings. Who selects places, times, and slogans, and who maintains information flows, shapes supposedly spontaneous movements. Digital media do not abolish organization but make some of its labor less conspicuous as curation, reposting, and emotional mobilization. Soft leadership also illuminates new representational problems. Highly visible accounts can coordinate effectively while acquiring the authority to interpret a movement without formal authorization. Network politics needs new accountability so communicative advantages do not automatically become unquestionable representative authority. Leadership and horizontal participation are questions of organizational design, not mutually exclusive choices.]

  8. Milan, Stefania. Social Movements and Their Technologies. Palgrave Macmillan, 2013. (Read: Chapter 2, pp. 31–54).

    [Note: This examines movements building their own communication and media infrastructures. Extending recursive publics to political actors reveals a potentially vast difference between owning and using media. Milan's Social Movements and Their Technologies, Gerbaudo's Tweets and the Streets: Social Media and Contemporary Activism, and Juris's Networking Futures bring the distinction among expression, infrastructure ownership, and democratic governance from macro judgments to mechanisms. Historical analogies are valuable only at that level. Declaring an epochal shift merely because algorithms, platforms, or models have appeared destroys theory's ability to distinguish continuity from rupture. Milan's Social Movements and Their Technologies contributes by returning this broad judgment to identifiable institutions. The distinction consequently remains open to empirical evidence and competing explanations beyond Milan's Social Movements and Their Technologies. Movement technologies concern not just which media to choose but whether relative autonomy over communicative conditions can be built. Independent servers, encrypted communication, independent media, and technical volunteers may constitute movements' own infrastructural capacities. Milan thus turns media use into media governance: an organization's degree of control over technological conditions directly affects action's continuity.]

  9. Juris, Jeffrey S. Networking Futures. Duke University Press, 2008. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–26).

    [Note: Taking movements against globalization as cases, Juris observes networked organization emerging in actual action, avoiding its reduction to a purely technical structure. Participant counts and communication speed cannot directly measure publicness. Juris's Networking Futures clarifies causal layers in publics' ability to maintain and modify media conditions. Juris's Networking Futures explains this ability only where corresponding institutional mechanisms can be identified empirically. Around Juris's Networking Futures, trace connections among mechanisms rather than seek one term covering every phenomenon. The ethnography in Juris's Networking Futures further shows networked organization is no direct projection of technical topology onto political form. Meetings, trust, resources, traditions of action, and interorganizational negotiation sustain networks together; horizontalism always involves coordination and informal leadership. The ethnography of antiglobalization movements shows networking as organizational norms and political culture as well as technical structure. Horizontal deliberation, autonomy, and diversity are practiced through meetings, mailing lists, and action networks, with coordination costs and informal power. Network organizations' democracy is an institutional achievement requiring maintenance, not an automatic property of connected nodes. Juris also shows horizontalism's practical difficulties: informal networks do not eliminate power, since technical skill, resources, language, and ability to travel still generate centers. Organizational analysis must examine both formal structures and informal hierarchies. Horizontalism is better treated as an ongoing practical norm than an accomplished organizational fact.]

  10. Papacharissi, Zizi. Affective Publics: Sentiment, Technology, and Politics. Oxford University Press, 2015. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on affective publics and networked storytelling).

    [Note: Papacharissi centers affect, emotional expression, and narrative structures in networked publicness. Publics form not only through rational arguments and information exchange: affective rhythms, hashtags, visibility, and circulating stories temporarily organize them too. After Warner and Fraser, this supplements overly institutional or normative tendencies while remaining distinct from Berlant: here the focus is public formation, whereas the next session concerns attachment in precarious lives. Mediation is not inherently antidemocratic; visibility, accountability, and reconstruction are the questions. Affective publics free affect from simple opposition to public reason. Circulating hashtags, images, and narratives assemble dispersed individuals into temporary publics of shared feeling; emotional intensity itself becomes political connection. Can such connection become sustained organization, and how does platforms' optimization of visibility and interaction amplify selected emotions? Affect does not necessarily produce superficial politics. It sustains memory, identity, and common concerns, or may be depleted by short attention cycles. Distinguish formation from institutionalization: the former explains how connections happen, while the latter still requires organizational theory. Endurance ultimately depends on organization, memory, and institutional supports; emotional intensity cannot replace long-term political capacity. Affect's circulation also clearly depends on platforms. Certain emotions travel readily through short texts, visual impact, and engagement metrics, and ranking may further amplify highly engaging content. Affective publics are not spontaneous psychological aggregates: media forms and algorithmic visibility shape them. This infrastructural condition must inform any account of digital political emotion.]

  11. boyd, danah. "Social Network Sites as Networked Publics: Affordances, Dynamics, and Implications" In A Networked Self: Identity, Community, and Culture on Social Network Sites, edited by Zizi Papacharissi, 39–58. Routledge, 2011. (Read: entire chapter).

    [Note: Boyd's networked publics explain how persistence, replicability, scalability, and searchability alter public interaction. The point is not that Facebook or Twitter automatically generate democratic public spheres, but to supply middle-range concepts explaining how affordances change speech's temporality, visibility, audience boundaries, and recirculation. Reading with Warner's circulation is especially productive. Low mobilization costs and organizational capacity are different measures. "Social Network Sites as Networked Publics: Affordances, Dynamics, and Implications" turns differences among publics, counterpublics, networked publics, and recursive publics from rhetorical propositions into institutional analysis. The framework emphasizes affordances' shaping of communication: persistence, replicability, scalability, and searchability change expression's time, reach, and retrievability. Social networks are thus not simply online traditional public spheres. Preserved visibility, copyable content, and blurred audiences bring identity management, context collapse, and participation together. Networked publics also alter imagined audiences. Speakers often address potential, invisible, algorithmically expandable audiences rather than defined groups, changing self-presentation and risk assessment. Context collapse is not individual failure to manage privacy: multiple social settings are technically compressed into one interface. The social tensions of network publics thus enter interface design.]

  12. Gillespie, Tarleton. Custodians of the Internet: Platforms, Content Moderation, and the Hidden Decisions That Shape Social Media. Yale University Press, 2018. (Read: Chapter 2, "The Myth of the Neutral Platform," pp. 24–44; Chapter 5, "The Human Labor of Moderation," pp. 111–140).

    [Note: The book analyzes platforms' content governance through policies and technical rules while emphasizing moderation's dependence on extensive hidden human labor. It corrects the image of automatic algorithmic governance: algorithms, rules, human review, and commercial risk management commonly govern together. Content governance thus resembles a quasi-public institution yet lacks public bodies' usual democratic authorization and procedural constraints. Rulemaking, automated detection, and human review jointly determine visibility's boundaries, while firms control both interpretation and infrastructure. Gillespie makes platform responsibility concern governance's legitimacy, not merely deleting or retaining content. Moderation also exposes a private-platform paradox: firms claim neutral intermediation while constantly making public-order-like rules. Scale forces reliance on automation and global human labor, so interpretation becomes a continuous organizational process. Disputes cannot be reduced to a single opposition between free speech and censorship. Moderation is simultaneously content policy, a labor institution, and infrastructural governance; together these determine publicness's actual boundaries. Platforms are private firms and de facto communicative infrastructures, a tension underlying governing disputes. Moderation's scale also creates continual friction between rules and cases. Uniform policies encounter linguistic, cultural, and political differences, while automated detection cannot fully understand context. Platforms constantly adjust between global consistency and local judgment. Research should focus not only on contested individual decisions but on how this vast institution produces executable categories and exceptions. The politics of moderation also appear in handling exceptions. The more complex contexts are compressed into uniform policies, the more borderline judgments are required; these are precisely where platforms exercise de facto public power.]

Session 6: Platform Labour, Precarity and New Class Relations

This session brings the political economy of platforms into the labour process and the time of everyday life. Platforms reorganize employment through task allocation, ratings, dynamic pricing, task decomposition, identity verification and automatic deactivation. The power of the "boss" can thus appear as interfaces, metrics and models, without always being exercised directly by a visible manager. Scholz, Woodcock, Rosenblat and Aloisi/De Stefano approach this from cooperativism, workers' struggles, drivers' experiences and labour law. They show that algorithmic management has not abolished labour relations; information asymmetry and dispersed responsibility may instead make labour control harder to identify.

Terranova's free labor, Casilli's research on microtasks, and Gray and Suri's account of ghost work extend digital labour to user participation, content moderation, data annotation and training support. "Automation" often depends on extensive human labour that is geographically dispersed and erased from its public narrative. AI systems therefore cannot be understood solely through models and computing power. Platformization further transfers work-related risks to individuals: waiting, accepting tasks, maintaining ratings, paying for equipment and remaining continuously available become parts of the labour process. Class relations are consequently expressed not only in wages, but also in information rights, conditions of exit, data ownership and control over time.

Berlant's Cruel Optimism adds an affective and temporal dimension to this structure of experience. Precarious labour persists not simply because of external coercion, but also because visions of "flexibility," "freedom," "entrepreneurship" and "self-realization" can become objects of attachment that sustain people's life narratives. Platform cooperatives, unions, collective bargaining and public infrastructure therefore confront more than ownership: they must also address the distribution of risk, the organization of everyday time, and whether workers can constitute a sustainable collective political subject. Institutional alternatives must reach these levels to move beyond the limited idea of simply changing a platform's owner.

Required Readings:

  1. Berlant, Lauren. Cruel Optimism. Duke University Press, 2011. (Read: Chapter 1, "Cruel Optimism," pp. 23–50; Chapter 6, "After the Good Life, an Impasse," pp. 191–222; Chapter 7, "On the Desire for the Political," pp. 223–264).

    [Note: Berlant does not offer a direct theory of platform capitalism, but provides a powerful concept for understanding why platform labour remains attached to "hope." Cruel optimism names a subject's attachment to an object that obstructs their flourishing. Chapter 6 situates this relation within the precarious present and the time of work and life; Chapter 7 develops the difficulties of political desire and action. Read after platform labour, it raises a question technical solutions often overlook: why do workers remain dependent on "flexible, autonomous, entrepreneurial" forms of work even when these continually erode security and the ability to plan a future? Institutional alternatives must change platform ownership and address an attachment sustained jointly by hope, everyday rhythms and precarity. Chapter 1's definition must be read alongside the impasse of Chapter 6 and political desire of Chapter 7. Berlant is concerned not merely with why people cannot relinquish a harmful object, but with how they improvise a life in a persistently unstable present after the infrastructures of the "good life" fail, and why political desire does not automatically crystallize into a collective programme. This matters especially for platform labour, since flexibility may be both a platform slogan and a real need under conditions of care, migration, education or unemployment. Only by acknowledging both the material rationality of attachment and its structural costs can cruel optimism avoid becoming the simplistic claim that "workers are brainwashed." Berlant offers an affective politics of attachment rather than an economics of platform labour. People may remain attached to promises of "flexible work," "self-employment" or a "good life" even as these undermine the conditions of a stable existence. The precarious present is therefore constituted not only by wages and contracts, but also by temporal experience, hope and everyday adaptation. Labour reform that ignores these attachments will struggle to explain the enduring appeal of precarious forms.]

  2. Terranova, Tiziana. "Free Labor: Producing Culture for the Digital Economy" Social Text 18, no. 2 (2000): 33–58.

    [Note: Terranova's free labor examines the relations between voluntary participation, social interaction and capitalist valorization in digital culture. It warns against reducing digital labour to "paid online work": users' creation, socializing and data production can themselves become conditions of capital extraction. Algorithmic management does not mean managers disappear. Rule designers, customer service, operations and risk teams, and capital owners remain; some commands are simply executed through interfaces, ratings and automatic deactivation. Tracing responsibility must therefore penetrate the organizational claim that "the system decided." "Free" participation, paid employment and microtask labour must remain analytically distinct, or digital labour loses its capacity to distinguish degrees of coercion. Algorithmic management has not abolished management relations; it converts some commands into task allocation, ratings, dynamic pricing and automatic deactivation. An impersonal interface can disperse responsibility without reducing workers' exposure to control. The strongest aspect of free labor is its recognition that voluntary participation and capitalist valorization can occur simultaneously. Enjoying creation, socializing or games does not stop users from producing value; conversely, calling every online activity labour erases differences in wage relations and coercion. Terranova thus offers an analytical continuum, not a simple formula that turns all of life into labour. She also reveals that capitalist valorization and cultural autonomy are not a zero-sum relation. Digital culture can genuinely create communities, aesthetics and knowledge while platforms convert these activities into traffic and data. Critique should not deny participants' autonomous meanings, but explain how value is captured within infrastructures they do not fully control. The force of free labor lies precisely in this duality: participation can be a real autonomous practice while supplying unpaid conditions for platform accumulation.]

  3. Scholz, Trebor. Uberworked and Underpaid: How Workers Are Disrupting the Digital Economy. Polity Press, 2016. (Read: Chapter 4, "Crowd Fleecing"; Conclusion, especially the sections on "Tactical Refusal, Defection, and Withdrawal from Data Labor" and platform cooperativism).

    [Note: The book's central concern is not "developing a workers' Uber," but reopening the questions of who bears platform-economy risks, who controls data and who owns platforms. Chapter 4 discusses crowd fleecing; the conclusion connects refusal, defection and withdrawal with platform cooperativism. This reading avoids reducing cooperativism to a business venture, restoring its place within worker ownership, collective bargaining and infrastructure governance. Discussions of automation must especially avoid substitution fetish: a machine replacing a task does not mean the disappearance of a profession or all labour. The institutional core of platform cooperativism is not "copy an existing platform and change its owner," but the reorganization of control, surplus distribution and data governance. Cooperatives that still depend on external cloud services, capital finance or closed algorithms may find their autonomy constrained by infrastructure. Scholz's questions thus ultimately concern governance capacity and technological sovereignty beyond ownership. Platform cooperativism must also confront scale. Cooperative ownership can alter returns and decision-making rights, yet network effects, finance, software maintenance and user acquisition can still force cooperatives to depend on incumbent giants. The viability of alternatives depends on a wider institutional ecosystem of shared technology, public procurement and alliances among cooperatives. The difficulties of cooperativism extend from business ownership to the technology stack, financing and market access: platform autonomy needs a fuller institutional ecology. Only when worker ownership combines with infrastructural capacity can it produce an organizational form meaningfully different from conventional platforms. The technical conditions of cooperation cannot be treated as neutral external resources.]

  4. Woodcock, Jamie. The Fight against Platform Capitalism: An Inquiry into the Global Struggles of the Gig Economy. University of Westminster Press, 2021. (Read: Chapter 3, pp. 45–67).

    [Note: Woodcock returns collective action in platform labour to workers' practices: stoppages, disconnecting, organizing, unions and cross-platform cooperation. This creates a tension with Scholz's route of institutional alternatives: even where cooperative platforms exist, workers still need real organizational capacity and bargaining power. Cooperativism is no technological panacea. Read within this session, Woodcock's The Fight against Platform Capitalism: An Inquiry into the Global Struggles of the Gig Economy gives a more concrete structure to the question of which layers of power cooperatives, unions, labour law and commons governance each change. Algorithmic management has not abolished management relations; it turns some commands into task allocation, ratings, dynamic pricing and automatic deactivation. The interface's impersonality can disperse responsibility without weakening control over workers. Woodcock restores platform conflicts to workers' organizing, beyond alternative business models. Strikes, collective log-offs, unions and cross-platform networks show that collective action has not disappeared even when labour relations are individualized and broken into tasks. Algorithmic management may itself create shared objects of discontent. Platform labour politics thus remains centred on organizing: how can scattered experiences become sustainable collective power? Organization must also confront the technical mediation of the labour process. Personalized task allocation and dynamic pricing can weaken shared experience, yet the same interface can help workers recognize similar injustices and develop new organizing tools. Technology is both a management medium and a potential object and resource of collective action. These practices show that platform workers are not passive objects of algorithms: they develop knowledge, strategies and collective countermeasures around algorithmic rules.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Srnicek, Nick. Platform Capitalism. Polity, 2017. (Read: Chapter 2, pp. 35–63).

    [Note: Platforms are understood as economic organizations for data extraction and market intermediation. This gives the session's problem of compute concentration a prehistory in capitalist economies of scale and network effects, but platform capitalism must not simply be equated with AI capitalism. Theoretical resemblance does not automatically imply institutional identity. Srnicek treats platforms as specific business models formed through data extraction, network effects and market intermediation, supplying an economic basis for understanding their concentration.
