Platforms are not homogeneous: advertising, cloud, industrial and lean platforms depend on different revenue structures and asset configurations. Distinguishing these types prevents conceptual overgeneralization when examining platform labour and concentrated computing power. This typology also explains why "platforms" cannot be treated as one uniform class relation: their reliance on fixed assets, labour contracts and data differs, as do their paths to concentration. Another strength of platform capitalism is its placement of data within business competition rather than an abstract "information society." Firms accumulate data because it improves services, locks in users, trains models and erects entry barriers. Concentrated computing power and data must therefore be connected to concrete profit models, not explained only by technological scale. Platform concentration arises from network effects and positive feedback among data, capital and infrastructure; every alternative policy must specify the level at which it acts. Platform typology is thus a prerequisite for policy analysis: different mechanisms of concentration require different regulations and public alternatives. Economic distinctions precede any uniform scheme of "platform governance." Srnicek's typology also reveals differing capital intensities. Asset-light platforms depend on outsourcing and risk transfer; cloud platforms need enormous fixed capital. Both are called platforms, yet their labour organization and entry barriers differ entirely. Connecting platform capitalism with AI infrastructure especially requires distinguishing these capital structures, or "platform" will conceal the compute industry's heavy dependence on assets.]

  2. Huws, Ursula. Labor in the Global Digital Economy: The Cybertariat Comes of Age. Monthly Review Press, 2014. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 11–38).

    [Note: Huws approaches digital labour through global divisions of labour and commodification. She reminds us that digital labour encompasses not just software engineers, but a new global labour structure formed by services, outsourcing, platforms and knowledge work. Algorithmic management does not mean that managers disappear. Labor in the Global Digital Economy: The Cybertariat Comes of Age offers not a definitive label for the relation between affective attachment to precarious life and labour institutions, but a theoretical opening that competing explanations can test; this openness is itself part of its research value. Huws situates digital labour within global commodification and divisions of labour, rejecting "knowledge workers" as the digital economy's sole subjects. Customer service, outsourcing, logistics, manufacturing and office work are all restandardized and organized at a distance through informatization. The cybertariat thus connects high and low skills, centres and peripheries, requiring digital class structures to be understood through global labour chains. A global view also corrects the equation of digital labour with remote white-collar work. High-end software and low-paid back-office services often occupy the same value chain; the former's appearance of automation may rest on the latter's standardized labour. Class analysis must address these spatially separated but functionally interdependent jobs together. It must attend to both software interfaces and supply chains, restoring visible knowledge work and hidden support work to one structure. Huws also brings households and social reproduction into the picture. Remote and flexible work does not eliminate care burdens and may allow working time to penetrate further into the home. Platforms' flexible schedules must therefore be examined with gendered reproductive responsibilities: the same "flexibility" may mean autonomy for some workers and the continual erosion of work–life boundaries for others.]

  3. Casilli, Antonio A. Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation. Foreword by Sarah T. Roberts. Translated by Saskia Brown. University of Chicago Press, 2025. Originally published in French as En attendant les robots: Enquête sur le travail du clic in 2019. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on micro-work, clickwork, data labor, and automation).

    [Note: The central point is that labour remains behind automation. Microwork, data annotation and content moderation show that AI training and operation often rely on highly dispersed, barely visible human labour. This connects "platform labour" with "AI labour." The 2025 English translation is used to bring the 2019 French study directly into dialogue with automation discourse after the rise of generative AI; its core remains hidden labour, and the book should not be misrepresented as a retrospective commentary on large models. Casilli's Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation brings the concealment of microtasks, annotation and maintenance by automation narratives into organizational and institutional analysis. His principal contribution is to decompose "automation" into the organization of extensive human microlabour. Clicking, annotating, verifying and moderating are not incidental patches outside machine intelligence; they are often necessary conditions of model training and service operation. Automation is thus not the simple disappearance of labour, but its rearrangement across space, contracts and visibility. Casilli further shows how human labour is embedded in automated feedback loops. Models continually need annotation, verification, correction and content judgments; platforms distribute these stages through crowdsourcing to global labour markets. Human-in-the-loop may be a lasting organizational form of large-scale AI services, not merely a transitional stage. Automation grows together with new labour markets. The global distribution of microlabour also complicates labour law's identification of employers. Workers may face multiple contractors, crowdsourcing platforms and the ultimate AI company, with a fragmented chain of responsibility. Automation ethics must therefore reconnect supply-chain responsibility with labour standards.]

  4. Gray, Mary L., and Siddharth Suri. Ghost Work: How to Stop Silicon Valley from Building a New Global Underclass. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019. (Read: Chapters 1–3).

    [Note: This book shows the microtasks, content moderation and platform-mediated human labour behind AI. Read with Casilli and Crawford, it reframes automation as labour redistribution and the production of labour's invisibility. Cooperativism is not a technological cure-all either. The question of which layer of power cooperatives, unions, labour law and commons governance each change, illuminated by Gray's Ghost Work: How to Stop Silicon Valley from Building a New Global Underclass, exceeds conceptual debate within the text. Ghost work exposes the infrastructural paradox of automation narratives: the more a system is described as requiring no human input, the more easily the human judgment sustaining its "intelligence" disappears. Global microtask markets split labour into discrete, on-demand units that are hard to organize, grounding technical efficiency in new forms of labour precarity. AI labour policy must therefore extend beyond technical occupations: microtask workers' wages, occupational safety, complaint channels and cross-border rights also belong to AI governance. Gray and Suri reveal an organizational paradox as well: workers are isolated into individual accounts yet rely on informal communities to exchange experiences, identify scams and help one another. Where platforms provide no stable work organization, workers create their own cooperative networks. The collectivity of digital labour has not vanished; it has moved from formal workplaces into more fragile spaces with less institutional recognition. This organization also shows that "on demand" does not mean demand arises naturally. Platforms actively shape labour markets through task decomposition, pricing and quality control. Worker replaceability is jointly manufactured by technical and contractual design, creating a direct institutional connection between labour's invisibility and technological myth.]

  5. Rosenblat, Alex. Uberland: How Algorithms Are Rewriting the Rules of Work. University of California Press, 2018. (Read: Chapters 2–4).

    [Note: Rosenblat examines algorithmic dispatch, prices, ratings and information asymmetry through drivers' experiences. Her concrete ethnography of algorithmic management prevents platform labour from remaining an abstract capital–labour relation. At the scale of Uberland: How Algorithms Are Rewriting the Rules of Work, platform labour's task decomposition, algorithmic management, risk transfer and collective action first appear as concrete relations. Automation is often achieved by hiding labour: annotation, moderation, microtasks and maintenance are distributed across global labour markets, so the claim that "machines perform the tasks" conceals new organization and risk transfer. Uber's algorithmic management does not eliminate management, but distributes commands across price signals, task allocation, ratings and information asymmetry. Drivers formally retain freedom of choice while continually responding to a platform-designed incentive environment. Rosenblat's ethnography therefore specifies how autonomy and control coexist within one labour regime. It also reveals information asymmetry as a managerial instrument. Platforms see demand, prices and driver performance together; drivers see only partial information on which to base decisions. Algorithmic management draws power not only from automated commands, but also from monopolizing a market-wide view and controlling when information is disclosed. This is a key difference from traditional on-site supervision: workers face a platform that can observe them but that they cannot easily observe. Such an information structure makes "autonomous labour" distinctly asymmetric: choice exists, yet rests on the platform's superior informational position.]

  6. Aloisi, Antonio, and Valerio De Stefano. Your Boss Is an Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence, Platform Work and Labour. Bloomsbury, 2022. (Read: chapters on algorithmic management and worker protection).

    [Note: This book approaches algorithmic management through labour law and institutional design. The "boss" need not be one person: it can take the form of scheduling models, performance ratings, automatic deactivation and rule systems, linking political economy with labour institutions. Aloisi's Your Boss Is an Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence, Platform Work and Labour, Rosenblat's Uberland: How Algorithms Are Rewriting the Rules of Work, and Irani's Chasing Innovation: Making Entrepreneurial Citizens in Modern India place the relation between affective attachment to precarious life and labour institutions within different intellectual traditions. Algorithmic management does not mean managers disappear. Aloisi's Your Boss Is an Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence, Platform Work and Labour releases this relation from overly abstract judgments about the age. Automation is often accomplished by hiding labour. The contribution of Your Boss Is an Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence, Platform Work and Labour to this relation lies precisely in keeping theory open to refutation. Aloisi and De Stefano approach algorithmic management through labour law, restoring institutional content to the popular phrase "your boss is an algorithm." Task allocation, performance management, pricing and deactivation may be automated, but businesses still design control within labour relations and bear its legal consequences. The central question is how traditional employment classifications, rights to information and collective negotiation can adapt to impersonal management, not how to hand responsibility over to software.]

  7. Irani, Lilly. Chasing Innovation: Making Entrepreneurial Citizens in Modern India. Princeton University Press, 2019. (Read: chapters on entrepreneurial citizenship, design and development).

    [Note: Irani studies how "innovation" becomes a moral language in governance and economic policy, and how entrepreneurial subjects are formed. Read with Berlant, she invites a question: when workers must become "innovators," "entrepreneurs" and self-managers, does power enter labour relations through the language of hope and self-realization? Through Chasing Innovation: Making Entrepreneurial Citizens in Modern India, the concealment of microtasks, annotation and maintenance by automation narratives can be broken into interconnected processes. Automation often works by hiding labour. From the perspective of Chasing Innovation: Making Entrepreneurial Citizens in Modern India, this concealment cannot be separated from institutional authorization and resource allocation: technical forms produce enduring social consequences only in conjunction with organizational power. Irani examines how innovation turns from an economic slogan into a mechanism of subject formation. Design thinking, entrepreneurship education and development projects encourage individuals to redescribe social problems as entrepreneurial opportunities, while turning structural risks into personal responsibilities. Alongside platform labour, entrepreneurial citizenship explains why "precarity" can be repackaged as autonomy, flexibility and innovation. The "entrepreneurial citizen" also changes how failure is attributed. Once innovation becomes an individual duty, project failure is more readily explained as personal inadequacy than as an outcome of infrastructure, capital and policy. Self-branding, ratings and freelance culture in the platform economy continue this subjectification, recasting labour risks as personal choices.]

  8. Schor, Juliet B. After the Gig: How the Sharing Economy Got Hijacked and How to Win It Back. University of California Press, 2020. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on platform business models, inequality, and alternatives).

    [Note: Through empirical research on sharing-economy platforms, Schor distinguishes business models, forms of labour participation and distributive outcomes, avoiding the reduction of every gig-economy experience to one model of exploitation. She is especially useful after Scholz and Woodcock: cooperativism and workers' struggles matter, but workers differ in their dependency, income structures and motivations, so alternatives cannot rely on one organizational template. Schor's After the Gig: How the Sharing Economy Got Hijacked and How to Win It Back, Irani's Chasing Innovation: Making Entrepreneurial Citizens in Modern India, and van Doorn's "Platform Labor: On the Gendered and Racialized Exploitation of Low-Income Service Work in the 'On-Demand' Economy" shift the question of which layers of power cooperatives, unions, labour law and commons governance change from broad judgments to mechanisms. Cooperativism is no technological panacea. The contribution of After the Gig: How the Sharing Economy Got Hijacked and How to Win It Back is precisely to return this question to identifiable institutional mechanisms. Automation often works by hiding labour. Schor distinguishes the sharing economy's early social visions from platforms' later commercialization, showing how venture capital and expansion reorganize narratives of efficiency, community and supplementary income. Her research indicates that the platform economy has no single path: labour conditions, ownership and community rules can produce different outcomes. The question becomes which institutional arrangements can turn sharing from marketing language into actual resource governance.]

  9. van Doorn, Niels. "Platform Labor: On the Gendered and Racialized Exploitation of Low-Income Service Work in the "On-Demand" Economy." Information, Communication & Society 20, no. 6 (2017): 898–914. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Van Doorn emphasizes that on-demand service work is not abstract "flexible labour," but highly gendered, racialized labour embedded in urban service relations. Connecting platform capitalism with existing low-paid services, migrant labour and social reproduction corrects analyses that begin only with interfaces or algorithmic dispatch. "Platform Labor: On the Gendered and Racialized Exploitation of Low-Income Service Work in the 'On-Demand' Economy" clarifies the causal levels of task decomposition, algorithmic management, risk transfer and collective action. By putting gendered, racialized, low-income services at the centre, van Doorn challenges the tendency to let drivers or highly skilled freelancers represent the entire gig economy. Cleaning, care and delivery already occupy unequal structures of social reproduction and migrant labour; platformization further digitizes ratings, matching and payment. Algorithms did not create these differences, but can recode and amplify them. Gender and race in the on-demand economy also show that technical mediation does not erase labour markets' historical stratification. Customer ratings, geographical matching and platform classifications can translate existing prejudices into apparently individualized transaction outcomes. Labour fairness therefore concerns algorithm design as well as institutions beyond platforms, such as migration status, care responsibilities and social protection. Platformization can shift prejudice from employers' direct judgments to dispersed customer reviews and system rankings, making responsibility for discrimination harder to locate. Algorithmization does not strip inequality of identity; it can instead sustain inequality through apparently individualized data feedback.]

  10. Graham, Mark, Isis Hjorth, and Vili Lehdonvirta. "Digital Labour and Development: Impacts of Global Digital Labour Platforms and the Gig Economy on Worker Livelihoods" Transfer 23, no. 2 (2017): 135–162. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Graham, Hjorth and Lehdonvirta situate digital labour platforms within global development and cross-border labour markets. They examine how online outsourcing expands opportunities while generating unequal bargaining, excess supply and geographical wage differences. This extends the session from Uber-style local gigs to global remote labour, reminding us of platform labour's different spatial scales. Algorithmic management does not mean managers disappear. Their global perspective examines online outsourcing's effects on development and geographical inequality. The internet lowers cross-border transaction costs without eliminating wage disparities, language hierarchies or dependence on place. Platforms can globalize demand while leaving workers in separate social-protection systems: digital labour both crosses and exploits borders. This market also produces new replaceability. Employers can quickly move tasks between countries, while workers remain constrained by local living costs, currencies and regulations. Remote platforms create asymmetric spatial freedom: capital and tasks move more readily, while workers' social reproduction remains intensely local. The spatial politics of cross-border digital labour is thus not the "disappearance of geography," but the conversion of geographical differences into cost advantages and bargaining inequalities. Its developmental effects are double-edged: it can provide new income in peripheral regions while exploiting low wages and weak social protection to sustain global cost disparities. Developmental value must be assessed not only by job numbers, but also by bargaining power, skills accumulation, income stability and opportunities to move up the value chain. Moreover, platform ratings and global competition individualize development: workers must improve their position through skills and reputation, while exchange rates, regional wages and platform bargaining power recede into the background. Digital development policy must restore these structural factors to the picture.]

  11. Karatani, Kojin. The Structure of World History: From Modes of Production to Modes of Exchange. Translated by Michael K. Bourdaghs. Duke University Press, 2014. Originally published 2010. (Read: Chapter 12, "Toward a World Republic," especially the discussion of Mode D, pp. 285–308).

    [Note: Karatani's Mode D is not a digital-currency proposal, but a rethinking of exchange within historical dynamics. Moving beyond capitalism understood solely as a mode of production, he places capital, the state and reciprocity within a longer history of exchange. Here, this confronts Web3, DAOs and platform cooperativism with a higher-order institutional question: if the mode of exchange remains unchanged, can changing the technical interface alone transform capital–labour relations? Through The Structure of World History: From Modes of Production to Modes of Exchange, the concealment of microtasks, annotation and maintenance in automation narratives can move from rhetoric to institutional analysis. Mode D's normative force lies in refusing to reduce alternatives to capitalism to a single change of ownership. Exchange, state and reciprocity are interwoven; every digital cooperative proposal must address public finance, social reproduction and coordination across regions. Karatani thus confronts "decentralized organization" with a world-historical scale beyond technical governance. His framework also makes the digital left rethink the state. Capital, state and nation are not links that can be dismantled in isolation: market expansion often works together with state redistribution and protection. Proposals to replace existing organizations with DAOs or cooperative platforms cannot easily assume the overall functions of social reproduction without addressing taxation, public services and coordination between communities. Mode D therefore cannot be reduced to a technological utopia. The real difficulty is establishing institutions that transcend the complementary structure of capital and state while providing public goods, redistribution and cross-regional coordination. Technology can only be one component.]

  12. Ostrom, Elinor. Governing the Commons. Cambridge University Press, 1990. (Read: Chapter 1, pp. 1–28).

    [Note: Ostrom's empirical research challenges the reduction of common-resource governance to the "tragedy of the commons." Read alongside DAOs, the questions are how rules arise, are enforced and revised, and which participant structures can sustain shared resources. Code can implement rules, but cannot automatically create trust, participation or responsibility. Cooperativism is no technical panacea. Rather than maximizing conceptual coverage, theory should remain refutable: this framework should extend only where evidence supports its core mechanisms. Governing the Commons ultimately makes the question of which layers of power cooperatives, unions, labour law and commons governance change open to further empirical analysis, instead of a completed diagnosis of the age. Ostrom is especially useful for correcting the idea that commons mean rule-free sharing. Durable governance depends on boundaries, participatory rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution, adapted to each community. Although digital commons have different copying costs from natural resources, open access alone cannot solve their governance problems. Ostrom's design principles cannot be mechanically transferred to digital resources. Software and data can be copied non-rivalrously, and membership may span the world; servers, maintenance and governance attention nevertheless remain scarce. What can travel is her empiricism about institutional diversity and self-organization, not a licence to call every open project a commons. The issue thus returns to institutional design: reproducibility does not remove the need for member governance, maintenance obligations and conflict resolution. Digital reproducibility reduces resource-depletion problems but heightens the scarcity of maintenance and governing attention. Code review, server costs, community management and conflict handling all require continuing investment. Ostrom reminds us that commons are never only about openness, but about durable governance suited to the character of the resource.]

Part IV: General Intellect and Technological Future (Weeks 7–8)

Session 7: General Intellect and Resistance to Compute Concentration

This session reconnects Marx's general intellect with contemporary AI infrastructure, without claiming that "Marx predicted large models." The "Fragment on Machines" in the Grundrisse addresses contradictions among social knowledge, fixed capital, labour time and the value-form: as scientific knowledge and social cooperation enter machinery more deeply, the relation between direct labour and productive power changes. Virno re-emphasizes general intellect as a living, public capacity for language and cognition, distinct from the stock of knowledge already congealed in machines. Their tension offers more productive questions about concentrated computing power than whether "AI resembles humans."

Generative AI converts socially produced text, code, images, feedback and judgment into training resources on a vast scale. At the same time, chips, data centres, energy, capital investment and specialized labour make it a form of fixed capital with high entry barriers. Pasquinelli's social history of AI, Crawford's tracing of its material and labour conditions, and studies of knowledge capitalism, cognitive capitalism and digital labour jointly show that "intelligence" is not a pure capacity detached from social relations, but an outcome of knowledge, labour, infrastructure and property arrangements together. Compute concentration is therefore first an industrial and institutional problem open to empirical analysis, not an a priori political conclusion.

Resistance cannot be reduced to "open source" or "a GPU for everyone." Open weights may improve access without altering training resources, cloud infrastructure, energy costs or governing power. Public computing resources can lower entry barriers but still face questions of data, maintenance, responsibility and distribution. Virno's exit, commons and non-state public sphere offer no ready-made solution, but a political direction for reorganizing general intellect: can shared cognitive capacities acquire institutions and infrastructure of their own, so that models, data and computation no longer exist solely as private fixed capital?

Required Readings:

  1. Marx, Karl. Grundrisse: Foundations of the Critique of Political Economy. Translated by Martin Nicolaus. Penguin Books, 1973. Originally written 1857–58; first published 1939–1941. (Read: "Fragment on Machines," pp. 690–712).

    [Note: We must resist the retrospective claim that "Marx predicted AI." Marx addresses historical contradictions among social knowledge, general intellect, fixed capital, labour time and value: as scientific knowledge and social cooperation become more embedded in machinery, labour time's place in production changes. AI can be treated as a new historical setting for this problem, but LLMs cannot simply be equated with Marx's "system of machinery." The question is whether contradictions among value, labour and ownership reappear in new forms as social intelligence increasingly congeals into privately owned computing infrastructure. The "Fragment on Machines" must be restored to Marx's analysis of fixed capital and productive forces. Machinery absorbs scientific knowledge and social cooperation, increasingly making workers supervisors and regulators of production; this creates a tension between labour time as the measure of wealth and the socialization of productive power. General intellect's place in Marx's text is not identical to its later autonomist interpretation, and this difference must be preserved. For AI, the most useful comparison concerns how knowledge enters fixed capital: do models, software, chips and data centres form a new combination of fixed capital, and which parts of training data and living cooperation resist fixation? This is first a theoretical question about social knowledge, common capacities and relations of production. Contemporary applications must explain how these capacities become fixed capital, rather than anthropomorphizing model parameters as humanity's shared mind. Marx's fragment addresses the contradictions of fixed capital, social knowledge and labour time, rather than predicting AI. General intellect's entry into machinery means that production increasingly relies on socially accumulated science and cooperation, even as the value-form retains labour time as its measure. Foundation models can provide a new setting for this contradiction, but models, data centres and GPUs are particular historical forms; they cannot retrospectively define Marx's concepts.]

  2. Virno, Paolo. A Grammar of the Multitude: For an Analysis of Contemporary Forms of Life. Translated by Isabella Bertoletti, James Cascaito, and Andrea Casson. Semiotext(e), 2004. Originally published 2001. (Read: Day One, "Common Places and "General Intellect""; Day Two, "Intellect as Score" and "Reason of State and Exit"; Day Three, "The Emotional Tonalities of the Multitude").

    [Note: Virno's crucial development of Marx's general intellect is his refusal to understand it merely as the "total stock of knowledge" congealed in machines, fixed capital and technical systems. In "Common Places and 'General Intellect'" and "Intellect as Score," it first appears as socially shared capacities for language, knowledge, judgment and cooperation: a general condition of living labour. The central issue for AI is then not whether machines have acquired human intelligence, but how existing social cognitive capacities are reorganized through platforms, models and infrastructure. "Reason of State and Exit" advances the political question: if capital absorbs general intellect, why does emancipation not follow automatically? Virno's exit asks us to find a politics whose sole aim is not taking over existing state–corporate organizations, but reorganizing public conditions of cooperation. Today, resisting compute concentration therefore cannot mean simply replicating big tech in a more democratic form. The real question is whether society can regain data, model, computing and knowledge infrastructures, making computation serve general intellect rather than turning general intellect into raw material for compute capital. "Compute multitude" must remain a problematic concept rather than being attributed directly to Virno: it tests whether new political connections can form among general intellect, infrastructural ownership and autonomous organization. The metaphor "Intellect as Score" is especially important: a score is not an accomplished performance, but a set of public capacities realized only in concrete action. General intellect is thus not merely an object stored in fixed capital, but the common condition of speaking, cooperating, learning and judging. "Reason of State and Exit" then turns to the relation between the state and non-state publicness. Exit is neither private escape nor a technical community's flight from regulation, but a reorganization of cooperation that withdraws support from old relations. Applied to open models, public computing or federated infrastructures, each proposal must be tested: does it really change power over the organization of common capacities, or merely make tools cheaper? Virno brings general intellect out of fixed capital and back to living language, judgment, habits and cooperation. It can be organized by capital as a productive force, yet also holds possibilities for non-state publicness. Exit is not simply leaving institutions, but reorganizing the conditions of cooperation. For contemporary computing, the political focus is not whether machines possess intelligence, but whether common cognitive capacities can establish their own data, model and computing infrastructures.]

  3. Pasquinelli, Matteo. The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence. Verso, 2023. (Read: Chapter 4, "The Origins of Marx's General Intellect"; Chapter 7, "The Automation of Pattern Recognition"; Conclusion, "The Automation of General Intelligence").

    [Note: Pasquinelli places AI back within histories of the division of labour and pattern recognition, rather than treating it as a computational miracle detached from society. Chapter 4 retraces Marx's general intellect; Chapter 7 examines pattern recognition and automation; the conclusion carries these histories into the automation of general intelligence. For this session, "model training" becomes a question of organizing labour and knowledge rather than a purely technical operation: does AI automate one person's skill, an occupation, or collective cognitive capacities already formed by society? The book's social history asks us to understand intelligence alongside the division of labour: machine intelligence often extracts rules, patterns and statistical order from human work, then reorganizes that work in automated form. Chapter 4 returns to general intellect not to announce that Marx already explained AI, but to ask how knowledge becomes a productive apparatus. Chapter 7's historicization of pattern recognition dismantles the myth of deep learning "learning by itself from data." General intelligence in the conclusion is therefore first a social and institutional question: which general capacities are formalized, who determines the patterns, and who must adapt to patterns recognized by machines? Reconstructing AI through labour division and pattern recognition means machine learning is no longer intelligence suddenly emerging from pure mathematics. Automation often first extracts and formalizes rules of judgment from social practice, then delegates their execution to machines. General intelligence's history connects to histories of organization, measurement and management. What AI "automates" is not an abstract mind, but already socialized cognitive operations.]

  4. Hardt, Michael, and Antonio Negri. Multitude: War and Democracy in the Age of Empire. Penguin Press, 2004. (Read: Part 2, selected sections on immaterial labor, biopolitical production, and the common).

    [Note: Hardt and Negri connect multitude, immaterial labour, biopolitical production and the common. As production increasingly depends on language, knowledge, affects and cooperation, they argue that political subjectivity need not take the homogeneous industrial worker as its sole premise. After Marx and Virno, they offer a more explicit vision of political organization, but one that must face empirical correction from platform-labour research: widespread social cooperation does not automatically produce autonomous subjects, and capital can still capture cooperation through property, platforms and infrastructure. In the context of this session, Multitude: War and Democracy in the Age of Empire makes the difficulties of moving from theoretical multitude/common to sustainable institutions more concrete. General intellect cannot simply be equated with model parameters, datasets or the internet. It first names socialized capacities for language, knowledge, judgment and cooperation; fixed capital can absorb these capacities without making them fully identical with machines. Hardt and Negri emphasize the conjunction of common productive capacities and differentiated subjects, seeking a politics distinct from a homogeneous people or the traditional working class. This openness connects well to digital cooperation, but is easily romanticized through network metaphors. The real question is how dispersed cooperation acquires institutional durability, resources and decision-making structures; otherwise, "multitude" may remain political rhetoric that describes connections. Its affinity with digital networks readily invites technological optimism. Networked common production does not automatically generate common politics, nor do different subjects naturally form a stable will. The difficult task is building institutions for decision-making and resources without erasing difference. This brings multitude theory directly to governance.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Vercellone, Carlo. "From Formal Subsumption to General Intellect" Historical Materialism 15, no. 1 (2007): 13–36.

    [Note: Vercellone examines the entry of knowledge, cooperation and social intelligence into capital accumulation. He bridges Sessions 6 and 7: questions of labour organization ultimately lead to who owns general intellect and knowledge commons. Theoretical resemblance does not automatically imply institutional identity. Compute concentration concerns industrial structure and infrastructure. The scale requirements of chips, energy, capital and cloud services shape who can train, deploy and maintain models, so open weights cannot by themselves remove dependence on private infrastructure. The account of general intellect, fixed capital, cognitive labour and concentrated computing power in "From Formal Subsumption to General Intellect" is therefore valid only where the relevant institutional mechanisms can be identified empirically. Vercellone connects general intellect with capital's absorption of social knowledge, emphasizing production's increasing dependence on cooperation and knowledge beyond factory walls. Cognitive capitalism places rent, intellectual property and socialized production within a shared contradiction. For AI, it offers not the conclusion that knowledge has replaced labour, but an analysis of how capital re-establishes scarcity and control over common knowledge that is difficult to enclose completely. It also returns rent to analysis of the knowledge economy. Where common knowledge resists full privatization, capital may increasingly earn returns through patents, platform gateways and infrastructure ownership. AI models' enclosure of knowledge and API access can be examined this way, but whether they constitute rent requires concrete analysis of competition, property and pricing. By connecting formal/real subsumption with general intellect, Vercellone also tries to explain capital's movement from directly organizing labour toward controlling conditions of socialized knowledge. Even if this periodization is contested, it asks an important question: when production depends on broad social cooperation, which institutions convert dispersed cooperation back into private returns? Platforms and AI infrastructure supply new empirical objects for this question.]

  2. Moulier Boutang, Yann. Cognitive Capitalism. Translated by Ed Emery. Polity, 2011. Originally published in French as Le capitalisme cognitif in 2007. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on knowledge, externalities, and cognitive labor).

    [Note: Moulier Boutang's cognitive capitalism places knowledge, innovation, cooperative networks and positive externalities at the centre of value production, explaining why production increasingly exceeds traditional factory boundaries. It is close to general intellect but not synonymous with it: Marx and Virno address social intelligence's relation to capital, whereas cognitive capitalism is an empirical–theoretical name for a particular capitalist phase. Reading them together tests what it means for knowledge to become the main productive force. Compute concentration is a matter of industry and infrastructure. Cognitive Capitalism offers not a final designation for the reorganization of common capacities through property, platforms and infrastructure, but a theoretical opening testable by competing explanations; that openness is itself valuable. Moulier Boutang describes knowledge, innovation and positive externalities as prominent in accumulation, incorporating cooperation beyond the factory into value analysis. "Cognitive" must not obscure material production, but it helps explain why networks, patents, education and knowledge flows become crucial to capitalist competition. Applied to AI, this requires attending both to models' cognitive resources and to the energy, hardware and labour supporting them. Cognitive capitalism also confronts labour measurement. Knowledge production relies heavily on cooperation, education and social interaction, making individual contributions harder to isolate; capital nevertheless distributes income through wages, intellectual property and firm boundaries. Model training amplifies this contradiction: its materials come from extensive social production, while returns concentrate among a few infrastructure owners.]

  3. Gorz, André. The Immaterial: Knowledge, Value and Capital. Translated by Chris Turner. Seagull Books, 2010. Originally published in French as L'Immatériel in 2003. (Read: selected chapters on knowledge, value, and the crisis of measurability).

    [Note: Gorz examines a contradiction: knowledge, capacities and living social experience resist complete measurement by conventional labour time, yet capital continually converts them into appropriable resources. He belongs in the general-intellect lineage because he restores knowledge from abstract information to subjective capacities and social relations while raising a crisis of value measurement. For AI, we must ask whether training commodifies knowledge itself, or turns its expressions, data traces and access rights into assets. The Immaterial: Knowledge, Value and Capital brings the distinction between openness, interoperability, public ownership and autonomous governance to organizational and institutional analysis. Compute concentration concerns industrial structure and infrastructure. Gorz locates cognitive capitalism's central contradiction between reproducible knowledge and the manufacture of scarcity. The easier digital knowledge is to copy, the more capital must recreate exclusion through intellectual property, platform enclosure and service provision. Foundation models and the API economy give this a new form: absorbed public knowledge re-enters the market through controlled access. By stressing knowledge's immeasurability, Gorz makes value impossible to explain fully through individual labour time. Knowledge often comes from long education, public research and social interaction, while copying costs approach zero; patents, closed platforms and brands must reconstruct scarcity. Generative AI's mass absorption of public text makes the contradiction between common knowledge and private access more visible. Gorz also helps explain model-access rights: capital need not own knowledge itself if control of computation, interfaces and service conditions makes access to common knowledge scarce again. Appropriation shifts from ownership of content to ownership of infrastructure.]

  4. Roggero, Gigi. The Production of Living Knowledge: The Crisis of the University and the Transformation of Labor in Europe and North America. Translated by Enda Brophy. Temple University Press, 2011. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on living knowledge, the university, and cognitive labor).

    [Note: Roggero examines the production of living knowledge through universities and knowledge work. Cognitive labour is not an abstract "creative class," but forms within educational institutions, labour markets, cooperative networks and conflict. This returns general intellect from grand philosophical claims to universities, research, training and intellectual-property regimes, making it useful for examining tensions between common knowledge production and institutional appropriation as generative AI enters education and research. The difficulty of moving from theoretical multitude/common to sustainable institution-building in The Production of Living Knowledge: The Crisis of the University and the Transformation of Labor in Europe and North America exceeds conceptual debate within the text. Compute concentration is an industrial and infrastructural problem. Roggero places living knowledge within university crisis and labour transformation, stressing that knowledge is continually generated in social cooperation, learning and networks, not only formal research institutions. Universities produce public knowledge while commodifying and quantifying it. Foundation models' mass absorption of academic and public texts intensifies the contradiction, creating new appropriative relations between open social knowledge and private computing infrastructure. For Roggero, the university is not a pure public space outside knowledge capitalism, but a laboratory of labour transformation: research, teaching and learning increasingly undergo performance measurement, project-based organization and competitive funding. Connected with AI, this perspective shows academic knowledge becoming open text for model ingestion while publishing, platforms and computing resources restratify it.]

  5. Beller, Jonathan. The Message Is Murder: Substrates of Computational Capital. Pluto Press, 2018. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on computational capital, attention, and racialized extraction).

    [Note: Beller places computation within histories of capital, visual culture, financialization and racialized violence. Computation is not confined to operations inside machines, but belongs to broader social extraction of value. This creates a necessary tension with general intellect: treating social knowledge only as an emancipatory common capacity risks overlooking its production within differentiated violence, attention capture and global divisions of labour. At the scale of The Message Is Murder: Substrates of Computational Capital, relations among general intellect, fixed capital, cognitive labour and compute concentration first appear as concrete connections. Beller understands computational capitalism as a system in which perception, attention and infrastructure jointly participate in valorization, extending digital labour's boundaries. His strong claims require empirical limits, yet identify a crucial issue: computation is not a neutral background tool, but may become a general substrate through which capital organizes vision, time and social relations. The concept of substrate connects visual culture, computation and material foundations. Screen-based attention becomes capitalizable only within systems of chips, networks, energy and labour. Computational capital is therefore neither a pure information economy nor a simple extension of industrial capital, but a form of value capture organized through multiple infrastructural layers. Computation's apparent immateriality is rematerialized: the valorization of attention, images and data always depends on equipment, networks and labour below. Its analysis needs a double view of the politics of perception and material infrastructure. Losing either side abstracts computational capital again.]

  6. Tronti, Mario. Workers and Capital. Translated by David Broder. Verso, 2019. Originally published 1966. (Read: "Lenin in England," pp. 78–88).

    [Note: Tronti's significance is methodological: begin not with what capital wants, but with how workers' struggles force capital to change. For today's platform economy, this is a research method, not proof that "workers' struggles produced AI." Workers and Capital, Beller's The Message Is Murder: Substrates of Computational Capital, and Doctorow's The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation situate the reorganization of shared social capacities through property, platforms and infrastructure within different intellectual traditions. Workers and Capital releases this question from overly abstract judgments about the age. The contribution of Workers and Capital lies precisely in keeping the theory refutable. Tronti reminds us that technological change cannot be explained only through capital's innovation strategies. Workers' refusal, mobility, organization and conflicts in production can also force capital to find new management technologies and labour arrangements. Applied to automation, this means tracing historical links between concrete struggles and investment decisions, not romanticizing automation itself as a direct product of workers' struggles. His workerism also insists that political knowledge comes from inquiry within struggles, rather than defining workers' interests in advance. For platform and AI labour, research should begin with specific conflicts involving drivers, annotators, moderators and engineers, examining how workplaces reinterpret technology. Theory must not position workers merely as passive recipients of technical change.]

  7. Doctorow, Cory. The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation. Verso, 2023. (Read: Introduction; chapters on interoperability, switching costs, and antitrust).

    [Note: Doctorow translates "seizing the means of computation" into concrete institutional tools—interoperability, adversarial compatibility, antitrust and exit rights—rather than an ownership slogan. This provides a valuable intermediate policy level: if platform infrastructure encloses general intellect, must resistance first reduce lock-in and restore interoperability and migration? We must also ask whether these reforms reach ownership of data centres, computation and capital, or mainly improve competition. The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation allows the distinction between openness, interoperability, public ownership and autonomous governance to be broken into interconnected elements. "Seizing the means of computation" restores competition policy, interoperability and user rights to the centre of infrastructure politics. Technical openness that leaves exit costs, data migration and market control unchanged often offers only superficial choice. This reformist path allows productive comparison with more radical public ownership or cooperative governance. Interoperability has a specific meaning for power: if users can take their data, social connections and content elsewhere and connect different services, lock-in decreases. Yet interoperability also brings complex costs involving security, privacy and standards governance. "Opening interfaces" is therefore no unconditional answer, but a mechanism of competition and autonomy requiring public rules. Its political significance is to shift competition from "more platforms" to whether users genuinely possess the institutional capacity to leave and migrate.]

  8. Tarnoff, Ben. Internet for the People: The Fight for Our Digital Future. Verso, 2022. (Read: Introduction; chapters on privatization, public ownership, and democratic control).

    [Note: Tarnoff connects the history of internet privatization with public control, rejecting explanations that attribute platform power only to a few bad firms or algorithms. His approach is infrastructural politics: ownership, public investment, democratic governance and decommodification. With Doctorow, this opens a debate over reform's scale: are interoperability and competition policy enough, or must some internet layers be reconceived as public infrastructure? Internet for the People: The Fight for Our Digital Future, Doctorow's The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation, and Schneider's Governable Spaces: Democratic Design for Online Life shift the difficulty of moving from theoretical multitude/common to durable institutions from broad judgment to concrete mechanisms. The contribution of Internet for the People: The Fight for Our Digital Future is to return these broad claims to identifiable institutional mechanisms. By treating privatization as historical, Tarnoff breaks with the assumption that networks naturally belong to markets. Public funding, commercialization and advertising together shaped today's platforms; decommercialization must therefore involve financing and public institutions, not merely appeals to corporate ethics. The internet's public character becomes a question of ownership and institutional design.]

  9. Schneider, Nathan. Governable Spaces: Democratic Design for Online Life. University of California Press, 2024. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on governance, ownership, and democratic design).

    [Note: Schneider begins with online communities' governance practices. Digital spaces are neither naturally anarchic nor governable only by corporations; rules, membership, ownership and decision procedures can all be redesigned. There are distant resonances with Virno's exit and Kelty's recursive public, but the focus here is institution-building: without sustainable governance, "exit" from platform power can amount merely to moving to another private platform. Governable Spaces: Democratic Design for Online Life clarifies the causal levels connecting general intellect, fixed capital, cognitive labour and compute concentration. Schneider treats online spaces as capable of constitutional governance, asking how rules form, members gain representation and power is constrained, rather than praising democracy abstractly. Democratization requires enforceable procedures, not simply a voting feature added to an interface. Governable spaces require more than community rules: members must have an institutional position from which to change them. Platform democracy cannot be equated with surveys or voting plug-ins. If servers, code and final enforcement remain with outside owners, participation may lack binding force. The substantive test is not whether a participation button exists, but whether members can durably constrain rules, infrastructure and enforcement. Only when governing rights can bind infrastructure owners does digital participation become institutional power rather than consultation. Democratic design must ultimately reach enforcement.]

  10. Söderberg, Johan. Hacking Capitalism: The Free and Open Source Software Movement. Routledge, 2008. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on free software, labor, and political economy).

    [Note: Söderberg explains free/open-source software through labour and political economy, recognizing cooperation's potential beyond conventional firms while examining capital's recapture of unpaid contributions. This tests a recurring question: does open code mean common ownership? Where cloud computing, deployment channels and data remain concentrated, where is the political force of software commons weakened? Free software shows that control of technical means of production can be institutionalized through licences, cooperative norms and shared code. Yet it can both challenge property and be absorbed by capital as cheap innovation. Openness is not a pure space outside capital, but a continually contested production relation. The movement also demonstrates non-state institutional innovation: copyleft repurposes law to protect sharing and resist private re-enclosure. "Exiting capital" need not mean exiting law; autonomous practices often use existing law to build lasting boundaries. This directly informs data and model commons. Commons do not require abolishing institutional boundaries: appropriate legal design can support public production. Licences and governance for public models and open data may similarly prevent re-enclosure. Sustained openness is itself an institutional achievement. Free software also develops material and institutional dependencies. Projects need hosting, maintenance, funding and contributor governance; if these concentrate again in a few firms, open code can coexist with infrastructural dependence. Open models likewise require distinct examination of property relations governing weights, training data, computation and deployment platforms.]

  11. Lazzarato, Maurizio. "Immaterial Labor" In Radical Thought in Italy: A Potential Politics, edited by Paolo Virno and Michael Hardt, 133–147. University of Minnesota Press, 1996. Originally published in Italian in 1994. (Read: entire chapter).

    [Note: Lazzarato's immaterial labour names the importance of information, cultural content, communication and subjectivity production under post-Fordism. Influential for general intellect, it requires a double reading today: it captures production's spread into social communication, yet "immaterial" can obscure chips, minerals, logistics, annotation and bodily labour. Reading it with Session 6 exposes this limit. "Immaterial Labor" can turn the distinction among openness, interoperability, public ownership and autonomous governance from rhetoric into institutional analysis. The concept captures language, affect, knowledge and cooperation entering value production, but its boundaries require care. Cognitive and communicative activities do not become detached from material labour; they depend on equipment manufacturing, logistics, energy and reproductive work. Reconnecting the two prevents "immaterial" from hiding the digital economy's material foundations. Historically, the concept links post-Fordism, communication and subject production, emphasizing labour's increasingly direct production of cultural content and social relations. Its difficulty is the potential concealment of equipment, logistics and bodies. It is better read as a change in labour's content and forms of control, not a declaration that material production has departed. Only then can it connect to digital labour's layered structure. Its greatest value lies not in the label, but in identifying value production's growing dependence on communication, signs and subjective relations. Digital capitalism concerns how these activities and material foundations are recombined, not which replaces the other.]

  12. Dyer-Witheford, Nick, Atle Mikkola Kjøsen, and James Steinhoff. Inhuman Power: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Capitalism. Pluto Press, 2019. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on AI, labor, and capital).

    [Note: This book examines AI automation and capital through Marxist political economy, rejecting an exclusive focus on whether future machines will be conscious. It studies how machine learning reorganizes capital's powers of control as it enters production, management and labour markets. This reconnects general intellect with AI's actual political economy while setting empirical limits for the next session's philosophy and future imaginaries. Inhuman Power locates AI within capitalist automation's historical logic, rather than treating it as an independent technical subject. Machine learning expands capital's capacities for prediction, coordination and supervision while depending on existing divisions of labour and property structures. "Inhuman power" is therefore first a technical capacity organized through social relations. Inhuman Power also juxtaposes AI's autonomy with capital's: machine systems appear to gain agency, yet their goals, deployment and expansion remain shaped by accumulation. Technical autonomy and capital's autonomy are different concepts. Distinguishing them prevents corporate investment and management decisions from being anthropomorphized as "AI demanding acceleration." Machine autonomy becomes an organizational question again: expanding capabilities do not remove capital's decisions over deployment and returns. AI's political economy must distinguish technical capability growth from the social direction given by capital's organization. The capitalist framework of Inhuman Power also corrects the philosophical image of AI as an autonomous actor. Algorithms' goals do not naturally arise inside machines, but are supplied by investment, strategy, competition and management needs. Capabilities may develop complexities beyond individual designers' expectations, yet deployment still has identifiable institutional actors. System complexity cannot justify anthropomorphically transferring political responsibility.]

Session 8: Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Posthuman Futures

The final session places AI at the intersection of philosophy, engineering, political economy and future imaginaries. Turing's classic questions about machine intelligence, Russell's account of human–machine goals, Bostrom's superintelligence risk framework, and Brassier's, Land's and Negarestani's different approaches to reason, technology and acceleration are not the same kind of argument. They involve operational tests, engineering control, thought experiments, normative philosophy and metaphysical inference, and cannot substitute for one another under a single evidential standard. Nor should AGI be treated as an empirical object with an already stable definition and timetable. It must be differentiated into questions of capability, autonomy, generality, deployment conditions and institutional power.

Haraway, Hayles, Braidotti and Hui reconsider the boundaries of "the human" through posthumanism, embodiment, relationality and technological plurality. Posthumanism does not mean enhancing humans or uploading consciousness, nor does it necessarily imply technological optimism. It first challenges the traditional placement of reason, subjectivity and political standing within the individual human. In another register, Crawford, Bender/Hanna, Narayanan/Kapoor and Hao repeatedly return grand intelligence narratives to data, labour, energy, corporate organization, industrial competition and marketing, bringing the "future" back into present institutions.

The session therefore asks how narratives of the future themselves become political forces. Industry roadmaps, risk discourse, accelerationism and emancipatory visions of technology predefine what counts as feasible, necessary or inevitable. AI critique must neither reduce every capability to hype nor accept the industry's unified category of "intelligence" because some systems do possess significant capabilities. Actual performance, speculative risk, political-economic structures and normative futures require distinct arguments. Only clear connections among these levels can take discussions of automation and the posthuman beyond oscillation between technological worship and fear.

Required Readings:

  1. Crawford, Kate. Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence. Yale University Press, 2021. (Read: Introduction; Chapter 2, "Labor"; Chapter 3, "Data").

    [Note: Crawford returns general intellect to planetary materiality. AI depends not only on algorithms and models, but also on minerals, energy, data centres, annotation, moderation and global supply chains. Chapter 2 makes AI's labour visible again; Chapter 3 shows how data becomes a resource. With Marx and Virno, this raises a concrete question: if AI privatizes social intelligence while hiding material labour and ecological costs behind models, why does "intelligence" consistently appear disembodied? Crawford corrects our understanding of AI's actual conditions rather than directly extending general intellect. Atlas of AI uses scales such as Earth, Labor and Data to examine an industrial system of extraction: minerals, energy and space make computation possible; annotation and maintenance are concealed by automation narratives; datasets carry histories of classification into models. Alongside Hao's organizational investigation and Bender/Hanna's critique of hype, "what is AI?" becomes a composite of technical capability, industrial foundations and institutional power rather than an abstract question of intelligence. This final session must distinguish present capability judgments from philosophical possibility. A system's inability today cannot logically prove machines will never do something; conversely, the conceptual possibility of superintelligence cannot establish the political priority of present deployments. Crawford's atlas disassembles AI into a planetary assemblage of minerals, energy, labour, data, classification and state power. AI is not floating software capability, but a highly material and institutional system. Restoring workers, mines and data centres changes risk's timescale: political consequences do not begin only with future superintelligence, but already exist in extraction, work organization and classificatory institutions.]

  2. Bender, Emily M., and Alex Hanna. The AI Con: How to Fight Big Tech's Hype and Create the Future We Want. Harper, 2025. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on AI hype, synthetic media, labor, and institutional power).

    [Note: Bender and Hanna first disassemble "AI" into industrial discourse, institutional choices and concrete technical systems, opposing the anthropomorphism of machine-learning products as intelligent subjects with a unified will. They examine how hype diverts attention: society may debate distant machine domination while overlooking data, labour, resources, business models and present automation harms. Published in 2025, this text returns discussion to the new narratives following generative AI, complementing Crawford's material politics. AI is a highly heterogeneous umbrella term. Predictive and generative models, robots, optimization systems and hypothetical AGI should not share one capability assessment. Judgments must identify their specific technical object, rather than allowing "AI" to replace classification. Critique of industry discourse must stay connected to particular systems, organizations and observable effects, avoiding another grand anthropomorphic story in place of technical myth. Their focus is not only model limitations, but how exaggerated abilities serve investment, concentration and policy agendas. Compared with technical-risk accounts, this turns attention to existing institutional consequences: who can define AI, who benefits from its myths, and who bears deployment costs? Hype has political effects because it changes resource allocation. Grand narratives of general intelligence and automated substitution influence investment, talent, regulatory priorities and public attention, marginalizing some current problems. Critiquing hype does not deny technical change; it demands a stricter evidential connection between capability claims and social decisions. Demystification therefore does not diminish technology's importance, but returns judgments to testable capabilities, institutions and resource relations.]

  3. Narayanan, Arvind, and Sayash Kapoor. AI Snake Oil: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference. Princeton University Press, 2024. (Read: Chapter 1, "Introduction"; Chapter 2, "How Predictive AI Goes Wrong"; Chapter 4, "The Long Road to Generative AI").

    [Note: Narayanan and Kapoor offer a technological-epistemological "disenchantment." They distinguish predictive AI, generative AI and broader AI discourse, stressing capability boundaries and deployment conditions. This is crucial here: critical theory must distinguish actual technical capabilities from the "AI" of industry promotion. AI Snake Oil: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference thus offers a limited but effective scale for explaining how resources, labour, ecology and organizational history constrain AGI futurism. It identifies mechanisms without replacing further analysis of institutions, law and material conditions. Different technical objects require different evidence; predictive failure, generative capabilities and AGI imaginaries are not interchangeable. Critique that treats all systems as one intelligence reproduces marketing's vagueness. Demystification begins with classification. A key method of AI Snake Oil is matching every capability claim to its use case. Benchmark performance cannot automatically demonstrate suitability for hiring, education or medical decisions; fluent text cannot demonstrate factual reliability. Evaluation must move from abstract abilities to deployment conditions, error costs and alternatives. This distinction is especially useful at the reading group's close, preventing philosophical futurism and real system capabilities from substituting for each other within one concept of "AI."]

  4. Hao, Karen. Empire of AI: Dreams and Nightmares in Sam Altman's OpenAI. Penguin Press, 2025. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on OpenAI's scaling strategy, data labor, compute infrastructure, and global environmental impacts).

    [Note: Through long-term investigative reporting, Hao reconstructs OpenAI and the AI race, connecting model expansion with computing power, capital, data labour, global supply chains and environmental conflict. Rather than abstract AI philosophy, organizational history and global cases show how "scaling" became industrial strategy. Its place among the final session's required readings demands that philosophical projections of AGI, superintelligence and posthuman futures face actual organizations and resource politics: who builds these systems, who bears the costs, and who can define the future? Posthuman critique must not escape material politics. Challenging anthropocentrism matters, but concrete institutions still allocate minerals, labour, energy, ecological costs and intellectual property; relational theories of subjectivity must be read with these structures. In this session, Empire of AI: Dreams and Nightmares in Sam Altman's OpenAI makes conflicts over technological futures among risk governance, emancipatory imagination and democratic institutions concrete. AI is first a heterogeneous collection of objects: predictive and generative models, robots, optimization systems and hypothetical AGI have different capability and risk structures. One undifferentiated concept of intelligence quickly blurs empirical judgment. Through OpenAI's history, Hao places AGI ideals, financing, organizational governance and the compute race in one narrative. Its value is not only corporate inside information, but showing how the normative aim of benefiting all humanity encounters institutional pressures in commercial expansion, competition for talent and infrastructure investment. AI futurism is not a history of ideas detached from organizations, but bound to governance and capital structures. Corporate history also shows why governance cannot rely solely on mission statements. Organization, boards, investors and computing resources alter how far a mission can constrain commercial decisions. Public interest existing only as corporate self-regulation is easily reinterpreted under competition to scale.]

Recommended Readings:

  1. Turing, Alan M. "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" Mind 59, no. 236 (1950): 433–460. (Read: entire article).

    [Note: Turing's most important move is not asking "Can machines think?" but reformulating the question. Through the imitation game, a catalogue of objections and learning machines, he asks which behavioural criteria can make machine intelligence an operational object of research. Read after AI discourse of the 2020s, intelligence appears not as a transparent natural property, but as something defined by tests, tasks and institutional expectations. This final session must distinguish actual capability from philosophical possibility. Theoretical resemblance does not automatically imply institutional identity. Turing's paper is better understood as a methodological shift in how to discuss machine intelligence than as an AGI roadmap. The imitation game temporarily suspends metaphysical debates about thought's essence, replacing them with operational behavioural criteria. This opens computational intelligence research while leaving a persistent question: tests can measure performance, but cannot automatically settle understanding, subjectivity or social responsibility. Turing also anticipates objections to machine intelligence and shows their logical weaknesses. The point is not that he proves machines think, but that he moves debate from essential definitions to testable questions. We should preserve this restraint today: passing a test warrants judgments about that tested capability. Behaviour can be evidence without immediately yielding conclusions about consciousness, understanding or subjectivity. Turing offers conceptual discipline for discussing intelligence, not a prophecy of technology's future. His operationalism also leaves an acute contemporary problem: increasingly diverse tests reveal systems excelling at some tasks while lacking robustness at others. Should intelligence remain a single umbrella term, or be differentiated into abilities? This directly concerns the scope and evidential standards of generative-AI capability claims.]

  2. Russell, Stuart. Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control. Viking, 2019. (Read: Introduction; selected chapters on objectives, uncertainty, and the control problem).

    [Note: Russell raises control and alignment from within AI research. Rather than predicting a definite superintelligence catastrophe, he critiques the design assumption that fixes machine goals in advance as a single utility function. He proposes that machines remain uncertain about human preferences. With critical theory, we should ask how those preferences form, who may represent them, and whether social conflict can be reduced to preference learning. AI is a highly heterogeneous umbrella term. Russell formulates advanced-AI risk through goal specification and uncertainty management: if human-given goals are treated as a perfectly certain utility function, increasing capability may magnify specification errors. This deserves dialogue with social science, because preferences are neither unified, transparent nor static. Alignment thus concerns not only control engineering but value conflict, democratic authorization and institutional representation. "Human values" cannot simply be entered into a system as one unified object. Groups genuinely conflict, and values change with context. Treating alignment only as preference learning risks compressing democratic disagreement, rights and non-negotiable principles into optimizable variables. Technical control necessarily leads to political philosophy. In actual institutions, Russell's problem must also handle multiple actors. When a system serves a hospital, company, state or individual, whose preferences prevail? Values cannot always be compressed into one objective function. Alignment therefore needs procedural justice, limits imposed by rights and democratic decision-making; otherwise, "human compatible" may presuppose a unified human will that does not exist.]

  3. Haraway, Donna. "A Cyborg Manifesto" In Simians, Cyborgs, and Women, 149–181. Routledge, 1991.

    [Note: Haraway's cyborg is not merely a prediction of human–machine fusion, but a theory of political subjects that dismantles boundaries. It asks whether politics must rest on a pure biological body and unified identity, offering the multitude an image of coalition without homogeneity. "A Cyborg Manifesto" brings the question of how resources, labour, ecology and organizational history constrain AGI futurism into institutional and organizational analysis. Cyborg politics rejects pure, unified, naturalized identities as foundations for coalition. Technical practices continually redraw human/machine and nature/culture boundaries, while heterogeneous relations constitute political subjects. Its relevance to AI lies not in a fusion prophecy, but in reorganizing responsibility and solidarity without an essentialist account of human nature. Cyborg politics is also anti-essentialist coalition-building: instead of pure womanhood, humanity or natural identity, Haraway stresses partial connections formed where technology, bodies and power intertwine. For the AI age, the point is not that everyone becomes half-machine, but that political subjects are already constituted through technical and social relations. Responsibility and solidarity cannot therefore rest on recovering a pure pre-technological humanity. The cyborg also challenges technology as an external tool. Bodies, medicine, communication and labour have long been remade by technical devices; humans have never been independent subjects outside technology. "Protecting humanity" in AI governance must specify the capacities, relations and conditions of life to be protected, rather than invoking abstract pure human nature. Haraway turns this hybridity into a political resource instead of a technology-induced identity crisis.]

  4. Hayles, N. Katherine. Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with Our Nonhuman Symbionts. University of Chicago Press, 2025. (Read: Chapters 1–2, 6–7, and 9–10).

    [Note: In this 2025 book, Hayles proposes an integrated cognitive framework, extending cognition and meaning-making from humans to living organisms and some artificial systems while retaining an emphasis on materiality, embodiment and relation. It is more suited than How We Became Posthuman to contemporary AI debates because it directly addresses GPT-era claims about machine cognition without equating language models with human minds. Its value is a third theoretical route between strong anthropocentrism and the declaration that machines are already subjects. Posthuman critique must not become an escape from material politics. The contest over technological futures among risk governance, emancipatory imagination and democratic institutions in Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with Our Nonhuman Symbionts extends beyond internal conceptual debate. Hayles distributes cognition across relations among humans, nonhuman life and technical systems, so intelligence is no longer simply an isolated subject's internal capacity. This 2025 account connects ecology with AI: technical systems are embedded in biological symbiosis while altering how humans understand cognitive boundaries. Posthuman futures are thus first reorganizations of relations, not upgrades to one species. Hayles further treats cognition as a process across scales: bacteria and technical systems may sense and respond to environments differently. Cognitive pluralism rejects human reason as the sole measure without equating all information processing with human intelligence. Its key contribution is a vocabulary for distinguishing forms of cognition, freeing posthuman debate from oscillation between human exceptionalism and machine anthropomorphism.]

  5. Bostrom, Nick. Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies. Oxford University Press, 2014. (Read: Chapter 8, "Is the Default Outcome Doom?", pp. 115–142).

    [Note: Bostrom offers an existential-risk framework quite different from accelerationist philosophy. One need not accept a doom scenario in advance; the task is to examine the argument: if we posit a highly autonomous, goal-directed agent, why does alignment become central? Comparison with political economy asks whether AI risk can be abstracted into a purely technical issue detached from property, labour and institutions. The final session must distinguish actual capability from philosophical possibility. At the scale of Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, distinguishing AI capabilities, industrial hype, philosophical intelligence and political-economic reality begins with concrete relations. Technological futures are not purely objects of prediction. Industry roadmaps, risk narratives and accelerationism affect investment, regulation and public imagination, so what will happen and who can define the future must be discussed together. Through Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, the distinction becomes a stricter question: which mechanisms actually change, which changes are only shifts of medium, and who bears their consequences? Bostrom assumes extreme capability growth and goal preservation to derive existential risk and the control problem.
